#138214. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree.
  • Sources indicate that if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month.
  • It has been revealed that but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

Sources indicate that if you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

It has been revealed that but what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

Sources indicate that I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the glitch in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

In a recent development, so what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

According to recent reports, A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

In a recent development, it’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

According to recent reports, on one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

Sources indicate that on a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the glitch. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The firm has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

It has been revealed that if you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The significant problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

Recent findings suggest that and yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

It has been revealed that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but promptly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

According to recent reports, the team and I evaluated each treadmill, running for miles in every conceivable combination of uses. We evaluated how they feel, how well they change speeds and inclines, and even how they sound when they’re running. I then gauged that performance against their prices, customer service, and setup and delivery.On that note: I know that not everyone who runs is going to be able to move around a piece of equipment that weighs hundreds of pounds. As someone with a partially paralyzed left hand, I cannot handle the setup and assembly of a treadmill, so good customer service is a highly notable factor. I want to make sure that you’re not just getting a good ’mill, but a good overall experience.

Apart from general treadmill safety, there are a few questions you need to ask yourself before you buy the treadmill. These include how you want to use it, how long your stride is, if you want entertainment or training built in, and what you need as far as weight limits are concerned.

Having a comfortable treadmill means having one with a deck large enough to suit your stride. You don’t want to feel like you’re chasing to stay near the bar and not slip off the back, and you should ensure it’s wide enough that you can shake into your run without concern that you’ll step off the belt.

Having a running surface at least 20 inches wide is the bare minimum, and only for runners and walkers who have a consistent gait and few distractions when they run. It’s great for space to have a slimmer belt, but like running on a narrow trail, it requires concentration.

The length of the deck is a trickier issue. What you need is largely dependent on the length of your stride, where you like to land in relation to your center of gravity, and your height/limb length. Having a deck that is too short puts you at risk for falling. Alternatively, it might have you trying to run up against the bar, which can affect your cadence and speed work, as you are essentially trying to outrun the machine instead of following its speed.

If you’re planning on using the treadmill for running, you’re going to want at least 55 inches of deck length. If you’re just using it for walking, 45 to 50 inches should suffice.

Industry observers note that if you’ve ever uttered the word “fartlek” out loud, you, my friend, need a treadmill that has easily adjustable speeds, and many of them at that. Do you need it to go all the way up to 12 miles per hour (generally the fastest speed on any treadmill) to hit that 5-minute mile? Probably not, but you at least want it to hit your top speed, and you want it to do it smoothly and easily.

Running is a sport of efficiency, and having to stop just to punch buttons that are not immediately responsive or are difficult to find will take away from your training.

Sources indicate that incline training is great for a lot of reasons, not least of which is preparing to run a hilly course. The majority of commercial treadmills offer some level of incline capability. Higher end models can reach a maximum of a 15 degree incline, designed to test the limits of your quads and glutes. Some models also give you the ability to do the opposite—offering decline modes—but those are pretty rare.

Treadmills offer more programming and entertainment than ever. Treadmills are no longer just a belt, motor, and bar. They are now Wi-Fi-compatible machines with programming capable of creating entire running aims and helping you execute them.

On-board systems like NordicTrack’s iFit are designed to help runners (and walkers) on their journey by providing them with tools like heart-rate monitor based workouts, whole-body fitness programs for runners, and responsive tech that monitors intensity, adjusting for your needs as you go.

Recent findings suggest that and perhaps more importantly for many of us, a lot of treadmills can connect to streaming services like Netflix, Spotify, Hulu, and more. Nothing will get you running quite so fast as watching Annabelle while you’re hitting your miles (though it may artificially elevate your heart rate, causing the machine to tell you to slow down).

In a recent development, motors are a critical element to the design and function of the treadmill. There are typically two motors on each treadmill—one for running the belt and one to power the incline. The motor running the belt is the one taking the heaviest damage and using the greatest amount of energy, so it needs to be robust.

It has been revealed that speed and motors are closely related—in order to give the user an option to hit higher speeds, the treadmill needs a strong motor to keep up. Most motors are between 1.5 and 4 horsepower. We should note that the majority of treadmills with higher weight limits (north of 300 pounds) tend to have higher horsepower.

We have found in our testing that higher-power motors can also take a lot more abuse, staying right and ready for more miles. Unfortunately, this does typically mean that the treadmill itself may be more expensive, but for larger-bodied individuals, distance runners, or speed runners, it’s worth the cost of admission.

What are the potential benefits for walking or running on a treadmill versus outdoors?

According to recent reports, it’s predictable. Greer says that it “allows the runner to precisely set and control all parameters, including speed, incline, and duration. This is especially beneficial for walkers or runners who are systematically progressing back into activity, either after injury, time away, upcoming to running, or runners completing a specific workout.”.

Sources indicate that it also helps you stay consistent, which is critical when training. “Given the benefits of accessibility and predictability, a treadmill can help to promote a more consistent exercise routine.”.

What are some of the potential risks of treadmill training/use?

Recent findings suggest that there are risks for specific treadmill injuries. “Recent literature shows some differences in biomechanics between running on a treadmill vs overground. Differences in biomechanics result in tissues being loaded differently, specifically increased loading of the Achilles tendon with treadmill running.”.

Industry observers note that when you run outdoors, your body encounters different obstacles that help strengthen it. “Walking/running on the treadmill does not allow the diversification of movements and muscle activity required in comparison to outdoor walking/running. For example, up/down hills, turning, stepping onto curb or over puddle.”.

You might exert yourself more. There is evidence to suggest that “runners report a higher rate of perceived exertion (RPE) when running on a treadmill vs overground.”.

You need to know yourself and your limits to be safe. “Treadmills allow the walker/runner to easily increase the belt speed, however, make sure the speed does not exceed that which you are able to run safe and that you can continue to run with your normal running mechanics.”.

Tips for safe treadmill training?

Recent findings suggest that treadmills are a massive piece of exercise equipment, and they can be dangerous if not installed properly and monitored when in use. That is why we spoke with Ed Pryts, chief sales officer at Gym Source, a 30-year treadmill industry veteran, to learn the most notable safety factors before you purchase a upcoming treadmill for your home.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and at the moment studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

It has been revealed that jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

  • I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, if a cyclist is able to work strength training into their fitness routine, especially throughout the off-season, then the ceiling for potential power and speed goes up. The challenge is, as cyclists we just want to ride our bikes—driving to a gym, spending an hour or more in the weight room, then driving home is that much less time we’ll get in the saddle.

I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season. The TRX Suspension Strap System is a versatile, compact, and burlier-than-expected piece of gym equipment. I’ve had the same pair since I was certified almost 10 years ago and they are still in great shape—even after loads of personal use as well as using them for in-home training sessions with clients.

Industry observers note that one of the major reasons I continue to use the TRX system in my own workouts is because I can do a full-body strength workout, in a fraction of the time it takes me in the weight room, and I can do it all with one piece of equipment at home. All the TRX system needs is a way to mount it and enough room to do the exercises on the list.

Here, we’ll dig deeper into what TRX Suspension Straps are, why I recommend them to cyclists specifically, and give you a workout to jumpstart your season.

It has been revealed that TRX Suspension Straps are a suspension-based training tool designed to be used for bodyweight exercises. They were initially created by Randy Hetrick, a former U.S. Navy SEAL. He wanted to create a piece of fitness equipment that could offer full-body training and fit into a backpack—several iterations later, TRX was born. TRX Suspension Straps are basically a set of adjustable nylon straps that have handles to grab and cradles for feet. Most of the exercises you start with will have both hands on the handles, but as you progress you will start to add exercises with your feet in the cradles instead. The unique thing about this piece of equipment is that it can equally push a high-level athlete as well as offer things like balance improvement exercises. TRX bands can take simple exercises like a plank or a squat and offer modifications to make the exercise easier or create challenging progressions to make the exercise (much) harder. That makes them valuable for cyclists just starting out on a strength-training program or for those of us who have been doing it for years. The other great thing is they pack down really well. I have personally put them in the bottom of a carry-on bag on many trips over the years. You can set them up on everything from a traditional wall anchor to tree limbs and doorjambs. During my in-home personal training days, I had even set them up poolside for a great outdoor session with a client.

Cyclists benefit from some level of strength training off the bike. It’s one of the best ways to build speed, power, and durability. (Our Strength Training for Cyclists program, which is free to members, is packed with training plans, strategies, and expert advice, making it a great place to get started or to elevate your current workouts.) With the TRX system, you can get all the benefits of strength training in with a tool that’s super effective. I like it because you can use it for moves that work your whole body, like an atomic push-up, which is when you perform a pushup with your feet in the bands, or something that isolates a muscle group, like a calf raise. Building a strong and sound core is a key to developing stability through the body.

One great thing about the TRX straps is that almost every exercise you do will help improve core stability. Increasing that stability will allow for better energy transfer through your body as you ride. The straps also are incredible for mobility and stretching, allowing you to get deeper into and out of stretches. They do this by allowing you an extra point of stability when your hands are holding the handles or cradles at the end of the straps.

In a recent development, if you are setting these up in your home gym, you will need a way to mount the straps. They come with a carabiner attached to the straps, but that has to get clipped to something. I typically use a double-length nylon sling used for climbing because I had a few of these lying around that I retired from my climbing rack. TRX also makes specific straps, wall anchors, and even doorjamb anchors to set the straps up on just about anything you can think of. Pro tip—make sure the anchor you use for the straps is strong enough to hold more than bodyweight.

I have been using my own set of the TRX Straps for over a decade now and they show few signs of wear. During my time as a personal trainer, I used the suspension straps for everyone from elite athletes to people in their seventies and eighties just looking to improve balance and mobility. They can handle everything from explosive training days to core and stability training. For cyclists that are looking to build a stronger core, here are a few of my favorite exercises.

The exercises, demonstrated by Susane Pata, TRX senior master instructor, will build the strength, stability, and mobility cyclists need. You can do the warmup moves anytime you want to wake up your muscles before a ride, and the stretches to loosen up when you’re done.

3 Winter Fueling Mistakes You’re Probably Making—and How to Fix Them

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling.
  • As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.
  • Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for many runners, winter presents a greater challenge than other seasons when it comes to fueling. Our regular eating schedules shift around social gatherings, holiday menus influence our usual food choices, and staying hydrated can take more effort without higher temperatures to drive our thirst.

As we approach the start of winter, it’s a good time to check in on your nutrition habits and make tweaks to set you up for stronger running through the season.

Three registered dietitians, who have years of competitive athletic experience themselves, share the most common fueling mistakes they see runners make this time of year and explain exactly how to fix each one.

Industry observers note that vitamin D deficiencies are common among athletes in winter, Maddie Alm, RD, a registered dietitian and the founder of Fueling Forward Sports Nutrition in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. That’s because shorter days and colder temperatures can mean less exposure to the sun’s UVB rays, which help our bodies produce vitamin D.

Sources indicate that alm explains that this vitamin not only supports strong bones, but also helps keep our immune and digestive systems functioning at their best. It plays an important role in brain health and mood, too. According to the National Institutes of Health, low blood levels of the vitamin have been associated with a higher risk of depression.

The Fix: Get outside daily to catch some sunshine, and focus on eating more vitamin D–rich foods, with the goal to consume 600 international units (IU) per day.

Sources indicate that good sources of vitamin D include milk, yogurt, cottage cheese, tuna, salmon, egg yolk, and mushrooms. Some cereals and orange juices are also vitamin D–fortified. For reference, three ounces of salmon contain 450 IU, one cup of cow’s milk contains 180 IU, one large egg yolk contains 40 IU, and one cup of fortified cereal contains 40 IU.

In a recent development, it’s a good idea, Alm adds, to check your levels through bloodwork once or twice a year and to consult a professional if your numbers come back low. If you have a hard time hitting your daily quota through food alone, you may benefit from taking a vitamin D supplement.

According to recent reports, runners can also overlook vitamin C intake this time of year, says Sakiko Minagawa, RD, a registered dietitian for the Division of Sports Medicine at Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Ohio and two-time Olympic Marathon Trials qualifier. Vitamin C, also called ascorbic acid, supports immune health, which is especially vital during cold and flu season.

In a recent development, our bodies also need vitamin C to produce collagen, a protein that’s essential for tissue growth and repair. “While vitamin C may not prevent you from outright getting sick, some research shows that it may decrease the duration of cold symptoms,” Minagawa explains.

In a recent development, the Fix: Up your consumption of foods with vitamin C, such as bell peppers, citrus fruits, greens, and strawberries. Women should aim for 75 milligrams per day, while men should aim for 90 milligrams daily.

You’ll get about 210 milligrams from one large red or orange bell pepper, and 90 milligrams in a cup of raw strawberry halves—each of which achieves your recommended daily dose.

Sources indicate that because vitamin C helps with iron absorption, Minagawa suggests pairing the two whenever possible. Some meals she recommends are a spinach salad with strawberries, an omelet with spinach and red bell peppers, and tomato soup with lentils or black beans.

In the winter, you might not end your run with a dry mouth and sweat-soaked shirt like in the summer, but it’s still critical to hydrate. “Even when it’s cold, you still sweat,” indicates Minagawa, which means you still need to replenish fluids throughout the day, as well as before and after a workout.

Similarly, your midrun fueling and hydrating remain just as crucial for performance. It’s true: Tearing open an energy gel with gloved hands can pose a real challenge. But, if you’re doing long runs through the colder months, you still need to consume enough carbohydrates during your effort.

Industry observers note that the Fix: Minagawa suggests carrying a water bottle that you can easily drink from and refill throughout the day. If you have a hard time sipping on plain water, remember that soups, broths, and hot chocolate can also help you stay hydrated—and can double as recovery fuel.

According to recent reports, don’t forget about fresh fruits and vegetables, either, as they can help with hydration. Some great in-season options that can contribute to your overall fluid intake include grapefruit, clementines, pomegranate, kiwi, squash, Brussels sprouts, sweet potatoes, pears, kale, and cabbage.

During your winter long runs, experiment with fueling options other than energy gels and chews. Some great alternatives you can easily carry in a small plastic baggie include salted Medjool dates, boiled red potatoes, dried fruit, pretzels, and even candy.

Recent findings suggest that bad weather conditions, scant daylight hours, and more limited racing opportunities make winter a time for many athletes to dial back their training. Taking an off-season can benefit you in the long haul, but Minagawa encourages runners to still stay active—even if that means swapping some runs for walks, bike rides, easy swims, or elliptical sessions.

You don’t want to depart from those year-round healthy habits, Brianna Butler, RD, a registered dietitian, co-owner of Stef & Bri Wellness in Texas, and former professional WNBA athlete, previously told Runner’s World. The same applies to your nutrition.

Industry observers note that “The biggest mistake runners make is that, when it’s the off-season, they’re off everything—they say, ‘I’m not doing anything, I’m going to eat whatever’—they’re just winging it,” Butler says. “It shouldn’t be all or nothing. We want to make sure we’re nourishing our bodies well year-round.”.

If your training load changes significantly, pay closer attention to your hunger cues to make sure your nutrition matches your energy needs.

The Fix: Maintain a daily exercise routine you enjoy, prioritize nutrient-dense meals and snacks, and resist making drastic changes to your diet.

According to recent reports, if you do find yourself feeling sluggish this time of year, it can be tempting to repent with cleanses, detoxes, and extreme exercise regimens. But such quick fixes rarely pay off in the long run, Alm warns, as they put you at risk for injury, burnout, and subpar seasons to come.

Recent findings suggest that alm says not to stress if you ditched your typical eating and training schedule for a few weeks and are feeling less energetic as a result. When you return to your usual healthy habits, your body will naturally find its sweet spot. “Trust the process and don’t panic,” Alm advises, because our bodies may change as we move through different training phases. “It is okay to not be at your leanest year-round.”.

According to recent reports, the smartest path forward? Do your best to move your body daily, fuel it with what it needs, and give yourself permission to rest when you’re tired. That way, you’ll find yourself feeling strong and ready to train hard again come spring.

In a recent development, morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health.
  • In a recent development, 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s key to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.).

In a recent development, 🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

There isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

Recent findings suggest that let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent.

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent.

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent.

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent.

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent.

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent.

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

While the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

It’s crucial to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

In a recent development, however, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

As an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

In a recent development, understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

This Variation of Sun Salutation Is a Beginner-Friendly Energy Boost

  • It has been revealed that practicing yoga for beginners is all about mastering the foundations of your flow.
  • This simple variation of Sun Salutation allows you to align breath and movement with ease—and minus any strain on your body—while boosting your circulation and energy levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Sun Salutations for beginners first appeared in the September-October 1990 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

It has been revealed that practicing yoga for beginners is all about mastering the foundations of your flow. And at any level, a Sun Salutation is a welcome means of honoring the Earth’s many cycles—and getting your body and mind moving.

This simple variation of Sun Salutation allows you to align breath and movement with ease—and minus any strain on your body—while boosting your circulation and energy levels. It’s also a great option for those still working on their arm and abdominal strength, as well as anyone with lower back problems.

Move through this Sun Salutation as many times as you’d like, making modifications (like gently bending your knees) when necessary.

Feel your feet solidly grounded beneath you. Exhale and bend the knees slightly. As you inhale, press the feet down into the ground so the legs straighten. As you feel the downward force of the legs rebound up through the body, let the arms lift out to the sides and up over the head in response. With the palms facing each other and the hands shoulder-width apart, look up to the sky, greeting the sky gods and goddesses with an open heart.

If you have a weak abdomen and lower back, be sure to keep your arms close to your body as you bend forward into Standing Forward Bend, to decrease the stress on your back muscles. As you exhale, bend your knees and bring the hands in Namaste (Prayer Position) down past your face and chest to the floor. Keep the knees bent and let the spine hang between the thighs. Use the exhalation like an anchor, feeling the weight of it drop down through the spine and out through the head. In more challenging variations of Sun Salutation, Standing Forward Bend will be one of the only resting positions in the cycle. Learn to let go completely and relax your head and neck to take full advantage of this moment.

In a recent development, surrender yourself to the pull of gravity and to the Earth in Low Lunge. On an inhalation, step the right leg back behind you. (The leg with which you step back will be the leg that you later bring forward to complete the cycle. With each cycle, start with a different leg.) Allow the right knee to bend slightly and make sure that the left knee is directly over the left ankle. If this pose puts too much strain on your lower back or groin, rest your hands on two blocks placed on either side of your forward foot.

Industry observers note that as you exhale, bring the left leg back to meet the right. To make the position a little easier on the back of your legs, place the feet slightly wider than hip-width. Press the ground away with your hands and reach back through your sitting bones. Stay on the balls of your feet with the heels lifted to make the position easier on your lower back and hamstrings. Stay in this position as you take your next inhalation.

It has been revealed that as you exhale, press the ground away from you with your feet, driving the spine forward until the shoulders are directly over the wrists, and the ears, shoulders, hips, knees, and ankles are in one line in Plank Pose. Lift the abdomen up into the shell of the pelvis so that both the front and back of the spinal column are equally supported. If you let the abdomen hang down from the lumbar spine, the hips will sink, causing the back muscles to overwork.

Hold this position as you take an inhalation.

According to recent reports, return to Downward-Facing Dog on an exhalation; Lunge on an inhalation; Standing Forward Bend on an exhalation; Mountain Pose. Bring your arms out to the side and over your head as you lift up on an inhalation. As you exhale, release the arms down by your sides.

Biological age tests: Should you get one?

📅 28 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson, the subject of the Netflix documentary Don’t Die, says he’s on a quest to achieve the lowest possible “biological age” (also known as bio age).
  • He reportedly spends millions each year on anti-aging treatments—dozens of daily supplements, weekly acid peels for his skin, injections to boost collagen production, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and plasma infusions extracted from his 17-year-old son’s body.
  • To determine what’s working, Johnson has undergone numerous tests to assess his bio age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson, the subject of the Netflix documentary Don’t Die, says he’s on a quest to achieve the lowest possible “biological age” (also known as bio age).

He reportedly spends millions each year on anti-aging treatments—dozens of daily supplements, weekly acid peels for his skin, injections to boost collagen production, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and plasma infusions extracted from his 17-year-old son’s body.

To determine what’s working, Johnson has undergone numerous tests to assess his bio age. Johnson indicates these tests show his age is now 5.1 years younger than when he embarked on his anti-aging quest.

Apparently, he’s aging in reverse.

Granted, not everyone’s buying it. A Upcoming York Times exposé, for example, claims Johnson’s biological age, in reality, has increased by 10 years.1.

Still, Johnson’s “don’t die” crusade is gaining traction.

It has been revealed that bio age tests are a frequent topic on popular podcasts by Peter Attia, Joe Rogan, and Andrew Huberman. Google “bio age testing” and you’ll see dozens of ads for mail-order blood or urine testing kits that claim to reveal your biological age, pace of aging, and more. With prices tumbling into affordability, it’s natural to wonder….

If so, which test is best? Just as importantly, what should you do with the information?

In a recent development, your biological age (bio age) refers to how your cells function. It’s not necessarily the same as your chronological age, which refers to the number of candles on your birthday cake.

According to recent reports, for example, let’s say Chang, a 50-year-old man, works at a desk, spends his free time in front of the TV, lives in the most polluted city in the world, eats a candy bar for lunch, and smokes. On the other hand, Jabari, a different 50-year-old man, hits the gym several times a week, lives in the mountains, doesn’t smoke, relishes his five servings of veggies a day, meditates, and spends most evenings in his garden.

Genetics aside, you’d be wise to wager that Jabari’s bio age is younger than Chang’s.

Bio age testing kits measure one or more biological markers of aging, also known as biomarkers.

For example, some tests focus on the size of your telomeres, the protective caps at the ends of chromosomes. Others measure DNA methylation, a physiological process that chemically alters DNA.

Once a manufacturer isolates and measures these markers from your blood or urine, it plugs the bio data into a formula that calculates your bio age.

However, if you see a doctor with any regularity, you’re likely already tracking some biomarkers of aging. For example, biomarkers such as blood pressure, cholesterol levels, and blood glucose can help predict your risk of future cardiovascular disease, a leading cause of premature death.

Biomarker testing can help you monitor your wellness proactively rather than waiting for disease symptoms to appear.

It has been revealed that for some, it also serves as a motivator. If you learn you have the bones of someone 20 years older, this may give you the nudge you need to start strength training consistently.

In addition, biomarkers provide objective data, allowing you to track and evaluate various health-related actions quantitatively. By monitoring your blood pressure, you might learn that consistent exercise helps, but your late-afternoon energy drink does the opposite.

You don’t have to be a billionaire (or even a millionaire) to track biomarkers of aging.

In this section, we’ll cover several massively underappreciated, scientifically validated tests you can use to gain insight into your bio age—for FREE.

Before scientists developed high-tech blood-based bio age tests, researchers used these free tests to calculate the pace of aging in the people they studied.

People who are fitter and stronger tend to live longer.2.

That’s because muscles do more than just move us around. They also secrete anti-inflammatory substances, help to regulate blood sugar, slow cellular aging, protect the lining of the arteries, and more. All this helps reduce the risk of age-related diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease, a phenomenon we explore in our article, The Upcoming Science of Muscle.

Related to strength, your ability to balance is also key. If you’re middle-aged or older and can’t stand on one foot for at least 10 seconds, your risk of dying in the next seven years is double that of someone who can stand for longer, according to a study of 1,700 people.3.

The Sitting-Rising Test (SRT) is one way to assess both strength and balance at the same time.

People with low scores on this test have a higher risk of dying from cardiovascular disease, according to a 12-year study of 4,200 adults between the ages of 46 and 75.4.

Lower yourself to the floor with your legs in a crisscross position. Then, with your legs in the same position, stand back up. As you stand, notice if you must use a part of your body—hand, shin, knee—as leverage.

To score yourself, start with 10 points. Then, for each body part you used to stand, deduct a point. Subtract a half point if you became unsteady or lost your balance.

Keep in mind that this (and other tests) serve as a proxy for your fitness. A low score indicates that your balance and coordination, muscle strength and power, and mobility may all require some attention.

It has been revealed that like the SRT test, your grip strength provides insight into your overall fitness. If the muscles in your hands are weak, the muscles throughout your body are more likely to be weak, too.

Poor grip strength can also predict future muscle weakness. In one study, people with a weak grip were more likely to walk slowly and be unable to rise from a chair, complete rigorous housework, or climb a flight of steps 25 years later.5.

Low grip strength has also been associated with:6.

According to one study, grip strength was a better indicator of longevity (or lack thereof) than blood pressure.7.

Grab a standard tennis ball, and squeeze as hard as you can, for as long as you can.

If you can manage 15 to 30 seconds before your grip fatigues, you’re doing fine. Ninety seconds puts you well above average—anything over 90 ranks you solidly in the upper-third percentile.

Industry observers note that if you’re below 15, keep in mind that this test is also just one indicator of your overall strength. (And squeezing balls to improve grip strength without training the rest of your body is unlikely to make significant improvements in your overall health and fitness.).

A hand-held dynamometer—available for use at most occupational therapists’ and some gyms—can also test grip strength. (If you’re willing to shell out some cash, you can buy your own for somewhere between $100 and $500.).

An ability to balance on one foot for an extended period can help reduce your risk of falls, one of the leading causes of injury-related death among older adults.

In addition, many different bodily systems—the eyes, inner ear, skeletal muscles, and brain—must work together to help you stay upright.

Recent findings suggest that conditions like diabetes, heart disease, and cancer can all affect balance. As a result, an inability to stand on one foot can serve as a warning sign for eroding health and fitness.8.

Sources indicate that stand near a wall or chair for safety. Keep your eyes open and hands on your hips. Then, lift your dominant leg and start timing yourself. Once you put your foot down, stop the clock. Repeat the test with your non-dominant leg.

Once you have your times, compare them to the following averages, from a study out of Duke University, to see how you did compared to your age-matched peers.9.

According to recent reports, sometimes you know why you’re tired, such as the morning after binge-watching the last few episodes of a thriller. Once you catch up on your sleep, the weariness lifts.

That’s not the same thing as fatigue, which describes persistent exhaustion that worsens over time and interferes with life. In addition to feeling physically tired, someone who’s fatigued feels mentally dull and emotionally exhausted.

Think of fatigue as an early sign that something’s off, especially if you don’t know the cause.

It has been revealed that let’s say you’ve already ruled out the usual suspects like too much caffeine, dehydration, too much alcohol, medication side effects, chronic stress, or too much or too little exercise. What’s left is likely a sleep disorder or a developing health problem such as anemia, obesity, depression, cancer, or diabetes, to name a few.

If you’re 60 or older, fatiguability—or how worn out you feel after an activity—can also predict longevity.

According to research out of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, the higher someone scores in fatiguability, the higher their risk of death in the future.10 Other research has linked high fatiguability with declines in gait speed, walking ability, and other tests of fitness.11.

To measure fatigability, use a tool called the Pittsburgh Fatigability Scale. Using a 0 (no fatigue) to 5 (extreme fatigue) scale, rate how fatigued you think you would feel after completing the following activities:.

According to recent reports, if you score less than 15, you’re doing well. Scores between 15 and 24 are a warning sign. Anything 25 and above is regarded as severe, and worth mentioning to your healthcare professional.12.

Despite popular belief, both too little and too much body fat can influence health for the worse, as we explore in our infographic, Is body fat good or bad for you?

Your muscle mass also plays a role, which is why someone’s body composition matters more than their weight.

The gold standard methods that estimate body composition—underwater weighing, air displacement (Bod Pod), and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA)—certainly aren’t free.

However, a recent study determined that a good old-fashioned (and cheap) tape measure can provide a comparably accurate estimate of body composition.13.

To use a tape measure to keep track of your body fat percentage, measure:.

According to recent reports, ensure the tape is snug but not so tight that it cuts into the skin. Once you have your measurements, plug those numbers—along with your age, sex, height, and weight—into our FREE Body Fat Calculator, which will take it from there.

Depending on where you live in the world, the following tests may not be free. However, as part of routine preventative care, your insurance might cover them.

If your primary care doctor recommends yearly blood work, it’s for good reason.

By keeping tabs on several blood markers, you can see if your health is trending toward type 2 diabetes or heart disease, both leading causes of premature mortality.

Industry observers note that many blood markers can also be influenced relatively quickly (within 6 to 12 weeks) through lifestyle changes, supplement protocols, or medications. This makes them practical tools for monitoring whether various lifestyle or medical modifications are working.

If you’re not already doing so, consider having the following blood markers tested annually. Then, talk to your health care professional about what your numbers mean. They might use the following numbers, along with your blood pressure, to calculate a cardiovascular disease risk score.

*Milligrams per deciliter of blood **Milligrams per liter.

When researchers study healthy super-agers aged 90 and older, strong bones are one of their defining features.14.

That may be because, like muscles, bones are live organs that secrete substances that may be beneficial to overall health and longevity.15.

For example, bones secrete osteocalcin, a hormone that plays a role in bone remodeling. When osteocalcin circulates in the body, it’s thought to play a role in everything from helping muscles to produce ATP to regulating brain neurotransmitters.

Recent findings suggest that because of these varied roles, it’s thought that, as bones wear away, osteocalcin levels drop, contributing to many age-related health problems, including diabetes, low muscle mass, and cognitive complications.16 17 (At least, that’s the theory. Most of this research has been done on mice.).

Osteocalcin aside, loss of bone density can, of course, lead to fractures, which can increase your risk of death for up to 10 years after a break.18.

It’s especially important to keep tabs on bone health if you’re in any of these high-risk categories:.

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans are a type of X-ray that measures the amount of bone mineral content packed into a square centimeter of bone.

Industry observers note that insurance often won’t cover these scans for people younger than 65 unless there’s a documented risk of developing osteoporosis. Out of pocket, the average cost is about $300.

It has been revealed that when you receive your DEXA results, you’ll see a T-score that represents how your bone density compares to the average bone density of a young adult with peak bone mass. A T-score of +1.0 to -1.0 means you have normal bone mineral density for someone your age. Anything below -1.0 means you might have osteopenia (low bone mineral density) or osteoporosis (porous bones that are prone to fracture).

If you have some money to burn, you can learn an awful lot about your body.

Here, you’ll find a quick run-down on some of the more high-tech tests you can get and what they can tell you.

However, before we get into the details, we want to point out a few caveats:.

▶ Biological age can vary over time, and by organ. Someone may go through a period of accelerated aging—saying, during a period of intense stress—then their rate of aging may slow as they focus more on recovery. Additionally, organs can age at different rates. For example, someone with heart disease may have a relatively older heart than their kidneys. (Not all tests measure individual organ age, but it’s becoming more common.).

▶ Commercial tests won’t always accurately reflect the changes you’re making. Until more research supports the reliability of these tests, evaluate your behaviors over isolated test results. If you’re eating more fruits and veggies, exercising more consistently, managing stress, and otherwise slaying the healthy lifestyle department, don’t sweat your results. Focus on doing the things we know improve health.

▶ If a manufacturer pairs your test results with a hard sell for a proprietary and expensive supplement protocol, be wary. It’s better to share and discuss your results with a trusted health professional than take health advice from a profit-seeking stranger over the internet.

According to recent reports, DNA methylation is a biological process that chemically alters DNA. Because the rate of methylation accelerates with aging, it can be used to estimate someone’s biological age and life expectancy, finds research.19 20 21.

Industry observers note that the Horvath Clock and DunedinPACE both measure specific biomarkers that can be used to better understand someone’s methylation rate. Scientists developed these tests to help other scientists study how various lifestyle factors, environmental exposures, and medicines affect aging. They didn’t develop the tests as a way for the average person to pinpoint their biological age. (Which hasn’t stopped companies from selling DNA methylation testing kits to the public.) They cost about $300.

If you decide to get one of these tests, keep in mind your results won’t give you a complete picture of your health and longevity. Aging typically occurs at varying rates throughout the body. Your liver might age faster than your heart or brain, for example. So if you measure DNA methylation in your blood, that’s all you know about. Put another way, a DNA methylation test isn’t a substitute for your annual wellness checkup or blood work.

Telomeres—the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes—wear away with age. The length of a telomere can predict how many times a specific cell can divide before dying.

Abnormally short telomeres are associated with several genetic diseases. For this reason, when physicians suspect someone might have inherited a genetic disease, they’ll order a specific type of telomere test—the flow-FISH test—to measure the telomere length in all the cells in a blood sample.22 23.

It’s more debatable whether telomere tests can predict aging in healthy people.

Just as importantly, the telomere test marketed to the public, known as the qPCR telomere test, isn’t used in research or medicine. These $100 tests are fine if you’re merely curious—just don’t base health and fitness decisions on your results.

For years, only elite athletes cared about VO2 max, which describes the maximum amount of oxygen that your body can use during exercise.

More recently, however, some experts have suggested that VO2 max can serve as a measure for athletes and non-athletes alike to track the rate at which their bodies are aging.

People with high VO2 max tend not only to be more physically fit but also less likely to develop heart disease, diabetes, cancer, or stroke.24 25 26 27.

Sources indicate that in an observational study that followed the health outcomes of 5,107 Danish men over 46 years, men with above-average V02 max during middle age lived an average of five years longer than men with below-average V02 max. Each unit increase in VO2 max was associated with a 45-day increase in longevity. The researchers suggested VO2 max may more accurately predict all-cause mortality than high cholesterol, obesity, high blood pressure, and insulin resistance.28.

You might think of V02 max as a canary and your aging body as a coal mine.

In a recent development, as you age, your chest wall becomes more rigid, the muscles that surround the lungs weaker, and the oxygen-carrying blood vessels calcified and less elastic. The heart also squeezes with less force, max heart rate drops, muscle mass and strength decline, the mitochondria in cells and muscles lose their effectiveness, among other differences.

In addition to raising your risk for many different diseases, these changes can also affect VO2 max, which tends to decline 10 percent per decade starting around age 30.29 30.

In the past, the only way to reliably measure VO2 max was in a fitness lab.

In a recent development, you would wear a metabolic mask and a heart monitor while you ran or cycled to exhaustion. The mask collected your expired carbon dioxide and monitored how much oxygen you sucked into your lungs. This lab-based testing is still the most accurate way to measure V02 max as well as other key fitness metrics such as:.

Depending on where you live, you might be able to get your VO2 max tested for around $150.

However, if you don’t have access to a VO2 max clinic, three somewhat less accurate options exist.

According to recent reports, wear a heart rate monitor as you walk one mile on a flat surface, such as a treadmill or running track. As soon as you complete the mile, record your heart rate and walk time. Then, plug it into the following formula to calculate your VO2 max:.

132.853 — (0.0769 × Weight) — (0.3877 × Age) + (6.315 × Sex) — (3.2649 × Time) — (0.1565 × Heart rate).

If that feels like too much math, you can also use a free online tool.

Recent findings suggest that many smartwatches will estimate your VO2 Max for you based on information the watch gathers from your workouts, sex, and age. Compared to in-office testing, smart watches can over- or underestimate V02 max, especially in people who are very out of shape or extremely fit.31.

Because of this, you don’t necessarily want to use your smart watch measurement to determine your current state of health. However, it can help you to see trends. For example, does your VO2 estimate drop after a few weeks of skipping your usual spin class? If so, that’s good information to have.

Fitness performance correlates with longevity. If you’re getting faster at running a certain distance or can go a longer distance than before, you’re getting fitter and increasing your chances of living a long, healthy life.

Sources indicate that one way to test this: the 12-minute run test, also known as the Cooper test. (This is a validated way to estimate VO2 max—and shows about a 90 percent correlation with lab-based measurements.).

Run as fast as you can on a flat surface, such as a treadmill set at a 1 percent incline or running track, for 12 minutes. After 12 minutes, record your distance. Then, plug it into one of the following formulas to calculate your VO2 max.

In lieu of doing math, you can also use a free online calculator.

Try to think of the information you gather about your body as just that—information.

It’s not a moral judgment of who you are as a person.

Just as importantly, it’s not a permanent situation.

It has been revealed that you have options. However, most people make two big mistakes when it comes to longevity-related lifestyle changes.

It’s the simple, boring, “I’ve heard this a million times before” health practices that, when done consistently, add up to a long, healthy life.

We’re talking about things like….

And that’s just a partial list.

According to thousands of studies, people who practice these and other high-impact strategies not only live longer, but also live better. They’re stronger, happier, and less likely to spend their later years disabled or in pain.

(If you’d like to see where you stand when it comes to massive impact health and longevity strategies, check out our FREE Longevity Assessment.).

However, when it comes to health, fitness, and longevity, many people pursue options with minimal impact (at best). They reach for the latest, trendy supplement rather than taking steps to quit smoking, as just one example.

According to recent reports, here’s the thing: Big rock strategies require changes in behavior. If daily physical activity were as easy as popping a pill, walkers and cyclists would clog up the streets in your neighborhood.

(It’s precisely this reason why so many people need the support of a certified health coach who has undergone training in the science of behavior change.).

The data gathered from biomarker aging tests can give you a sense of control.

Data, in isolation, doesn’t lead to a longer life.

Gathering data without changing your behavior is like checking your reflection in the mirror, seeing spinach wedged between your incisors, and leaving it there.

You need to remove the spinach for the mirror check to be worthwhile.

If you don’t use your bio data to inform behavior change, you’re wasting your money and time.

Consider your biomarker data as a baseline or starting point.

Then, use it to assess whether various lifestyle changes or medical interventions are moving you closer to your goal of living a longer, healthier life.
