#138195. Who’s ready for coaching? 7 GLP-1 clients, from “not yet” to “let’s go!”

📅 11 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4499 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Precisionnutrition ↗ Open Full Page

Who’s ready for coaching? 7 GLP-1 clients, from “not yet” to “let’s go!”

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Precisionnutrition

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.
  • According to recent reports, though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat.
  • Now, in 2026, over 1 in 10 US adults are taking a GLP-1 medication.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD.

That’s the thought many health and fitness coaches had when GLP-1 medications first hit the mass market.

According to recent reports, though semaglutide (Ozempic) became available in 2017, it initially felt like a theoretical threat. Prescription rates were still very low, and it seemed like no one actually knew anyone who was taking it.

Now, in 2026, over 1 in 10 US adults are taking a GLP-1 medication. Most of us know someone on it (or we’re on it ourselves).

Sources indicate that with wider use, opinions towards the medication have softened too. Most coaches no longer see it as a threat, and instead appreciate it as a valuable tool for certain clients, with coaching as an additive complement.

Many coaches still have concerns though, primarily about their clients’ long term health on the medication. (Among the worries: Loss of muscle mass! Using a “band-aid” solution! Bypassing foundational health habits! And more!).

However, whether you count yourself as a GLP-1 supporter or a GLP-1 skeptic, there’s a framing that might change the way you think about your work in this field:.

As Kate Solovieva, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Community, indicates: “As a coach, you’re not in the GLP-1 world; you’re in the GLP-1 support world.”.

That’s actually good news. Because trying to coach everyone taking a GLP-1 just isn’t possible. And spending time thinking about all the people using GLP-1s “the wrong way” is, bluntly, wasted energy. Some of those people just don’t want, need, or aren’t ready for your help.

Meanwhile, there is a subgroup of people on GLP-1s who are ready, willing, and able to receive your support. Honing in on this group is where you can actually make a difference (and where your business can thrive).

In a recent development, in the following article, we’ll cover seven GLP-1 clients you’re likely to meet. Each reflects a different point in the GLP-1 medication journey, and a different level of readiness for coaching. Based on our experience coaching over 175,000 clients (of which an increasing number are on GLP-1s), we’ll offer strategies to work with each.

Before we begin, a reminder: People change, and readiness isn’t fixed.

A person who starts off saying “I’m doing fine on my own” may eventually morph into “I’m flailing and really need someone else in my corner”—and vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that if the person in front of you sounds like one of these clients, that’s where they are right now. So listen carefully to how your client speaks at every session, and respond dynamically.

In general, Coach Kate claims someone is usually ready for coaching when they demonstrate two things:.

Keep that in the back of your mind as you interact with client prospects, and as you read about each client, summarized in the table below.

Now, on to the different GLP-1 clients.

This is the person who’s started a GLP-1 medication—and they love it.

They’ve experienced minimal side effects, and have gotten great results on a relatively low dose.

They haven’t changed much about their exercise habits or their diet (except the eating less part, which the medication has taken care of), but they’re seeing what they want to see on the scale, so they don’t feel motivated to change anything.

It might be tempting to “lure” this kind of client in by warning them of the dangers of using a GLP-1 medication without adding in long-term health behaviors (like resistance training and strategic nutrition), but this type of approach can backfire.

At best, you may sound like a downer. At worst, you may sound like an active antagonist.

In Motivational Interviewing, a communication approach commonly used in coaching, this is called the “righting reflex.” It’s the urge that coaches, counselors, and therapists often have to help or “correct course” for their client. You see them doing something “wrong,” and you want to help them “fix” it.

However, following this instinct may actually strengthen a client’s defenses, and prevent change.

If a person is flying high on their current approach, their readiness for coaching is extremely low.

As Coach Kate says, “they’re just not my person yet.”.

Your best move with this client is to genuinely celebrate their current results, then plant the seed for support should they need it in the future.

Recent findings suggest that for example, you could say: “It must feel so good to see all these positive results! If you ever feel like you want to work on another layer, like resistance training or optimizing your nutrition, I’d love to work together.”.

Then, just stay available. (“My door is always open!”).

This is the person who hasn’t started a GLP-1 medication—and might never, despite being a great candidate for one.

Maybe their doctor has already suggested the medication to them and they’ve read everything they can on the topic.

Industry observers note that and yet, they’re frozen with fear at the starting line. They’re afraid of side effects, of being on medication for life, of not holding up their end of the bargain. (“I’ve been trying to start strength training for years. If I take this medication it matters even more… What if I still can’t do it?”).

Toni Bauer, Super Coach and PN’s Director of Coaching and Education Operations also indicates that, in some cases, a client’s hesitation isn’t about side effects. “Some of our clients wonder, ‘Am I a good person or a bad person if I start taking a GLP-1 medication? Am I weak? Am I giving up?’” Coach Toni says these concerns aren’t unique to GLP-1 medications, but they seem to be especially common.

She reasons, “If you have high cholesterol, are you weak for taking cholesterol medication? No. But often people don’t view obesity as a disease at a societal level, so the conversation is different here.”.

Regardless of the root cause of this person’s hesitation, the advice below can help them find clarity.

First, let’s be clear: Deciding whether or not to take a medication isn’t a coaching decision, and falls out of your scope of practice. That choice is ultimately up to your client and a medical provider who can assess whether a GLP-1 is appropriate given their medical history.

That said, clients may still come to you wanting to discuss their options.

So the question becomes: How do you support someone through a decision you can’t make for them?

It has been revealed that coach Toni advises: “You can share facts and data. For example, study results and what you’ve seen with other clients. But you can’t say, ‘For you, this is the right choice.’”.

Instead, the biggest coaching opportunity here is to help clients articulate what’s actually driving their hesitation.

This hesitation about whether to do something different or stay the same is called ambivalence, and it’s a normal (albeit uncomfortable) stage of change.

According to recent reports, problem is, without the right tools, a person can stay stuck in ambivalence for months or even years. And, much like being stuck at an airport in between two destinations, it sucks.

But at PN, we have a cool exercise to deal with client ambivalence. It’s called the 4 Crazy Questions. Essentially, you explore:.

In this context, the questions can help a client explore the risk of starting a GLP-1 (which they’ve probably already voiced), but also the risk of not starting, which they may not have considered yet.

Our 4 Crazy Questions worksheet can encourage clients to explore the pros and cons of both choices. With these considerations laid out explicitly, most people feel a lot more clear about their next steps—or at least what questions they need to ask their medical provider before they can move forward.

Importantly, this exercise doesn’t have a “right” outcome. Some people work through it and fill the prescription. Others decide the medication isn’t for them, and that’s fine. (It’s also worth reminding clients that starting isn’t necessarily permanent: With their provider’s input, a trial run on the medication is a perfectly valid way in.).

Sources indicate that either way, there are opportunities to support your client. As Coach Toni puts it: “Whether you go ‘natural’ or whether you go GLP-1, the foundational habits are essentially the same.”.

This is the person who started a GLP-1 with lots of optimism—and now feels like they have a plague that won’t end.

In a cruel twist, this person might actually be seeing great fat loss results. And yet, they’re nauseated, exhausted, dreading their next dose, and wondering whether it’s worth continuing this medication.

Adding to their sense of defeat, they may also be comparing themselves to a “Honeymooner” in their life, so they might also be wondering if there’s something wrong with them. (“It worked so well for my friend! I must be broken in some way.”).

First, offer some neutral education to depersonalize their experience.

In a recent development, namely, they should know that side effects are extremely common: About half of people report nausea, a third report diarrhea, and a fifth report vomiting.1 So, what this person thinks is exceptional might actually just be a normal adjustment. (This doesn’t make the experience suck less, but it can give them some hope.).

Also, getting GLP-1s right is a process of trial and error: the right medication, the right dose, and the right nutritional strategies to reduce symptoms.

According to recent reports, if their symptoms are severe, get them to loop in their doctor. Medication type and dosing is under the purview of a medical professional, so involving them is essential.

After that, your best coaching move is to suggest an experiment.

▶ Ask about dose. To be clear, you’re asking about it, not adjusting it. Indicates Coach Toni: “Often, when people are experiencing extreme side effects, they’ve ratcheted up their dose too rapidly. Sometimes the easiest way to keep somebody on a GLP-1 who’s experiencing high side effects is to lower their dosage.” Coach Toni makes clear that while dosage isn’t a coach’s domain, you can help draw a client’s attention to it.

▶ Start a food journal. It doesn’t need to be every day—just around the meals that precede the worst symptoms. You’re looking for three things:.

▶ Try smaller portions, eaten more often. Coach Toni indicates if you only try one thing, this one is the most reliable strategy. GLP-1 clients may be tempted to cut meals when symptoms are high, but this increases the likelihood of undereating and nutrient deficiencies. The goal, in her words: “Can we get small enough, frequent enough meals that we get nutrients in, but they never feel overwhelmed or super full?”.

To stay within your scope of practice, language matters.

Don’t say: “You’re nauseous, so you should eat smaller meals.”.

Instead, say: “Folks who are nauseous sometimes do better with smaller, more frequent meals. Want to try it this week and see what you notice?”.

Recent findings suggest that in the first example, you’ve offered a “prescription” (which coaches can’t legally do). In the second example, you’ve offered an experiment to consider.

Industry observers note that side effects (such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, and/or diarrhea) are extremely common among GLP-1 owners, and typically last one to two weeks after initiating the medication. Some symptoms can last longer (particularly constipation), but most are mild to moderate, and usually improve within a few weeks.

Symptoms can also return each time a dosage is increased, though they’re usually milder and more short-lived. These too tend to improve after the first week or so.

However, you should strongly encourage a client to reach out promptly to their medical provider if they notice:.

Industry observers note that reassure your client they’re not being dramatic by reporting these symptoms. Their medical team needs to hear this kind of information to help them get the best results, while preserving overall health.

Also: Your client will get better care if they show up prepared. So, get them to jot down and bring:.

This is the person whose results look great, but less visible changes are creating longer term risks.

Sources indicate that this person is likely to be quite sedentary, and when you ask what they do for exercise, they might tell you “I walk.” But they’re not the outlier kind of walker who consistently gets 20,000 steps a day. They just… walk a little.

Women are more likely to fall into this category, especially if they come from a generation or culture where strength training simply wasn’t a thing women did (or were welcomed to do).

Additionally, this person might be running on a decades-long plain-toast-and-coffee breakfast habit, with lower protein intake already ingrained before medication further reduced appetite.

In a recent development, the scale is dropping though, so they’re thrilled. It’s just that nobody’s measuring what kind of weight is dropping.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that this description is a starting hypothesis, not a diagnosis. Low activity and low protein raise the risk of muscle loss, but they don’t confirm it. That’s what the measures below are for.

Your job is to bring awareness to the invisible. Because once this person sees what’s at stake, they’ll be more likely to see the value in changing their habits, and in coaching.

However, theoretical warnings about muscle loss are easy to dismiss.

This is one of the reasons why Coach Kate says, “I don’t care if I coach you or not—please just get a DEXA as a baseline.”.

When a person has a quantifiable, objective measure of their muscle composition, it’s often more motivating than any amount of abstract concern.

Ideally, every person who begins a GLP-1 medication should get a DEXA scan before they start, then again at six or twelve months to see how they’re progressing.

If a client can’t or won’t do a DEXA, assess strength and function in other ways. Ask: “How do the stairs feel compared to a few months ago? What about carrying groceries?” Gather objective data too, recording baselines for squat, deadlift, and bench press (or other accessible exercises) to compare to over time. Declines in any of these areas can reveal potential muscle loss, and can motivate a client to take action.

Without protective strategies, up to 40 percent of weight lost from GLP-1 medications can come from lean mass, with a majority of that being muscle.2.

In order to prevent that from happening, there are two behaviors to prioritize:.

▶ Protein at every meal. When appetite is suppressed, every bite has to earn its place. Aim for 25-40 grams of protein at every meal and 15-20 grams for snacks. (On days when appetite is severely suppressed, protein powders can be a more palatable way to reach that target.).

It has been revealed that ▶ Strength training, scaled to what they’d actually do. The term “weight lifting” might overwhelm a person who’s never set foot in a gym, so don’t start there. Start where PN always starts: Ask what they could do twice this week that they’re 9-out-of-10 confident they’d actually do. Sit-to-stands off the couch. A few moves with a resistance band. Bodyweight anything. Scale up from there, one week at a time.

This is the person for whom the medication has worked a little too well.

Their appetite hasn’t just decreased—it’s gone.

Recent findings suggest that they’re not eating enough, and often don’t notice until you ask. “When did you last eat?” you say, and they say, “Ummm… Yesterday afternoon? I think?”.

Their protein and overall calorie intake is plummeting, and soon their energy levels will too.

Plus, something more subtle might also be happening: Food stops being a pleasure and becomes a chore, or even a source of dread.

According to recent reports, for some, this might seem like an upside down world. They may have spent their whole life fighting to eat less. The idea of fighting to eat more feels completely absurd—and entirely off their radar.

It has been revealed that before anything else: If there’s an active eating disorder in the picture, this medication likely shouldn’t have been prescribed. A vulnerability to disordered eating can both contribute to or be triggered by the above scenario.

So, scope of practice first. Ask this person if they’ve ever struggled with disordered eating. If the answer is yes, refer out to a doctor or a dietitian. You can absolutely stay involved as a guide, but not as the only professional in the room. Have your referral network ready before you need it.

It has been revealed that but sometimes, you won’t know. Your client may have been screened and cleared. Or, they may not have disclosed. So your job is to figure out what you’re actually looking at—and that starts with what Coach Toni calls the “show me” approach.

Sources indicate that as with every client here, treat this one as something to investigate, not a label. Rather than acting on a hunch, collect something concrete, such as a few days of food logging (in writing or via photos).

From there, it branches two ways.

▶ If they’ll track, do some food math, and the numbers may do the work for you. When some clients see that their calorie intake is hovering around 800 to 1,000 Calories per day, it’s the only wake up call they need. They weren’t intentionally restricting; they genuinely just had no idea.

For this client, establishing an eating routine is the best next action.

Your client may be used to following appetite as a cue to eat, but now that medication has removed it, they need a different cue. That means eating on a schedule, likely every 3–4 hours, including protein at every one of those occasions. Portions can be small if appetite is very low, but they should be nutrient-dense.

▶ If they won’t track—and especially if they resist in a way that feels purposely avoidant—that resistance itself is information.

Coach Toni suggests that if you suspect that disordered eating is in the picture and a client is really resistant about tracking, it might be time for a crucial conversation—an often uncomfortable, but honest and essential conversation between a client and a coach.

Recent findings suggest that she suggests leading with non-judgement and safety. For example:.

Industry observers note that “I want you to know this is a safe space to talk. My goal as a coach is always to prioritize your overall health. However, there have been a couple of things you’ve shared recently that have me wondering whether we’re protecting your body’s basic needs.”.

Then name the specific things you noticed, sticking to facts. (“You’ve mentioned you’ve been losing hair and struggling more during workouts. Those can both be signs of undereating. Would you be open to revisiting food journaling for a short stretch so we can see more clearly what’s happening, or telling your doctor about your symptoms?”).

If this conversation is enough to help a client see the value in tracking, follow the advice after “If they’ll track” above.

If what surfaces is a genuinely troubled relationship with food, refer out, while offering to stay involved for support as needed.

This is the person who got the results they wanted with the medication, and is now choosing to wean off.

They’re not quitting because of crappy results or intolerable side effects, they’ve simply decided they don’t want to be on a GLP-1 forever.

The coaching opportunity here is, in part, about tempering expectations.

Most people imagine coming off as the finish line. Instead though, it’s more like starting a different endurance course: The medication has been managing their appetite, and now they have to.

In a recent development, ideally, you start working with this client while the medication is still doing some of the heavy lifting with appetite regulation. If you can have six months to build the right habits as well as prepare mentally for the tapering off period, your client will be in a much better position.

Make sure the previously mentioned habits—like resistance training and optimizing protein—are already firmly established. If your client is managing those habits consistently (not perfectly, but consistently), even on their busiest, most stressful, most side-effect-disrupted days, then they’re more likely to be able to maintain them when they’re off their medication and food distractions re-enter the picture.

After that, work on how you’ll continue to define success. This client has been accustomed to measuring it on the scale, but the scale will move—some regain is normal. So, ask them early: What does success look like if the scale ticks up eight pounds but your habits hold?

It has been revealed that be honest about the odds, too. People who changed nothing while on the medication almost universally regain most of the weight—usually within the first year and a half or so3—because the appetite that went down comes right back up.

However, people who integrate and sustain healthier nutrition and exercise behaviors while they’re on medication are four times better at maintaining a ten percent or higher weight loss when they come off the medication.4.

This is the person who was also getting great results on the medication—except instead of choosing to go off it on their own time, they’re forced to quit due to external circumstances.

Maybe their insurance stopped covering it, or they lost the job that came with the benefits, or the one drug they tolerated turned out to cost four times as much as the one they couldn’t tolerate.

About 50 percent of GLP-1 people stop the medication within the first year of using it.5 Some stop due to side effects, and others stop because they’ve gotten the results they want and they want to see if they can maintain them drug-free. But many are simply priced out. The latter is an especially frustrating scenario because, for this person, a “solution” exists. It’s just that, for them, the solution is out of reach.

Recent findings suggest that understandably, this person may be angry or even ashamed that they can’t afford this medication. Those feelings may or may not show up in your coaching, but it’s good to prepare for them anyway.

First, reassure this person that this is a system failure, not a personal one.

Sources indicate that whether someone can access affordable medication comes down to their insurance strategy, the region they live in, and their socioeconomic status—also known as the social determinants of health. Those forces shape health outcomes far more than willpower does, and none of them are a measure of how hard someone has tried or how “worthy” they are.

Acknowledging that reality isn’t about throwing up your hands and saying, “Well, I’m screwed!” Rather, it’s about accepting some miserable truths about the world, and then shifting from self-blame to problem-solving.

Once they’ve had a chance to process some (very valid) anger and disappointment, it’s time to focus on what they can control.

Sources indicate that at PN, we call this the Spheres of Control exercise. The image below shows you how it works.

Access, price, and coverage are not on the list of controllables, and fighting those realities may only compound frustration.

Meanwhile, they can control other influential factors, like their protein intake, their training, their sleep, their food environment, and maybe their next insurance appeal.

Use the image above to begin a conversation with your client about what is within their control, and lean in hard on those factors.

The truth is, you can’t predict how a client will respond to medication. And, some regain after stopping it is expected.

However, diet and lifestyle habits hugely affect what kind of weight clients lose, plus the rate and amount of that regain.

“I can’t promise anyone they’ll lose a specific amount of weight or that they’ll never regain it—and I’d be suspicious of any coach who did. What I can tell you is that the habits we build while the medication is doing its work are the ones that’ll still stand when it isn’t.”.

Of course, “coming off” isn’t the endpoint for everyone. Many providers now treat obesity as a chronic condition and these medications as long-term therapy—the same way we’d treat cardiac disease. Again, whether someone stays on, tapers, or stops is a conversation for them and their provider.

Sources indicate that but for those who do come off, Coach Toni indicates the people who hold their results share one thing: “They maintain consistency with their behaviors as if they were still on the medication. Like nothing changes.”.

She shares an analogy for why that works:.

It has been revealed that “Think about the Oregon Trail. Wagon wheels made ruts in the trail by hitting the same ground over and over and over. You can still see those ruts today. Habits are the same way: If you lay down those neural pathways and reinforce them enough times while your client is on the medication, they’ll have a better chance of continuing on the same path even when they go off the medication.”.

It’s not: “You’ll keep it off.”.

It’s: “While the medication is doing its work, we’ll cut ruts deep enough that those pathways will still be there after the medication is gone.”.

Practically, that means regular resistance training, rock solid nutrition, appetite awareness, and attending to the parts of health that never show up on a scale—sleep, energy, mood, relationships, and identity, which is where Coach Toni lands:.

“Ideally, your client will have embraced the identity of a ‘upcoming person.’ As in, ‘I am the person who wakes up at 6 a.m. and walks two miles. I am the person who eats protein at every meal. I am the person who does resistance training because it builds the tissue I need to age well.’ That’s the client who maintains.”.

The seven client examples above help you answer two questions:.

Is this person ready for coaching?

How do I meet them where they are?

Once someone becomes your client, the question changes to:.

And when nausea, fatigue, stalled results, and weakening strength and physical function all show up at once in the same client, that can be tricky to answer.

Knowing where to start is one of the core skills taught in the upcoming GLP Coaching Institute Certification, developed in partnership with Precision Nutrition.

According to recent reports, the certification combines GLP-1-specific science and practical coaching frameworks with PN’s proven coaching methodology. You’ll learn how to use a framework called The Five GLP-1 Types: Strength, Fuel, Fitness, Recovery, and Results.

Industry observers note that unlike the profiles in this article, the Five Types aren’t about how ready clients are. They’re coaching priorities: a way to decide what to work on first, and when to shift focus as a client’s needs change.

To learn more, join the waitlist. You’ll be the first to know when the certification launches, with early access before enrolment opens to everyone else.

The Triathlete editorial team has been around long enough that we’ve collectively written dozens of holiday gift guides — from stocking stuffers to price point round-ups to personality-based ideas, always solid ideas but usually pretty generic.

Industry observers note that but this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

In a recent development, and we are happy to share our IRL gift ideas with you for your own gifting or wish list creation. Below, you’ll find out a little bit more about some of our favorite contributors, what we gifted them, and why we think they’ll enjoy it.

It has been revealed that about the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

What we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

It has been revealed that about the contributor: Sierra is a skilled writer who has lent her talents to highlight the need for more athlete-friendly pregnancy and postpartum deferral policies and to advocate for clearer policies around breastfeeding and pumping during races. She’s a mom to an active toddler.

What we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

—Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

About the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. From her home in Boulder, Colorado, she interviews experts, talks to today’s top pro athletes, and writes to make changes and news of the sport understandable to all athletes.

According to recent reports, what we gifted (and why): Winters in Colorado are long and cold, making training challenging. As a tri nerd, I think Emma-Kate will enjoy keeping up with her training indoors using the latest swim tech. While I don’t think ZWIM will keep her from the gym (I’m not sure anything could), I do think it will complement her training nicely to make the winter not feel so long.

Recent findings suggest that about the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): Naturally, when I read Mike Reilly’s book, Finding Your Finish Line, I thought of Tim. Reilly, also known as the “Voice of Ironman,” announced over 350,000 athletes across the finish line during his career as a race announcer before retiring in 2022. He, too, has seen it all, and some of his best tales are in this book. If I could get Tim and Mike in the same room to swap stories, it would probably be the best day of my triathlon career.

Reilly’s book, co-written with Triathlete contributor Sarah Wassner Flynn, is a masterful piece of storytelling. It’s inspirational, aspirational, and will leave you feeling proud to be a triathlete.

About the contributor: Susan is a board-certified sports dietitian, accomplished Ironman athlete and Kona qualifier, and runs her own business helping endurance athletes dial in their health and performance goals through their nutrition. She is our go-to writer whenever we need a sports nutrition concept or topic broken down in a way that triathletes can apply to their own training and racing.

According to recent reports, what we gifted (and why): I’ve been a long-time fan of Skratch Labs for its simple ingredients and clean flavors. When we saw Skratch now offers a make-it-yourself gel-making kit using its super high-carb sports drink mix, we thought the nutrition expert who literally wrote our guide on high-carb fueling might enjoy easily customizing her nutrition intake. More than the fueling customization, the kit also provides a less gooey gel texture and planet-friendly reusable soft flasks. I’m eager to hear how it works for her!

—Bethany Mavis, contributing editor.

About the contributor: When college student Saqib came on board as an intern in our Endurance department, the first question I had for this gangly cross-country runner was, “Have you done a triathlon?” The answer was no, and I am making it my life’s mission to change that.

What we gifted (and why): Did Saqib ask for resources on triathlon? He did not. In fact, he thinks of himself as a land animal and has no interest in swimming, which is why I’m gifting him this book from Triathlete contributor Alison Freeman – just to plant the seed. Isn’t that what holiday gifts are for, anyway? Subtle hints wrapped in shiny paper? I think of my brother-in-law, who always gifts his wife exercise equipment even though she is a couch potato; or my mother, who has given me countless hairstyling tools to tame my wild mane into something she deems more respectable.

In a recent development, but this book will actually serve its purpose, because Freeman has a real talent for making a big, scary goal like a first triathlon approachable and achievable. Her book is a start-to-finish roadmap that eliminates guesswork and leaves the reader feeling like they can not only do a triathlon, but also have fun along the way.

About the contributor: Jon Dorn is a former editor, longtime triathlete, and lifetime gear geek. He’s qualified for six age-group world championships, and loves to bust his butt training for long-course tri. If I hear about a cutting-edge piece of gear, an unconventional training method, or something that’s just plain weird, I call Jon. That stated, he’s not afraid to call a spade a spade and let me know if something is just pricey junk; he’s no fanboy.

According to recent reports, what we gifted (and why): I had heard about red light therapy in the context of the general health/beauty space for a few years, but it wasn’t until I was wandering the expo in Kona at this year’s Ironman World Championship that I encountered a red light therapy device that not only targeted triathletes but is also portable. Sadly, the one I checked out on the Significant Island was bonkers expensive and didn’t make sense for a gift, so I shopped around for something similar that wouldn’t break the bank. I landed on the reasonably priced Valo Spark that had decent reviews.

On one hand, I’m not 100% sold on the efficacy of red light therapy — and the science is still out on how it works with sports-related aches and pains — but I know Jon trains super hard (his next race is Boulder 70.3 in June), I know he has his share of aches and pains, I know he loves to travel, and I know he likes trying fresh things. Whether he loves it or uses it as a portable night light, I can’t wait to find out what he thinks!

The SP Force AXS is our flagship triathlon bike, with a full carbon fiber frame and bars, built with SRAM Force electronic shifting and Zipp 404 Firecrest Carbon wheels. If you want the best performance along with the best value in triathlon, now’s your chance. Our limited BFCM sale is live now.

Sources indicate that about the contributor: Arguably one of the most accomplished triathletes in Triathlete’s contributor lineup, with hundreds of triathlons and well over a dozen Ironmans under her belt, Jordan knows the sport from every perspective. She’s also one of the industry’s best-known and loved figures, representing professional athletes and helping brands grow their businesses.

Few people know the triathlon world better than Jordan, past or present. (She’s our first pick for a triathlon trivia team.) With her finger on the pulse, she gives pros and age-groupers a voice and digs into the stories shaping the sport.

Sources indicate that what we gifted (and why): Jordan might spend more time in the saddle than any of us editors, and she knows her gear as well as anyone, especially what the pros are presently using. While she’s currently on the road to recovery from a meniscus tear, we wanted to send her something custom and pro-level to test whether the 3D investment matches the marketing as she rebuilds her fitness on the bike.

In a recent development, but saddles are tricky to gift. Finding this fully adjustable, 3D-printed option gave us the versatility we were looking for: a fit she could fine-tune herself, without being limited to the stock setup straight out of the box.

—Travis Mundell, social media manager.

Sources indicate that about the contributor: Zach Nehr is another one of our key tech/gear editors, especially when it comes to indoor training. Blessed (or cursed) by living in the not-winter-compatible state of Wisconsin, Zach is a die-hard Zwifty and has used probably just about every indoor trainer or virtual training platform that exists (or has existed). As much as Zach rides inside, I trust that if he says something is great, it’s great; if it’s not, it’s probably in the dumpster. Because you don’t ride inside as much as he does with junk.

What we gifted (and why): The Profile Design Zwift Ride Supersonic Aerobar was a medium-quiet release during this year’s Hawaii Ironman World Championship week – mostly because you don’t think much about riding in the pain cave when you’re in a tropical paradise prepping for the biggest race of your season. As incongruous as the setting was for an indoor release, I was excited to see that Profile was taking its triathletes seriously by announcing the first-ever triathlon-specific Zwift-integrated aerobar for indoor training.

I wanted to gift this to Zach because if you dedicate enough time to training indoors, you should really dedicate your indoor training setup as well, not just make do. Being able to control your avatar from a dedicated set of Zwift Ride–compatible aerobars is the pinnacle of tri gear, as it completes the perfect pain cave: the kind that could prep you for next year’s Ironman World Championship, anyway.

About the contributor: When it comes to explaining sports psychology and neuroscience studies to triathletes, there’s no one better than Daya. As a neuroscientist, certified mental performance consultant, and yogi, Daya helps all types of athletes train their brains through her business, and she can make even the nerdiest psychology studies understandable and applicable for triathletes.

Industry observers note that what we gifted (and why): When we heard about the Muse Athena S Headband, a “brain-sensing headband,” we thought of Daya. The headband claims it can do everything from tracking your brainwave activity for better focus to tracking your blood oxygenation in the prefrontal cortex to help you build mental endurance. If anyone can sort through the science behind the Muse, it’s Daya, so we’re excited to hear how effective it seems to be in her own athletic performance.

#138193. Latest Update: Time Off Feet Will Change How You Think About Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1292 w)

Latest Update: Time Off Feet Will Change How You Think About Recovery

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress.
  • Now, as a Newly introduced York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training looks.
  • While time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that back when Kerri (Gallagher) Inman was training for professional track races, she told her coach that between runs she would be working as a waitress. Absolutely not, was his answer. “It’s not as if he would have assigned me a specific time off feet metric,” Inman says, “but my feet needed to rest, and being a waitress was too much time on feet for someone racing the way I did.”.

Now, as a Newly introduced York City-based TeamRunRun coach, Inman carefully considers her runners’ jobs when creating their training looks. For example, a nurse who is “always on her feet,” can’t have runs that overload her so much that she couldn’t keep training or working after a race, Inman says.

While time on feet is a metric that many coaches use to quantify a runner’s training volume, few of them use time off feet in a measurable way. “We do have an old saying, ‘Never stand when you can sit and never sit when you can lie down,’” states Will Baldwin, USATF and VDOT-certified running coach. Like any generalization, though, that rule isn’t very helpful.

Additionally, despite the many ways runners dig into their metrics and researchers look at small running form and running shoe discrepancies, there is little hard science regarding how much time off your feet you need and how you should best spend that time.

“Instead, you want to use comfort as your paradigm or framework on whether your recovery method is working for you,” says Jim Jastifer, MD, a fellowship-trained orthopedic surgeon specializing in foot and ankle reconstruction with OSMC Orthopedic and Sports Medicine Center in Indiana.

🏃🏻‍♀️The Runner’s World Guide to Recovery is your home for a smarter—from managing soreness and fatigue to easing back into running after a race, offseason, or injury.

In fact, “be comfortable” and “do what makes you happy” may be the best metrics for recovery, according to Jastifer. That’s because it’s not just your feet that need a break—so does your brain.

Are joy and time off feet really related? Turns out, they are. Kara Goucher, distance runner extraordinaire and cohost with Des Linden of the running podcast Nobody Asked Us, has her own way of making sure she gives herself enough time off feet.

Sources indicate that “I love playing Sudoku!” Goucher remarked on the pod, and she considers her game playing part of her rest and recovery. “It’s time off feet that really does calm my mind and it’s so much better for my brain and mental health than doom scrolling on my phone! It's time to reset my body and my mind.”.

In fact, according to the experts, your goal around recovery and time off feet should be to become self-aware of what your body needs, what your feet need (which may be different than what your larger muscles and soft tissues need), and what your brain needs.

It has been revealed that your feet may actually be the best way to determine how to spend your recovery time; your wearable likely doesn’t correlate its opinion of your recovery to the stress that your feet feel, Jastifer says. “If your Garmin says you’re ready to run, but your feet hurt, you should listen to your feet,” he adds.

Sources indicate that “Someone who is running 70/80/100 miles a week isn’t going to recover more by going for a walk,” notes Baldwin. This is precisely why Inman’s coach didn’t want her, a professional runner at the time, to add waitressing on top of her training schedule.

“Instead, I try to get my athletes to do low-level movement, such as time on the bike.” For his own time off feet, Baldwin saves his favorite shows to watch during these sessions so he has less mental taxation.

In a recent development, “Swelling and pain are really the only two reasons you absolutely need to stay off your feet,” states Baldwin. However, you’ll need to be aware of the difference between swelling due to injury and swelling that occurs simply because fluid has gone to your feet because of extensive motion.

Industry observers note that “Keeping your feet in motion can actually help swelling,” states Jastifer. Walking can stimulate the movement of blood and lymph (a fluid that carries nutrients to your blood and tissues), which can help recovery, but only if your feet aren’t fighting injury. Signs of injury include pain and discoloration.

Recent findings suggest that of course, you don’t always have to walk—or do anything with impact—to move your feet. Making circles, rolling a ball under them, or stretching them can reduce the swelling. Again, though, if you feel pain, stop and go to a doctor before you run again.

Percell Dugger, Runna run coach, suggests that you always consider rest and recovery within the context of your training plan, and, if your feet hurt, balance that important metric against the intensity and effort of a planned workout, even if it’s active recovery.

“In practice and by observation everyone recovers differently,” Inman indicates. “So, you want to be responsive to whether your feet are telling you they need to rest. If so, maybe get in a pool or get on a bike.”.

Even though there is no clear time or method for recovery, the most vital thing to do between runs is sleep and eat, advises Kristine Sweezey, PT, DPT, CSCS, a physical therapist in Rock Hill, South Carolina, and Charlotte, North Carolina.

Sources indicate that jastifer agrees, adding that rest, cross-training, and time off feet are not at all the same as sleeping. “They serve different functions,” he adds. Without sleep and proper nutrition, athletes cannot actually begin to recover. Moreover, any tricks or tools you use outside of sleep and proper fueling won’t add anything to the recovery equation without a commitment to the basics.

In a recent development, between sleep, time on feet, and time off feet, the experts recommend that you add foot strengthening to your routine. Because improving the abilities of your intrinsic foot muscles will help your feet cope with long and hard miles on the road. So, what are your intrinsic foot muscles? The small muscles that connect within your foot, but not to areas outside of it, such as your Achilles. The muscles in your toes and arch are intrinsic.

“By analogy, we have all the same muscles in our feet that we have in our hands, and while they aren’t significant from a force standpoint, they help regulate the force proprioception in ankle stability and are part of a neuromuscular feedback loop so you don’t have to think about how your feet land which will provide you with stability,” Jastifer notes. “If you have foot pain, it might be from these muscles.”.

Sweezey agrees and indicates you should do all the toe scrunches and toe lifts that you can. “I keep a lacrosse ball under my desk to roll around with my feet,” she says. “It helps decrease the soreness and flushes things out.”.

In a recent development, finally, when you are ready to get back on the road with your revived feet—whether it’s been a day or a week—make sure you don’t pair two long runs or speed workouts back-to-back, notes Dugger. “Progressive loading is better than high spikes and a dive.” If you and your feet (and your brain) need a break, don’t push too much on your next run.

Sources indicate that donna Raskin has had a long career as a health and fitness writer and editor of books and magazine articles. A certified run coach who has practiced yoga for many years, she also loves to lift weights, dance, and go for long walks with her hound dog, Dolly.

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers.
  • Sources indicate that the right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers. Besides being uncomfortable, numb hands can make it difficult to shift gears or feel your brake levers, turning a cold ride into a potentially unsafe one.

Sources indicate that the right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls. But finding that pair isn’t always as simple as checking the temperature rating on the packaging. How warm your hands get, the weather conditions, and the type of riding you do all play a role.

According to recent reports, for example, on a 35-degree road ride, you’ll likely want a much warmer glove than you would for a mountain bike ride at the same temperature. Higher speeds on the road mean more windchill, while a slower, harder effort on the trails can leave your hands sweaty in gloves that are too warm. If you ride throughout the winter, it’s worth owning a few different pairs to cover the range of conditions you’ll encounter.

I tested more than 40 glove models in temperatures ranging from the low 60s to below 20 degrees, then narrowed the field to my six favorites. I’ve included recommended temperature ranges for each, but consider those a starting point. If you tend to run cold or have Raynaud’s syndrome, you may want a warmer glove; if your hands sweat easily, a lighter, more breathable option might work better.

More Winter Gear Advice: Our Expert Swears by This Three-Layer Trick. ● The Best Men’s Winter Cycling Jackets ● The Best Winter Cycling Hats.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps my all-time favorite version of my all-time favorite glove, DeFeet’s Duraglove has been around for ages and has remained mostly unchanged. It’s very comfortable, has great dexterity, and provides good grip. Plus, it has touchscreen functionality. DeFeet offers two versions of this glove: The plain Duraglove ET and the Duraglove ET Wool Blend featured here, which uses a merino wool blend.

Sources indicate that I’ve found this version to be the warmer of the two. I’ve worn this glove into the low 40s during high-intensity rides and stayed comfortable. Because this knit glove is incredibly breathable, it’s still comfortable to wear as the day warms into the mid-to-high 50s. The Duraglove is unsuitable for rainy rides as its knit construction will rapidly soak up water.

These Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be as warm as they are. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no issues.

Industry observers note that they use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a big fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

Sources indicate that near-freezing temperatures with rain are probably the most challenging conditions to ride in. But for some, it’s unavoidable. Glacier Glove’s Ice Bay is as good as it gets for these conditions. It’s constructed with 2mm-thick, fleece-lined neoprene and is as waterproof as any piece of clothing could be.

These gloves have incredible dexterity given their warmth. The long cuff is easy to tuck under your rain jacket to keep water out. The downside of a neoprene glove is that it does not breathe at all. That’s partly how it keeps your hands warm, but it only works as long as you keep the gloves on. If you take them off, your now-sweaty hands will get quite cold quickly, and your formerly toasty gloves (lacking body heat) will be cold and wet with sweat. Despite these drawbacks, if it’s cold and rainy and I need to be out riding, these are the gloves I reach for.

Sources indicate that these pricey gloves are the warmest five-finger gloves I’ve tried that still let me move my fingers. Gore took inspiration from high alpine mountaineering for the design. The outer shell uses a Gore-Tex ePE liner that is highly wind- and water-resistant. For insulation, Gore used a PrimaLoft lining. It features one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios. All of this results in a glove that can be comfortable down to and below freezing, depending on your pace and specific riding conditions.

Industry observers note that I’ve used similarly warm gloves from other brands, and they've often been far too bulky to feel useful. These still maintain a good bar feel and let me freely articulate my fingers. While they have touchscreen compatibility, I found them a little too bulky to promptly type out a text message on an iPhone.

We’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

It has been revealed that the gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

The secret to the dexterity is the PrimaLoft Gold insulation, which provides exceptional warmth without adding bulk. Most very warm gloves are also very thick, which makes it difficult to locate the proper shifter and grip your brake levers. This pair keeps my hands warm on long weekend rides and daily commutes, even when temperatures dip below freezing, without getting in the way.

Bar Mitts may look unconventional, but riders who use them swear by their added warmth and control. Designed to work with gloves, these neoprene covers attach to your bar and enclose your bike’s shifters and brake levers. They add significant wind protection and help keep your hands shielded from the elements.

Several Bar Mitt variants are available for road, mountain, and townie-style handlebars. Be sure to check details and confirm fitment with your bar/shifter combo before you order.

Recent findings suggest that glove fit is subjective. They should fit in the Goldilocks range. If your gloves are too big, you risk losing grip on the handlebar and controls. But a glove that’s too tight can prevent you from comfortably grasping the handlebar or grips.

It has been revealed that an easy way to spot a glove that’s too big is if you have a lot of fabric bunching in your palm. It’s always worth trying upcoming gloves on your bike to see how they feel on the bars, since labeled sizing can differ from brand to brand.

If you’re riding in temperatures below the mid-40s or closer to freezing, you want a glove with some insulation. In the most basic definition, insulation is filling used to capture and hold onto warmth. The most familiar insulation for outdoor use is down, often found in puffy jackets. In gloves, you are most likely to find down in very bulky mittens, which are very warm but lack the dexterity for cycling.

Recent findings suggest that most cycling-specific gloves use synthetic insulation from companies like Polartech or PrimaLoft. These materials are most often used on the back of the hand to protect from wind and minimize interference with the handlebar feel. Thin, grippy material is generally found on the palm. Many brands use leather on the palms for improved grip and durability, so watch out for this if you avoid buying animal products.

For the interior of the glove, look for polyester or Merino wool. You want something that wicks sweat and keeps your hands dry—sweaty hands can rapidly turn into frozen prunes.

It has been revealed that gloves with appropriate breathability for the temperature and your riding effort keep your hands warm and dry. The warmer the temps, or the higher your effort, the more breathable you’ll want your gloves.

In a recent development, regionally, humidity also plays a part in selecting the right glove. If you ride somewhere cool and dry, such as Colorado, where it might be in the 30s with low humidity, you likely will be able to use a lighter pair of more breathable gloves. These can do a much better job keeping you warm because they transfer moisture away from your hands more effectively. If you ride in the Northeast, the same pair of gloves might feel too cold at the same temperature, since humidity is often much higher. For these conditions, you’ll want a glove with better wind and waterproofing at the expense of breathability.

Once you figure out the glove warmth you need for your riding, consider other features before buying. Something I find very important in gloves meant for frigid weather is long cuffs. Cuffs make it easy to tuck the glove under or sometimes over your jacket sleeve, keeping your wrists warm and stopping cold air from entering your jacket.

It has been revealed that the palm construction of a glove is also worth careful examination. A common feature is padding. Some riders prefer padded gloves, while others do not. Padding matters less the warmer a glove gets, since the palm becomes bulkier with insulation. For thinner gloves, a seamless palm is the way to go. It minimizes any chance of irritation and improves handlebar feel.

If you ride with a smartphone or have a touchscreen computer, gloves that interact with these devices are great. The less you need to remove your gloves in the cold, the happier your hands will be.

Finally, a soft, large terrycloth nose-wipe section (preferably along the thumb or index finger) is good if you’re a heavy snotter.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Latest York City bike messenger but swiftly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

Save Massive Without Sacrificing Comfort With These Editor-Tested Running Shoes Under $130

📅 30 Oct 2018 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Editor’s Note, November 19, 2026: Black Friday sales are in full swing.
  • Sources indicate that “All you need is a pair of shoes to start running” isn’t exactly truthful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 19, 2026: Black Friday sales are in full swing. Several of our already low-priced trainers are discounted for as high as 30% off, including our Best Overall, the Latest Balance 680v9.

Sources indicate that “All you need is a pair of shoes to start running” isn’t exactly truthful. If you hate your toenails and heels, by all means, wear Converse high-tops. A good pair of running shoes will spare your digits and the skin on your feet—but that doesn’t mean you have to drop cash on expensive trainers.

Recent findings suggest that cheap running shoes, models less than $130, are a respectable choice for beginners and vets wanting to save. From plush to moderately cushioned, we’ve listed affordable running shoes on this list that’ll help you save up for more run gear, like a fancy GPS watch or that next destination race.

Sources indicate that to find the best shoes under $130, we performed comprehensive research on top-rated trainers by well-known brands, and called in shoes for our shoe program testers and staff to evaluate. These shoes were vetted by scrutinizing fit, ride, and comfort. To give you both options, we included our premium recommendation for each shoe from our Best Running Shoes buying guide, just in case you want to spend some extra cash.

🏃 For even more choices, head to The Best Running Shoes of 2026.

We also spoke with Footwear Buyer Jon Notary, who works at the local running store Aardvark Sports Shop in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. Notary provides insight on what you’re compromising on when buying cheap shoes, and gives advice on what to look for when you’re out shopping for your next pair.

Recent findings suggest that buying an affordable trainer doesn’t necessarily mean subpar features. Brands will sometimes incorporate “old” technology into these shoes, like midsole foams, to mitigate a high price. But you are sacrificing some premium specs, like plush cushioning and more durable materials.

Below is a comparison chart of our Best Overall budget trainer, the Newly introduced Balance Fresh Foam 680v9, versus the brand’s premium daily trainer, the Fresh Foam X 880v15. The latter has the next generation of Fresh Foam, Fresh Foam X, and more cushioning. You save almost half the money with the 680v9, but you get what you paid for with the 880v15.

Industry observers note that the 680v9 is still a reliable shoe for everyday runs and light workouts. If you’re an efficient runner (you don’t wear down your shoes’ soles faster than the average runner), you may even get more mileage out of the 680v9s. It comes down to what you’re willing to give up and what you’re willing to spend.

All the trainers on this list are Best Value material, but the 680v9 deserves the title for its consistency with each patch. Though not as plush or responsive as, say, the more expensive 1080 or 880, the 680 still encapsulates Upcoming Balance’s soft-cushioned feel, absorbing shock and promoting comfort on every run.

Sources indicate that its Fresh Foam midsole provides a supportive, plush, lightweight ride, making the 680v9 an excellent choice as an everyday trainer that can handle base-building mileage. A breathable, cozy upper makes this a comfy running shoe and great for casual wear, as well.

Recent findings suggest that 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best Value Shoe → Latest Balance Ellipse (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com.

You can’t go wrong with the Launch 12 for a speed shoe, especially when it has DNA Flash v2, the foam featured in the Hyperion Elite 4. The nitrogen-infused supercritical foam is lightweight and responsive; it provides plenty of pop for fast workouts on the road and track.

One drawback, at least for runners with wide feet, is that the midfoot area is quite narrow.

Sources indicate that “No matter how many times I loosened and re-laced my shoes, it always felt too tight through the midfoot area, causing some noticeable discomfort,” stated RW editor Ashley Tysiac. “While I can appreciate its secure fit, I think this system could have been reimagined to be a bit more forgiving in that area to provide more comfort.”.

Despite her distaste for the Launch 12’s tightness, she praised the shoe’s lightweight and responsiveness. Tysiac found the shoe’s simplicity refreshing in our max-cushioned era of trainers.

“I think the weight of the shoe is the best part, as it’s very light yet provides a pretty stable ride,” she said. “That made it the perfect shoe for runs where I wanted to pick up the pace a bit without being dragged down by heavy shoes, and even a good option for those recovery days when I still wanted to feel light on my feet while running at a slower pace.”.

It has been revealed that 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best Overall Shoe → Adidas Adizero Evo SL (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com.

The GT-1000 15 provides stability without overbearing, rigid foam pieces, or a high price tag. The shoe has Asics’s 3D Guidance System, which uses a broader platform and reshaping in the heel and forefoot to help with inward foot rolling.

The shoe has high-abrasion Ahar rubber that can withstand aggressive gait patterns and provide reliable traction on slippery surfaces and sharp corners. The fit is slightly narrower than past models, so you may want to size up.

The shoe is also great for long runs thanks to its PureGel tech and FF Blast midsole; you’ll have a soft ride that absorbs impact.

According to recent reports, 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best Stability Shoe → Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26 (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Recent findings suggest that the FloatZig 2 looks bulky with its unconventional, zigzag midsole rim around the shoe. But we found it surprisingly lightweight during testing. Its soft cushioning—that midsole isn’t just for looks—provided a supportive bed for testers’ feet.

“What I found most enjoyable about this shoe was how lightweight and balanced it is,” said tester Mike Parmer. “The fit and comfort allowed longer training runs and no sore feet or toes. This shoe is one of the better shoes I have tested recently and would compare equally to Hoka.”.

The Superfloat+ midsole promotes high energy return, giving a much-needed boost when the road feels long.

👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Shock Absorption Shoe → New Balance 1080v15 (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at reebok.com | Shop Women’s at reebok.com.

Anta proves you can have premium cushioning on a budget. The PG7 3 has an incredibly plush feel, making the shoe versatile for easy runs, long runs, and casual wear. The cushioning stays soft and also supportive, allowing you to run hard and fast.

In my runs in the PG7 3, I’ve found the ride and feel comparable to the Saucony Triumph and Brooks Glycerin.

Recent findings suggest that “Budget shoes always feel cheap,” said Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “There’s an undeniable compromise you have to make to pay less. And that stinks. In this case, the PG7 doesn’t really feel like it’s holding anything back. It’s comfortable, cushioned, and supportive. It’s going to work as a daily driver for a lot of runners.”.

In a recent development, 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Long Runs Shoe → Nike Structure Plus (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Though the C202 7 costs the most on this list, it’s more than worth the $130 price. Compared to racing shoes that are upward of $200, the C202 7 has a full-length carbon-fiber plate sandwiched in its midsole of DAN cushioning, a TPU supercritical foam.

The shoe feels snappy and responsive. And it has good traction too. Furrer tested the shoe during a rainy 5K in San Antonio, Texas. While other competitors wiped out on slick turns, Furrer stayed vertical cutting corners and accelerating on waterlogged sidewalks and muddy dividers.

Sources indicate that 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Racing Marathons Shoe → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s).

Trail running demands a lot from your shoes. Between the hard-charging descents and scraping against rough rocks, the last thing you want is a cheap, flimsy shoe that won’t hold up. The Saucony Excursion TR17 has Versarun, which absorbs impact and provides comfy cushioning over trail debris.

One knock is the shoe is quite heavy, and it runs a little small and narrow, so consider sizing up and trying on the wide version.

All models of the Excursion TR17 have 4.5mm lugs to keep you on your toes when things get dicey.

Recent findings suggest that 👟 Want to go premium? Try our Best for Trails Shoe → Hoka Speedgoat 7 (Men’s/Women’s).

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

According to Notary, the two main sacrifices you make when buying cheaper running shoes are comfort and longevity. That doesn’t mean you’re stuck with choosing uncomfortable shoes when you’re searching for cheaper pairs. It just means you have to do the extra, er, footwork, when considering more affordable shoes.

Sources indicate that notary notes the materials are not as premium or as durable. “That being said, the industry does benefit from what I call the technology trickle-down; many of the materials on lower priced models were once used on a ‘fancier’ one.” For example, the Brooks Launch 12 has DNA Flash v2 foam which was used in its Hyperion Elite super shoes.

According to recent reports, “A lower cost shoe will use older foams and fabrics, possibly less outsole, or no outsole, and less involved construction techniques. All of those realities typically lead to less overall comfort than what else is at the moment available,” indicates Notary. A cheaper shoe will be comfortable, it just won’t have the same max plush and support of a top-shelf trainer.

Notary claims comfort is king. “If it feels heavy, stiff, and firm in the store, don’t expect that to change. Conversely, if it feels hyper-light, super flexible, and marshmallowy soft, there is a good chance it won’t be as durable.”.

It has been revealed that perhaps you’re leaning toward one end of the spectrum of cushioning or somewhere in the middle. The best way to find if a cheap shoe—or any running shoe—is right for you is to try it on first and go for a test run in the store. Some shoe stores allow you to run on the sidewalk or on a treadmill to see if the shoe’s a good fit.

In a recent development, cheap running shoes have a shorter shelf life. “Because the materials are less premium they typically break down faster even when they’re not being worn,” says Notary. “This isn’t always true and is somewhat of a generalization, but higher grade materials generally offer more durability. If we’re considering mileage, a lower-cost shoe typically yields fewer miles.”.

Notary adds, however, that some of the most expensive running shoes on the market right now, i.e., super shoes or shoes with a carbon plate, also have a shorter mileage life, which is another thing to put in perspective.

According to recent reports, we took pains not to include discounted models on this list but shouldn’t be overlooked when buying running shoes. In some cases, the differences between last season and the current season are unnoticeable.

When the Price Is Too Good to Be True.

In a recent development, beware of dupes on sites like Amazon. A usually expensive model slapped with a too-good-to-be-true price tag is probably just that. The model in question likely isn’t the shoe promised, is poorly made, and could cause injury due to poor quality materials. Check the seller to see it’s from the actual brand (and make sure it’s not someone posing as a well-known brand).

It has been revealed that for models by lesser known brands, Notary gives us some pointers when choosing running shoes. “Things to look for are a rubber outsole and a removable footbed/liner,” he indicates. “These are two quick check aspects of a viable running shoe. Also, look for fewer sewn overlays on the upper, more will only cause problems with flexibility and add excessive weight to the shoe.”.

Will cheap running shoes make me run slower?

In general, a cheaper shoe will not have as much pop or energy return as a more expensive one which in theory should make it slower. Lower cost shoes will likely lack plating or supercritical foams found in today’s ‘fastest’ shoes. However, a lot depends on how comfortably the shoe moves with you. Some of the ‘fastest’ shoes on the market today don’t agree with my body’s mechanics, and I find them slower than more conventional shoes in my rotation.

Are cheap running shoes a good choice for fresh runners?

According to recent reports, in my world, any shoe that gets someone running is a good choice. That mentioned, a well-fitting, comfortable technical running shoe will have a much better chance of keeping a upcoming runner in the sport.

It has been revealed that it’s a shame that with so much great and relatively affordable product available, many people start the sport in the wrong shoe and quit, never knowing a different reality exists for them. Unfortunately the ‘running shoe’ category is a bit of a catch-all, and there are plenty of shoes categorized as ‘running’ that have no place being labeled as such.

How old can a past shoe model be for it to be ok to run in?

It has been revealed that unworn shoes will definitely lose some cushioning after about two to five years due to oxidization, which hardens the midsole foam. Glue also weakens over time, increasing the risk of delamination in shoes that have been sitting around a while, primarily between the upper and the midsole and the midsole and the outsole. They can be used, sure, but they won’t have the typical 300 to 500 mile range of usability nor the comfort of a ‘fresher’ pair.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

What the Full Moon in Gemini Means for You

It has been revealed that gemini is the sign of the twins, ruled by the planet Mercury and the element of air. In a recent development, the twins also represent duality. Gemini reminds us that we are complex, that we can hold two feelings at once, and that life is rarely black or white. There are shades of gray everywhere, and within that uncertainty exists endless possibility.
