#138150. Industry News: An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3990 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: An Unimaginable Tragedy Took Her Children. They’re the Reason She Keeps Running—No Matter How Much It Hurts.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running.
  • Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world.
  • According to recent reports, erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story was originally published in June 2021.

According to recent reports, there are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.

Karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.

According to recent reports, erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.

In a recent development, karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she claims. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.

She thinks about Reagan and Grant.

On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that plan, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.

The trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.

On the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.

It has been revealed that he’s killing my kids, she mentioned, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.

Her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? Why didn’t she race to her car and drive 190 miles an hour to reach them? She can’t explain. She only kept rocking back and forth, back and forth. The next thing she remembers is her uncle walking through the front door. He kneeled beside her and whispered in her ear, “They’re gone.”.

It was her best friend, Brandy, who got her running. Brandy was once a lost teenager who shot up heroin; now she’d become a sober woman who found release through her body in motion, and she wanted Karen to find it too.

She did, but often it felt like anguish. She muttered and cussed and yelled. This is stupid. It hurts. Why am I doing this? Karen didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer. She ran a half marathon less than a year after the tragedy, a full marathon the next.

Sources indicate that still, the grief escalated. The shock and adrenaline wore off after two years, leaving a fathomless despair. One night in May 2018, she laid out hydrocodone, Valium, and Xanax. The strategy was to wash them down with vodka and wine and not wake up.

Sources indicate that her memory of that night is spotty, but she remembers looking at a picture of Reagan and Grant. She was desperate, sobbing. She did not want to die, but she could not understand what she was doing on Earth without them. I need you to intervene, she begged them. Soon after, she remembers getting a text from a cousin checking in on her, then another cousin, then a friend, then her sister. Karen took it as a sign. She threw away the pills.

Industry observers note that two weeks later, her father checked her into a residential treatment center outside Nashville that specialized in trauma. It was a serene place, acres of rolling pasture, and Karen spent hours on the wooded trail out back, running. Some people who lose their children don’t make it. Alcohol and drugs take them; the suicide rate is higher than average. Eventually Karen came to accept that if she died, then Reagan and Grant died with her, and she couldn’t let them die twice.

She discovered the trail at Erwin Park after returning home to North Texas. Over the next two years her race distances ramped up promptly, from 50 miles to 100K. Karen, who had once made fun of Brandy’s cracked and blistered feet, was now the one peeling off toenails, running her fingers over the watery bubble of a blister. The fifth anniversary of her children’s death was the first time she ran 100 miles. As the hours went by, she checked her watch, trying to place each of her children’s last moments. This is when he was pouring the gas, this is when he texted.

According to recent reports, she could feel Reagan and Grant on that trail. She always does. A cardinal fluttering past, a heart shape in the stumps of the trees, a pair of blue jays—they’re reminders that although she lost her children, they are with her still. Reagan and Grant are the reasons to keep going—not just over the 100 miles, but in the life she is still figuring out how to live.

Recent findings suggest that karen Sparks had a different life once. She was 25 when she met David Small at the mortgage organization where they worked. A clean, good-looking man, a real charmer. He was eight years older. She liked the salt-and-pepper hair, the goatee. She was wearing pink corduroy pants and a floral top that day; he complimented the outfit. Karen needed compliments. Ever since adolescence—the glasses, the braces—she’d struggled with a sense that she was not pretty enough, not thin enough. Not enough.

It has been revealed that karen already had a boyfriend and kept a photo of him at her desk. “He won’t be that for long,” David told her. “I’ll have you.” She laughed, because obviously that was a joke. A bit arrogant, too, though she liked the feeling of being coveted. He was smirking, a micro-movement that struck her then as benign.

To understand why Karen fell so hard for David Small, it helps to understand how badly she wanted to escape. Garden-variety teenage rebellion had escalated fast. She’d been a cheerleader and athlete, the daughter of a charismatic high school football coach who became the principal, but in her 20s, she watched Brandy rope off her arm with a rubber tube and plunge a needle into a vein. Around that time, Karen was arrested for drunk driving. She knew she needed to find a better path.

And she did, but she didn’t. She traded the nice boyfriend for the charming bad boy at the office. She’d dropped out of college, which was probably a mistake, and the working world had been a series of dull cubicle gigs. More than anything, she wanted a family. She wanted to be a wife and a stay-at-home mother. Motherhood felt like a purpose. She’d never been a star student or athlete, but she had heart. She was the kid on the team who got the “hardest worker” award. And maybe because her own father had been so powerful, she believed that marrying David could give her those things.

Her mother didn’t like the guy, but Karen’s father urged his wife to give him the benefit of the doubt. Duke Sparks is a Santa Claus of a man, big laugh, big smile. The eldest of 10, with an alcoholic dad, he raised his siblings. Maybe his mistake—he thinks about this all the time—is that he couldn’t stop saving his daughter. Whatever she wanted, he gave it to her, so when she fell for this man, he wasn’t going to stand in her way. When she asked for the fairy-tale wedding, he gave it to her, even though $30,000 was a chunk of change for a school administrator and his schoolteacher wife.

She bought the gown at one of those big bridal warehouses. Silver-ivory beads embroidered on the straight corset, a long flowy bottom like a princess at a ball. She took bridal photos in front of black-eyed Susans at a Dallas park that was popular with brides-to-be. She sits on the lawn with a tiara nestled in her brown beachy waves, the diamond ring with three bands fitting together like interlocking puzzle pieces conspicuous on her finger as she rests her cheek in her palm. Karen doesn’t recognize the 27-year-old woman in that picture. It’s like she’s wearing a mask.

The newlyweds moved to a one-story in McKinney, about a half hour north of Dallas, and then a two-story a little farther north in the small town of Van Alstyne. In 2006 she had a baby girl named Reagan, and 17 months later a baby boy named Grant, and the way those two came into the world was the way they walked through it: Reagan swift and bold, Grant taking his time, circumspect. Reagan was Karen’s mini-me. The girl of a thousand smiles, with a smattering of freckles. She was a gymnast who loved to climb the walls, climb the refrigerator, climb anything. The summer before the fire, Reagan learned the backstroke and Grant had just gotten comfortable in the pool. Out on the field, though, he was a heck of a ballplayer. He was very particular about his clothes—everything had to match—and had a thing for neons. Those two loved tricking their grandfather into eating Sour Patch Kids. They’d promise him the candy wasn’t sour—definitely not sour, no way was it sour—then when he popped one into his mouth and his face puckered, they’d fall to the floor laughing. They were happy kids. The marriage was rocky, surely they heard things, but Karen is pretty sure they were happy.

In a recent development, david had trouble keeping a job, though. He had trouble keeping the electricity on, keeping the mortgage paid. In a word, he had trouble. He pawned her ring shortly after Grant was born. Karen sat on the steps of their lease-to-own home, weeping. How could this happen? We have to make sacrifices, that’s what he said. He promised it would never happen again, but it just kept happening. Karen’s credit card started getting declined. David once bought the kids scooters for Christmas, only to pawn them. He kept the car parked in the back to keep it from repo men.

After the fire, Karen visited the house. She had to retrace the steps, witness the damage with her own eyes. She pulled back the canvas that investigators had draped over the carpet in the master bathroom. She had to see it: The silhouettes of her children’s bodies, soot outlining their final positions like sidewalk chalk. Some mothers never want to go back, she gets it, but she needed this. What also stands out from that visit is the enormous engagement photo of her in that wedding dress. Flames had licked the canvas, so the picture-perfect image had crackled and turned blister-black.

Why did you stay? Karen could torture herself with this until the end of time if she wanted to. Did you ever think he was capable of such wickedness? Of course not! He never hit her. He never hit the children, never even threatened it. No drinking problem, no drug addiction, no gambling, as far as she can tell. But when Karen scans for warning signs, she thinks about his charm. The subtle manipulation, gaslighting, coercion. How many serial killers, how many con men, how many two-bit criminals get described this way by some innocent bystander? He was so nice, so good-looking, so charming. David’s favorite movies were The Talented Mister Ripley and Catch Me if You Can. So yeah, that was a clue.

Recent findings suggest that some signs were more obvious, especially to people who weren’t Karen. Her sister trailed him twice to see if he was going to work. (He wasn’t.) Though their memories of the incident are foggy, Karen remembers that her sister tried to show her a photo of him meeting another woman. Karen couldn’t hear it. David loved her. He loved their kids. Karen had gone on antidepressants for postpartum depression after Grant was born, and she wonders if the meds kept her hazy.

Recent findings suggest that also, Karen did not quit things. The little girl who got “hardest worker” trophies would not give up on her marriage so easily. Resilience would be her strength, and her undoing.

It was her father who finally convinced her to leave. Duke had run a background check and found David had an outstanding arrest warrant for unpaid traffic tickets. He called his daughter from the football field. He’s driving around with your kids, he told her. If they arrest him, they’re taking those kids to social services.

That startled Karen. Reagan was 9. Grant was 8. Her instinct to protect them overrode any fear of leaving.

It has been revealed that she pulled David into the bathroom one night so they could talk in private. The bathroom had a worn brown carpet that led to a walk-in closet. She leaned against the countertop with the double sink and spoke in a voice more defeated than angry. This was over. No fighting. His voice was calm, too. I’m sorry, baby. I’ll fix it, baby.

According to recent reports, the fire began in the garage. He’d poured gasoline through the house, dousing the walls, dousing the furniture. The investigators had never seen so much gas. The children lay on the carpet inside the master bathroom where he and Karen had stood just a month before, when she’d told him it was over.

How he kept the kids compliant is a mystery. No drugs were found in their system, no sign of struggle. The children were arranged the way they usually slept, Reagan on her side, Grant on his tummy. David’s body was curled in a ball at the back of the closet, holding down one of the dogs. That sorry coward had placed his kids closest to the flame.

In a recent development, karen had finally left him on October 19. Her attorney had recommended that she go without warning, so she moved the kids to her parents’ place. After David was served divorce papers, he told her he didn’t see it coming. He just didn’t think his wife would do this.

“You got me,” he texted her that day.

She shot back, “I learn from the best.”.

Halloween had been his first weekend alone with the kids. Karen saw no reason to punish him, even though he seemed to be punishing her. He took Reagan and Grant trick-or-treating, but he didn’t send one photo to Karen of them in their costumes.

Sources indicate that then came Sunday, November 1, 2015. He started texting her at 6 a.m. Are you coming to church with us?

Sources indicate that was he kidding? No, she wasn’t going to church with them. She wasn’t playing “happy family” anymore.

The texts kept coming, all morning long. I need to talk to you. There’s something I need to tell you. Her family told her to ignore him. Do not go back, it’s a trap. Karen had gone back so many times. She stayed firm. The texts stopped around noon.

Her mind runs alternate scenarios of what might have happened if she’d gone that day, and though she’ll never know, she believes he would have killed her. She thinks he wanted to take them all down together. Instead, he took her children, the pets, most of her belongings, her unshakable faith in God, nearly everything she had, and left her the lone survivor.

According to recent reports, from what Karen can piece together, it seems his proposal was to blow up the house, leaving nothing but ashes. But the trail of fire never reached the master bathroom. The bodies did not burn. Cause of death, carbon monoxide poisoning and smoke inhalation. Karen hates the phrase “at least”—at least you got them for nine years, at least you were a mother for a while—but this part really is an at least. He’d left a suicide note. Some nonsense about seeing her in heaven. How long had he been plotting this? Some answers she’ll never get.

According to recent reports, was he unstable? Clearly. Narcissistic sociopath turned psychopath, that’s her best guess. Karen has spent the past five-plus years puzzling out the question of why, and she hasn’t gotten far. Part of her trauma therapy at the treatment center was reenacting that day, placing herself in the scene she never entered in real life, a technique known as psychodrama. The benefit was profound, but it never gave her the “why.” There is no word in the English language for a mother who loses her children, the way there is for widows and orphans. It’s like language itself cannot admit the possibility.

Industry observers note that the fourth year was even harder than the first three. Grief kept amplifying. She got tattoos. Their names on her outer left forearm. Their birth dates in Roman numerals on her inner right wrist. Angel wings on her ankles, which she got with another mother who’d lost her kids. And on the tender ivory of her inner bicep, the phrase that has become her motto: Love never ends. She dyed her hair magenta and started painting her nails in bright neons. The look is a bit out there for a 43-year-old woman in small-town Texas, but the wildness fits her soul, and she likes to think her kids are proud. She believes they see her the same way she sees them.

Sources indicate that on November 1, 2020, Karen ran the 100 miles by herself, but she wasn’t alone. People had flocked to support her. One woman ran alongside her for 50 miles. Another flew in from Indiana to crew. Karen didn’t even know some of these people. But they had heard her story and wanted to help. At pit stops, her coach and his wife massaged her feet. It felt nearly Biblical. Her feet. Her dad was there from beginning to end, sleeping in his truck at night.

Industry observers note that karen had never seen a pit crew hustle so hard; it felt like NASCAR. They changed her clothes, popped her blisters, fed her when her stomach could take it. Pringles, PB&J sandwiches, ice-cold Coca-Cola. Her favorite was mashed potatoes and ramen. Sounds disgusting, but it went down smooth and easy as night fell.

In a recent development, somewhere in the dark, she started to hallucinate. The trees came alive. They turned into fairyland creatures, with swooping limbs and kind faces. Karen was Little Red Riding Hood, running from the Major Bad Wolf. She was Katniss Everdeen, an ordinary girl who never asked to be a hero. The sun came up, she scarfed down pancakes and syrup, and she could see the faces of the people who indicated up for her, and the feeling was golden.

Around mile 70, she started to crumble. She broke down when she briefly couldn’t find her dad at the pit stop. Duke wondered if it was time for his daughter to call it quits, but he knew her better than that. She would crawl to the end if she had to, but she would finish.

It has been revealed that it took Karen 31 hours to complete the run, an hour longer than planned. She beat herself up about the extra time until her team reminded her that what she’d done was harder than most races, not just because of the personal stakes but because she couldn’t feed off the energy of other runners, spectators, all those passing people. Even Karen had to admit: One woman, 100 miles. It was a triumph.

Recent findings suggest that karen had never wanted this. She only wanted to be a mom. But this loss summoned a strength she didn’t know she had. Back in her previous life, she did not have the courage to stand on her own. This part is confusing, it fills her eyes with tears, because losing Reagan and Grant was the worst thing that had ever happened to her—but it also made her more like the woman she wanted to be.

Recent findings suggest that she’s working on a memoir with her sister, and she plans to keep racing. Another 100-miler in October, a 200-miler after that; her dream is the Moab 240. Reminders of her loss never go away. Kids playing on a jungle gym. An empty swing. The memories can bring a smile, or they can bring a tear. She has learned to live with both: happy and sad, furious and grateful, lucky and cursed. Sixty-eight months. That’s how long it’s been since her world split open. Every first day of the month marks another notch in that marathon.

Sources indicate that most people want to outrun emotional pain. Not Karen. She runs into the pain. “Run toward the roar” is a line she read in a book about grief, and it’s why she can tell this story to a stranger in a cozy cafe, because she’s learned that sharing the pain is a better path. Allowing herself to be angry and difficult and complicated and hurt, swiping away tears and muttering cuss words only to apologize because she knows this is for a magazine—that’s better than pretending.

It will tell you about her spirit, and the radiance of this woman who never asked for any of this, that as she tells the worst story of her life, a man stops to comment on her smile. Another man stops, an hour later, to compliment her hot pink nails. In other parts of the world, and to other women, such comments might not go over well, but Karen flashes that smile. “It’s them,” she states, finger pointing upward, and maybe that’s true. It’s also true her smile was here before they were. And though she will never stop running for Reagan and Grant, maybe one day she will run for herself. It’s the next step.

The Real Grand Theft

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Everything has a price, and I think the cost of Grand Theft Auto 6 — the much-anticipated sixth installment of one of the most successful video games in history — is far too high.
  • Triathletes know all about expensive things: Tri bikes now start around $3,000 and rise (rapidly) up from there; running shoes now routinely crack $200; and now we’ve got $270 swim caps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor-in-chief Chris Foster on why Grand Theft Auto 6 costs more than you think (Photo: Donald Miralle/Getty Images).

Everything has a price, and I think the cost of Grand Theft Auto 6 — the much-anticipated sixth installment of one of the most successful video games in history — is far too high.

And I’m not talking about the cost to your wallet.

Triathletes know all about expensive things: Tri bikes now start around $3,000 and rise (rapidly) up from there; running shoes now routinely crack $200; and now we’ve got $270 swim caps. And don’t even get me started on entry fees — the 2026 Hawaii Ironman World Championship, for instance, topped $1,800, granted that’s easily our sport’s crown jewel, but even a upcoming event like 70.3 Utah still rings in around $500.

And even once you factor in the hard out-of-pocket expenses for equipment, entry fees, pool access, coaching, travel, accommodations, and so on, there’s still that looming cost of your time.

If a midpack triathlete did our most popular 70.3 training proposal, they’d spend about 150 hours of training over the 20-week plan. For our 16-week Olympic-distance plan, a triathlete would rack up about 65 hours of training. That’s a pretty significant chunk of life, but I know I’m preaching to the choir, as all triathletes know that our sport requires a big time commitment.

It has been revealed that however, there’s good news: We know that much of that time can be spent outside; we know that — when done correctly — swimming, biking, and running are very healthy endeavors; and we know that much of that time can be spent with others. To that last point, for better or for worse, even just the act of going to a race forces us to participate within a community.

In a digital world that competes ferociously for our attention (think: social media, TV, AI, and so on), giving your precious and valuable attention — your time — to swimming, biking, running, and triathlon will do more for your physical and mental health than getting hooked and strung out on a screen for hours.

So it’s here, in the obsession over the release of GTA 6, that as the leader of an outdoor-related title — and within the context of an era of critically dangerous social disconnection and physical isolation — I find myself confused about why the larger culture is celebrating the creation of something that will drain our attention and time like a dystopian plug in the back of a Matrix battery-person’s skull. I just can’t celebrate.

Recent findings suggest that on one hand, a video game centered on crime and violence is probably more of a sign of the times than a cause for rising crime rates in real life. I’ll succumb to a little bit of Qoheleth-level despair recognizing here that “what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing upcoming under the sun.”.

It has been revealed that and of course this is an outdoor sports publication, not Morality Weekly, but I still can’t shake another quote from the bestselling book of all time: “The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness.”.

Sources indicate that GTA 6’s content notwithstanding, from my position in outdoor/endurance sports, I certainly can’t quite abide when our culture treats the release of a video game like a high holy holiday. Especially when it comes at such a high cost.

Set aside the hard price tag of a gaming console and game (let’s say less than $1k), which is actually relatively low compared to a hobby like triathlon, and keep your eyes fixed on the time cost and quality.

Industry observers note that experts from IGN note that Grand Theft Auto 6 took their editors between 42 and 115 hours to complete the new release. It’s probably a good guess that the average gamer would spend 80ish hours to noodle around in that virtual environment. That’s a lot of “life spend.”.

And unlike many other video games, it’s time spent, well…alone.

GTA 6 has no multiplayer mode as of this writing (though it could come). This means there’s no opportunity to connect with other people — even remotely — during gameplay. You can’t commit crimes alongside your buddies in the living room; you can’t fire at police alongside friends in Sweden, Hong Kong, or France. You’re alone, for 60 hours, stealing cars and shooting people. You interact only with that world and the characters coded into it.

Now I won’t be entirely obtuse here — not everyone can physically train for a triathlon; not everyone has time or safe access to a place where they can spend 65-150 hours outdoors, even if they wanted to.

However, there is a large proportion of people whose time spent playing a video game (alone) will prevent them from being outside (with others) — moving their bodies through nature in some way, shape, or form.

That’s why, rather than relish the empty streets and bike paths that have been reported across major metropolitan areas this week, I’ll be hoping that once the game ends and the credits roll (do video games have credits?), folks will head back outside to get a refund for time better spent.

Industry News: 5 Yoga Poses to Get You Through Any Holiday Gathering

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If leaving isn’t an option—just kidding, we know you probably want to be there—there are ways to find grounding and calm within your own being.
  • According to recent reports, these yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva).

In a recent development, certain seasons come with a lot, and we mean a lot, of socializing. On the one hand, this means a chance to spend quality time with family and friends, which is always a win. But if you deal with any amount of social anxiety, gatherings can also come with stress and general overwhelm.

If leaving isn’t an option—just kidding, we know you probably want to be there—there are ways to find grounding and calm within your own being. You can practice breathwork, take a walk, even excuse yourself and enjoy a yoga pose or two for a minute. Or, if you resonate with the asanas on this list, perhaps five!

According to recent reports, these yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible. Escape for a few moments to try one of the more involved poses or enjoy a super subtle modification mid-party!

Recent findings suggest that holiday gatherings tend to involve a fair amount of standing around—which is where your casual Tree Pose (Vrksasana) comes in. Popping one foot up—whether against your upper or lower leg or, more stealthily, your ankle—can be done at literally any time: while you’re doing the dishes, chatting with loved ones, or experiencing a lull in activity. The reminder that you’re in control of your sense of balance can help you feel steadier on your own two feet in all ways.

Social gatherings can feel all over the place, making grounding of all kinds welcome. Sinking into Squat (Malasana) calls for strength and stability. And though households all over the world perform chores and even eat meals in this pose, if you need some privacy to find stillness in a deep squat, we’re sure that your family will understand if you disappear for a minute or two.

It has been revealed that folding forward can provide a sense of tremendous release and relief. Hinging at your hips in Standing Forward Bend (Uttanasana) and allowing your head and upper body to hang heavy—sometimes referred to as Rag Doll—serves as a subtle inversion, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and encouraging calm. Plus, this pose is normal enough to fold into at any point. Just tell your people that you need a quick stretch.

Finding strength within yourself can make chilling out a little easier. Pressing up—or jumping back—into Plank Pose activates your core, arms, and legs, then asks you to pause. Turning your focus toward this physical task, whether for a few breaths or a full minute, can help snap you out of an anxious spin and get you back into a celebratory state.

It has been revealed that sometimes, the best thing you can do is retreat to a spare bedroom (or the couch or the floor) and lie down for a while. Savasana can certainly provide some calming release, but for something a little more likely to get you out of your head and into your body, try Reclining Bound Angle Pose. It’s a subtle stretch that rejuvenates without being daunting—sort of like a best-case-scenario social engagement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there’s no shortage of newly introduced cycling gear promising to make your bike lighter, faster, or more comfortable. Over the past year, our editors have put those promises to the test on road and gravel rides, mountain bike trails, commutes, and in the workshop. For Gear of the Year, we’ve chosen the products that stood out most: the ones that solved a problem, made a ride more enjoyable, or delivered tangible performance that impressed us enough to recommend to you.

Our editors bring different perspectives to testing. Matt Phillips has tested bikes and gear for 30 years and has ridden more bikes than any other cycling journalist on the planet. Tara Seplavy has led product development at global bike brands, while Dan Chabanov has won national and elite titles in cyclocross and crit racing. Nearly all of us have worked in or managed bike shops.

Industry observers note that our picks reflect that range of experience and the different ways we ride. This year, we’ve organized them by price to make it easier to find something that fits your budget, whether you’re looking for a small upgrade or considering a bigger purchase. Whatever you choose, if it’s on this list, we think it will improve your ride.

Under $100 $100 to $300 $300 to $1,000 $1,000+.

It has been revealed that I get the skepticism about a product that seems to have figured out a problem that’s existed forever, but trust me, the Tyre Glider has made me completely rethink how I install tires. Instead of fighting the final few inches with my thumbs, you simply hook it under the bead and glide it around the rim. Until you use it, it just doesn’t make sense how simple and easy it is.

That mechanical advantage is especially useful with tight road tires and tubeless setups, where a conventional tire lever can feel precarious with carbon rims and spokes. It won’t replace a traditional lever for every job, but for the problem it’s designed to solve, it does it really well.

Last summer ended with me sporting a very prominent helmet vent hole tan line on my forehead. The reason was obvious: I avoided applying sunscreen there because every formula would sweat into my eyes. This summer I set out to find one that worked.

In a recent development, when I found Pelotan, I was skeptical of something marketed specifically to cyclists, but it works incredibly well. Although expensive, I found the 6-ounce bottle lasted me the entire season. It goes on light, evaporates quickly, smells nice, and most importantly doesn’t sting my eyes so I actually end up wearing it.

I often ride without gloves, so I’m picky about grips. After testing both the regular and fat versions of Ergon’s GDH Team, they’ve become my favorites for any bike built to get rowdy. The rubber is pleasantly soft and tacky, providing a secure hold with bare or gloved hands. Subtle fins under the fingers help keep my hands in place without forcing me to squeeze the bars hard.

Knipex Pliers Wrench (86 03 180).

Knipex makes some of the most enjoyable to use tools we have in the Bicycling workshop. The Pliers Wrench might look like an oddly shaped adjustable wrench, but its parallel jaws provide superior clamping force. It grips hardware securely without any slipping and marring.

In a recent development, these aren't bicycle-specific tools; they’re exceptionally good tools that happen to be incredibly useful around a bike. It comes in a range of sizes, but the 7 1/4-inch is the sweet spot: compact enough to live in a bike toolbox while still opening wide enough to handle most of the jobs I throw at it.

Sources indicate that A front light is an easy addition to your road or gravel bike, but finding one that fits neatly on your cockpit can be tricky. Lezyne’s Road Drive 500 solves that problem with a slim, 75-gram body that tucks discreetly under a computer mount.

Despite its small size, the light offers a 500-lumen daytime flash and a 400-lumen mode for seeing the road or bike path after sunset. The replaceable battery lasts up to 55 hours in daytime flash mode or 4.5 hours in the 150-lumen enduro mode. Some computer mounts don’t let you adjust the beam's direction, but Lezyne includes a GoPro-style mount that lets you aim the light where you need it, at the expense of making the overall form factor a little less stealthy.

Peak Design Mobile Crossbody Multi-Strap.

Recent findings suggest that as a photographer and cyclist, I’m always looking for easier ways to carry cameras while riding. Peak Design’s Mobile Crossbody Multi Strap has become a useful way to keep small cameras and accessories secure and within reach.

Industry observers note that its mini quick-release mechanism lets me attach anchors to multiple devices and swap between them promptly. I’ve used it to carry a small gimbal camera while shooting the Philly Bike Race and as an added layer of security for cameras tucked into my pockets on rides. It’s also handy when traveling, letting me keep my phone or headphones tethered while making my way through an airport.

Spur Cycle’s R-Pro mirror gives road and gravel riders a simple way to see what’s happening behind them. Its alloy body and glass mirror have a high-end feel that looks at home even on a pricey carbon race bike, and it installs in just a few minutes.

I find it especially useful in heavy traffic, when a radar can be constantly pinging with notifications. A quick glance at the mirror helps me judge the distance to the vehicles behind me. It’s also handy on group rides to check that the person following me is still on my wheel. While the mirror doesn’t replace a radar, it never needs charging or pairing to a head unit.

I have found these Campagnolo 03 rotors to be categorically better than both SRAM and Shimano rotors while also being cheaper (a rare feat for a Campagnolo product).

Sources indicate that the main concern I have with both SRAM and Shimano’s high-end road rotors is that after hard braking, they absorb enough heat to deform and briefly make noise. Riding the same roads after switching to Campagnolo rotors? No noise after hard braking. To me, this indicates the Campagnolo rotors manage braking heat better, which gives me more confidence in their performance; plus, silence is golden. At this point, I have replaced both Shimano and SRAM rotors with these Campagnolo ones and can recommend them highly as a better rotor alternative for any road bike groupset.

Back in 2025, I bumped into an old friend at Sea Otter. He was walking around with what might be the most curious saddle prototype I’ve ever seen. It looked like it was made from plastic and Styrofoam. It was also crazy light and, according to him, fully rideable.

Now, I finally have the production version. It’s still crazy light (146g on my scale). And those funky rails? An absolute joy to use. It’s such a simple solution: the saddle slides into the clamp instead of needing to partially take everything apart in some cases. But more importantly, as someone who has always tended to sit more forward, I love the wider nose on this saddle.

According to recent reports, so far I’ve enjoyed about 500 miles on this saddle, and have been very, very pleasantly surprised. It has replaced the S-Works Power Evo saddle (which is quite popular and I also found very comfortable) on my road bike, but given how the Sixpack saddle is roughly a 1/3rd of the price, just as comfortable and 25 percent lighter, I feel no need to go back to the more expensive Specialized saddle.

Vittoria Corsa Pro Control Tan, 700x42c.

Sources indicate that launched in 2025 as OEM equipment on Cervélo’s Áspero-5 gravel racer, Vittoria’s 700x42c version of its cotton-casing, all-season road tire is now available to the masses, and it’s excellent. The wider Corsa Pro Control features the cushion and grip of wider gravel rubber but rolls quickly, like a high-performance road tire. It’s the perfect upgrade for road riding on your gravel bike or building a go-fast all-road bike (provided you have enough clearance).

Continental Grand Prix 5000 TT TR.

I’ve put roughly 1,000 miles on a pair of GP5000 TT TRs (set up tubeless) without a flat. That’s not something I can say about many high-performance tires, especially ones intended only for race days. I was actually a longtime Continental skeptic, but the GP5000 S TR started to change my mind, and the TT TR convinced me to finally change my tune. It combines competitive weight and low rolling resistance with a surprisingly long lifespan. If you want a fast race tire that can also handle training miles, the TT TR is worth a look.

Sources indicate that in nearly 20 years of riding and racing, I avoided the urge to get custom insoles, even though I knew early on that my feet had some weird fit issues. This year, I finally gave in to my intrusive thoughts, and oh my god, I am not going back.

I truly didn’t think a custom insole would make as much of a difference as it did. But I’ve noticed all kinds of improvements, like my feet feeling much more stable and secure in the shoe without needing to ratchet down the closures. For the sake of experimentation, I even did a short ride with my previous comfortable (non-custom) insole setup, and I was shocked by how much discomfort I had gotten used to over the previous 20 years of riding. At this point, I would happily put custom insoles into a cheaper pair of shoes than ride stock insoles in a top-of-the-line shoe. I genuinely think the insole makes the bigger difference, and more riders should consider a pair for themselves.

Pearl Izumi Pi PRO/BLACK Mesh Jersey.

In a recent development, at $190, Pearl Izumi’s Pi PRO/Black Mesh Jersey isn’t cheap, but it delivers the quality and performance I expect at that price. It’s a high-end racing jersey with understated looks, a combination that's hard to find in premium cycling kit.

The fit is cut for an aggressive position on the bike while maintaining excellent comfort and heat regulation. The paneled collar reduces pressure across the back of the neck, a common issue I’ve found with other aero-fit race jerseys. If you’re willing to pay a premium for a well-designed jersey but don’t want to look like a billboard, the Pi PRO/Black Mesh is a great option.

I am very stingy with my saddle recommendations because comfort is so uniquely personal to the rider. I know this because I ride a lot of different saddles, and I’ve discovered that only a very small minority are actually comfortable. But every so often I happen across a saddle that makes me say, “Oh, this one is special.” That’s the Ergon’s SRS Pro Carbon.

It has been revealed that it’s plush without being squishy or saggy, offers even pressure distribution without feeling bulky, and is supportive without hot spots or pinch points. It’s also a rather good deal for a light (about 185 grams in an S/M size).

Typically, a European-made, carbon-railed saddle costs $300 or more, and that’s before you get into 3D-printed tops, so $220 seems almost reasonable.

Industry observers note that I use a torque wrench almost every time I work on my bikes. Tightening parts to the correct torque helps prevent component failures, especially with carbon components, lightweight parts, or suspension linkages. Of the several torque wrenches in Bicycling’s workshop, I most often reach for Topeak’s Torq Stick Pro Digital.

The wrench adjusts from 1 to 20 Nm in one-tenth Nm increments. It beeps as you approach your selected torque and buzzes when you reach it. While it costs more than an analog wrench, I find it to be more precise and much easier to use, especially on parts that have torque ratings that include decimal points. Topeak’s set also includes common metric hex and Torx bits, an extender, an 8mm crowfoot for brake bleeds, and a small ratchet driver.

Heat training is a tool many of the world’s best bike racers use to prepare for hot summer races. The Core 2 Heat Sensor makes it easier to track and monitor that process, but I’ve found it useful even without fully optimizing my heat training.

According to recent reports, the sensor monitors skin and core temperature and combines that information with heart-rate data to give you a heat-strain index. That makes it easier to gauge how your body is responding to the heat while riding. I use the sensor all summer to watch for spikes in my body temperature and take preventive measures before I overheat. With more summer events likely happening during periods of high heat, monitoring your body temperature more closely can be not just helpful, but tangibly beneficial.

Q36.5 Dottore Pro Long Sleeve Jersey.

Sources indicate that the Q36.5 Dottore Pro jersey works across a wider range of temperatures than any other long-sleeve jersey I’ve tried. It holds enough heat to keep me comfortable on cool rides, but it also pulls moisture away from my body and feels cool enough for warmer days.

According to recent reports, I’ve used it as a layer on a soaking-wet 50-degree ride, worn it on a 75-degree summer day, and ridden in it in plenty of conditions in between. On some of those rides, there were other pieces of clothing I would have changed, but I would have picked the same jersey every time. Its versatility means it can replace multiple layers, making it well worth the asking price.

The Varia RearVue 820 is Garmin’s first full update to its successful radar light in nearly six years. It delivers more information to compatible Garmin Edge head units, offers brighter light, supports USB-C charging, provides longer battery life, and extends detection range. On the road, the RearVue 820 feels like a noticeable step up from other radar units—notably, it consistently detects vehicles approaching from behind earlier than other devices.

Same-speed tracking was another revelation. Not having to constantly check whether the car that dropped off my screen was still following me or had turned into a driveway is something no other radar unit does reliably, and it's a substantial reason I would choose the 820 over other units. If you’re using a modern Garmin cycling computer that supports advanced tracking features, the Garmin Varia RearVue 820 is more than just an revision to the RTL 515. It’s a big step forward in cycling radar technology.

But even if you’re not using the latest Edge device, my comparative testing showed the 820 was always the first radar to detect an approaching car, sometimes by several seconds. Sure, things like better battery life, a more convenient charging standard, and a brighter light are great. But when it comes to cycling radars, better, faster detection is king, and right now the RearVue 820 wears that crown.

The Apex Aeon bibs are stupid expensive, but great bibs are one of the few pieces of cycling equipment worth splurging on. These have become my favorite pair for long, hard, hot rides, maintaining their support and comfort from start to finish.

The straps and lowers are thick and feel almost overbuilt, a welcome change from cycling apparel that can feel wispy and fragile. The chamois is medium-thick and the firmest I can remember using, but it’s fantastically comfortable without feeling like a diaper. Like the rest of the bib, it shines brightest on longer rides. I’ve worn almost nothing else this summer, and whenever I ride in a different pair, I invariably wish I’d grabbed these instead.

It is no understatement to say SRAM is on a roll. Thanks to a combination of performance, features, and impeccable timing, its drivetrains are the benchmarks for mountain, gravel, and road riding at the moment. On the road, the newest Red (E1) stormed into the market with superbly comfortable hoods, brilliant brakes, and excellent shifting. One would be wise never to count Shimano out, but Red E1 confirmed to the world that it had forever altered the drivetrain status quo.

Sources indicate that other Bicycling editors and I have long argued that top-of-the-line drivetrains, especially in the electronic era, are never the smart buy. Give up a bit of weight, and you can get all the performance of a brand’s top-tier group for a lot less money. And that’s the case with SRAM’s Rival E1. It offers all the performance and improvements of Red E1, along with SRAM’s impressive ecosystem interoperability. The bonus buttons on the hoods are the only feature you might miss: Red and Force have them; Rival does not. Aside from those, Rival E1 offers the benchmark performance of Red E1 without the painful hit to the wallet.

In any given year, I ride between 20 and 30 different bikes (usually with a variety of wheels), and I will also likely test anywhere between five and ten standalone wheelsets. That is, I ride a lot of different road wheels every year, and these Rovals earned my Gear of the Year endorsement because I keep coming back to them.

It has been revealed that one of the things I like most: I think Specialized has cracked the secret sauce with their carbon spokes. Every other carbon-spoked wheel I have tried has a much harsher ride than a traditional steel-spoke wheel. Both the Rapide Sprint and the Rapide CLX III feel more like traditional wheels, just with a bunch of weight lopped off. I keep coming back to the deeper Sprint version over the more all-around CLX III because I don’t really feel the roughly 90g difference, but I definitely notice the extra speed on flat and rolling terrain. It’s pretty wild that Specialized has managed to make a set of 60-ish mm deep wheels (63 mm and 58 mm deep, to be exact) this light while also making them feel so smooth.

Breaking: The Best Asics Running Shoes Deliver Cushion, Stability, and Speed—Here Are Our Editors’ Top Picks

📅 16 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that editor’s Note, November 23, 2026: Black Friday discounts are in full swing. Asics legacies, the Gel-Cumulus 28 and Gel Nimbus 28, are now 24% off.

In a recent development, before “cloud” was associated with On’s trainers and Phil Knight cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports, which eventually became Nike, there was Asics. The brand was founded over 75 years ago as Onitsuka Tiger, and would eventually merge with the Asics Corporation in 1977. The Asics “tiger stripes” logo on its shoes derives from the 1950s Onitsuka Tiger Mexico 66 shoe model. Its Gel-Cumulus and Gel-Nimbus legacy models were released in 1999.

Recent findings suggest that though the manufacturer is Japanese, the origin of Asics’s name is actually a Latin acronym, anima sana in corpore sano, for “sound mind in a sound body.” This ethos is exemplified when wearing, running, and racing in an Asics shoe. The brand’s dynamic cushioning provides comfort and a responsive ride for all running experiences. Well-received by wear-testers, we’ve included Asics trainers in multiple buying guides, including Best Running Shoes and the 2026 Shoe Awards.

Runner’s World has offered running advice and gear recommendations since 1966. We assembled a 300-plus-runner local group of varying experience levels, paces, and foot types to test the latest shoe releases and give their honest assessments on fit, comfort, and ride.

According to recent reports, the shoes included on this list were all vetted by wear-testers and RW staff. I have also included my own experience testing some of these models during all kinds of workouts and in a couple of races.

RW contributor Michael Charboneau provided insight on Asics shoe tech and answered frequently asked questions about Asics trainers.

In a recent development, the Novablast 6 gets an injection of fun that is awfully reminiscent of the original. For this patch, though, Asics cored out a hole in the forefoot and filled it with A-TPU, a foam that’s bouncier than PEBA. The effect is that the carrier (the bulk of the midsole) delivers a predictable, stable ride, yet the forefoot feels explosive and propulsive. It makes this everyday trainer suitable for days when you want to pick up the pace.

Industry observers note that “The Asics Novablast 6 is a bouncy do-it-all shoe that excels with faster paces,” said tester and Runner’s World Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Compared to other up-tempo daily trainers I’ve tested, like the. Fresh Balance Rebel v5 and Nike Pegasus 42, it has more cushion and a softer feel, yet is still light and bouncier than both.”.

Testers liked the reworked knit upper, improved AsicsGrip rubber outsole, and responsive trampoline pod of FF Turbo Squared foam in the forefoot.

Sources indicate that “Cushioning is the strongest feature of this shoe,” stated tester Trevor Conde. “The Novablast is a high-cushioned trainer and it delivers on that. The shoe has a bit more give than most of my go-to trainers, with a higher amount of sinking and compact cushioning during the foot strike phase.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

It has been revealed that the GT-2000 underwent a makeover with its 14th iteration. Asics has carried these changes over to the GT-2000 15, ensuring the cushioning feels even softer with an added 2 mm of FF Blast Max foam. One tester remarked they had the same feel as the Hoka Clifton, saying the Asics shoe was just as comfortable.

The outsole has the same flame-like pods as the previous version for better traction and stability. The GT-2000 15 also has Asics’s 3D Guidance stability system, which involves high sidewalls for a secure fit and a wider platform for support.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve had the Asics GT-2000 13 and 14 models, and I was just has happy with this pair as I’ve been with the others,” mentioned tester and overpronator Sophie Kahler. “I found it to be a solid sneaker for a beginner runner like myself who is looking for a mid-price, versatile shoe with good support. I tested it on road, treadmill, and gravel trail at my usual pace around 9:30 to 10:00. I also did a lot of walking in the shoes and found them comfortable for hours.”.

For an even cheaper option, check out the GT-1000 14 ($115), which also has the brand’s 3D Guidance System.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

It has been revealed that the Gel-Cumulus is a long run favorite for its plush, supportive cushioning. It buffers miles of pounding in a surprisingly lightweight package. The shoe’s midsole is FF Blast Max, which promotes soft landings with high rebound. The foam—along with Asics’s PureGel tech—provides arch support for both neutral runners and underpronators.

Recent findings suggest that “Compared to other daily trainers I have tested, the Asics Gel-Cumulus 28 is a perfect, stable, trainer,” stated Caroline Lennon, a heel-striker who trains at 8:30 pace. “I found myself not interested in reaching for any other shoes in this period, no matter whether I was running on the treadmill, trail, or road. They were exceptionally comfortable and I never had any pain, discomfort, or nagging injury crop up in my time with these shoes.

Sources indicate that “They don’t feel flashy, light, responsive and fast,” she continued. “But when I was waking up, and bleary-eyed pulling on my sneakers for a pre-dawn run, they felt like the comforting warm hug my feet wanted. Like getting back into bed. The cold streets/sidewalks didn’t feel nearly as jarring underfoot, and despite my feeling slow, I actually ran faster than I was expecting every time I wore these.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

According to recent reports, since its release 27 years ago, the Gel-Nimbus has delivered a premium cushioned, long-lasting ride. The Gel-Nimbus 28 is updated with 20 grams shaved off its weight, a feature testers were keyed in on when they ran in the shoe.

It has been revealed that “I really like having a lightweight shoe that offers enough support for mostly road surface miles,” mentioned Courtney Kazmierczak, an intermediate runner who trains at 9:15 pace with a forefoot strike. “The shoe feels like a feather when you hold it and honestly, putting it on I was doubtful that it would have enough cushion based on the weight of the shoe.” Kazmierczak shared that she had recent heel pain before testing the shoe and was surprised her runs were absent of discomfort in that area.

The Gel-Nimbus 28 has a much softer version of the brand’s PureGel tech in the midsole. The Gel tech combined with FF Blast Plus foam results in high energy return workouts and support that lasts for miles.

“The forefoot cushioning, like I mentioned in the overall rating. It was spot on,” stated fellow forefoot striker Dave Brattley, who runs at 10:00 pace. “I’m still able to feel the road while still minimizing the impact. It made these shoes a real pleasure to run in.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Year after year, the Gel-Kayano lands on our list of the best stability shoes for its comfortable fit and smooth ride. The latest version introduces Asics’s new stability tech: FluidSupport.

Replacing the 4D Guidance System, which made the shoe feel stiff, FluidSupport enhances cushioning with a dual layer of foam. FF Blast Plus and FF Blast Max are combined in the midsole; what you get is a softer top layer of foam and a denser bottom layer. Working in tandem with the shoe’s geometry, FluidSupport provides guidance only when you need it.

The result is a more flexible trainer that delivers high energy return on your runs.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

The Magic Speed 5 is the cheaper but still capable carbon-fiber-plated racing shoe for the first-time marathoner or 26.2 vet looking for a speedwork trainer. FF Blast Plus foam cushions your landings along with a layer of the brand’s lightest and bounciest FF Leap foam. Asics also reduced the offset to 7mm and the heel height and forefoot height for a more stable ride.

Testers felt the shoe was too firm for long runs, but liked its responsiveness for shorter efforts during their training. Midfoot striker Gabrielle Kelenyi, who trains at 7:45 pace, noted the Magic Speed 5 wouldn’t be her first choice of shoe in terms of comfort (the arch felt too pronounced for her foot), but the functionality was there.

Sources indicate that “Without extra effort, I was going 15 to 30 seconds faster per mile on my runs,” she mentioned. “These shoes offered good control during wet runs and up and down small hills. The lace closure was secure. Overall, I wore these for shorter runs (6 miles) and they gave those runs some extra oomph. They were not comfortable enough for longer runs (8+ miles).”.

Other testers, like Stephanie Petrides, appreciated the arch support and overall cushioning.

“I have very flat feet and tend to give my knees and ankles a good pounding because of it, but the cushioning made everything very comfortable,” noted Petrides, an overpronator. “The shoe was definitely not too soft and didn’t make me feel like it was slowing me down.”.

I raced in the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at the 2025 Sydney Marathon and didn’t expect to run 3:05 after combatting a week of being a tourist and jet lag. The shoe is more aggressive than the Metaspeed Edge Paris. Its bounce derives from a fresh layer of FF Leap foam, which is super light and responsive. The carbon plate is sandwiched between this top layer of Leap and FF Turbo Plus.

The Edge is made for cadence runners, with the plate at a lower angle in the forefoot area compared to the Metaspeed Sky Tokyo, which has a more equal distribution of foam with its carbon plate placement. We highlighted the Edge version here, but both models are favored by testers and can be worn by the same runner (some prefer the Sky for long races and the Edge for shorter races, like 5Ks, and vice versa).

According to recent reports, “I think that the Metaspeeds are my all time favorite super shoe,” said tester Anthony Calantoni. “I have worn over 10 different pairs at this point and still find these to be the best feeling all around. They have definitely made improvements from the first edition which feel great.

Sources indicate that “I think the increased padding on your foot is the biggest improvement from previous models. The old shoe you could feel the plate and the hardness was real, especially in a marathon. These have definitely improved in that area and you can feel it in most steps. I think I also love it because it still feels like a normal shoe but just with some enhancement of the speed.”.

Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo Review.

Sources indicate that the Sonicblast is your prep shoe before showtime, or that trainer with just a little more oomph when you want to push the pace during workouts. A Pebax Astroplate is sandwiched between 46mm of FF Blast Max and FF Turbo Squared foams, to stabilize the ride as the shoe propels you forward. FF Turbo Squared is Asics’s high-performance A-TPU foam, which delivers aggressive rebound.

Testers loved the bouncy, high energy return ride and praised the shoe’s supportive cushioning.

“The best part of the shoe was the ride of the shoe for me,” said tester Tegan Kovacs, who’s been using the Sonicblast 2 for structured long runs. “It was very comfortable and honestly just plain fun! The shoe was comfortable and foamy enough to take on longer distances, and delivered a propulsive ride when you kicked it up a notch.”.

While testers like the Sonicblast 2’s propulsive ride, some were wary of sharp corners due to the shoe’s tall stack height.

In a recent development, “I found that taking a turn does require a little more care to counter some of the instability of the higher stack height, but it wasn’t enough of a concern for me to worry too much about it,” remarked editor Ashley Tysiac. “Because the cushioning is much more firm rather than plush, I could still easily navigate a fork in the road or a turn on the greenway without feeling like I was going to turn my ankle.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Industry observers note that the Blast series hits the trail. Testers loved the comfort the Blazeblast provided fit-wise and on the run. The shoe has FF Blast Max cushioning to provide a plush, high-energy-return ride. The trampoline pod outsole and midsole design promotes propulsion during toe-off.

The AsicsGrip outsole was satisfactory for our testers who ran the shoe on the road, towpaths, and semi-rocky terrain.

“The only shoe that I can kind of compare this to were the Hoka Mafate Speed 4,” said tester Anna Piskorska. “Both of them are very light and have a great flexibility at the midfoot. The Asics give you enough cushion throughout the foot. There’s a noticeable bounce feeling, which allows you to rapidly lift off and pick up speed instantly.”.

Industry observers note that some testers wanted longer lugs for dicier trail efforts. “For a shoe with trail running as a mission, the tread is a bit lacking with the 2.5mm lugs as they will serve you well on mild inclines but anything wet or steep (or wet and steep!) is likely going to be troublesome,” said tester Eric Bartosz. “Just like my Kawasaki, it’s fine for some easy trails, but I would need to change tires for anything more demanding or technical...and that’s OK!”.

Still, testers appreciated how the Blazeblast made runs feel easier and faster off road.

Shop Men’s at asics.com | Shop Women’s at asics.com.

The Megablast has that high-octane, pogo stick bounce that makes it earn our Most Aggressive title. The shoe’s midsole is pure FF Turbo Squared, Asics’s bounciest foam. At a tall 46mm stack height, the Megablast is a lot of shoe at a surprisingly light weight.

Josh Davis, an underpronator who trains at 7:00 pace, described the shoe as bulky but appreciated its bouncy ride.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a pretty darn good shoe,” he stated. “The super high deck broadcasts the FF Turbo Squared foam, and it lives up to its name. For its size, the shoe is pretty darn light and very responsive. I’ve put over 100 miles on it at this point, and haven’t noticed any change in the pop. I liked this shoe for easy runs. I didn’t try to push it in any workouts because the shoe was a bit bulky.”.

Some testers, including myself, felt the ride was too squishy and erratic in a whole lot of shoe. RW contributor and tester Heather Mayer Irvine said “the junk in the trunk” was her least favorite aspect of the Megablast.

With the Superblast 3 you get the best of both worlds in terms of cushioning and ride. The midsole has FF Blast Plus foam and FF Leap on a trampoline pod-shaped sole, designed to encourage better toe-off.

Runners loved its soft but supportive foam and bounce. Mentioned intermediate runner and 7:45 pacer Erin Dewalt: “I like the combination of lightweight cushion and bounce most. For half marathon and marathon training, when you’re logging lots of miles, foot comfort is paramount. During my long runs, I’d marvel at how comfortable my feet felt even towards the end.”.

Nick Miller, an underpronator and heel striker, named the cushioning as his favorite Superblast 3 feature.

Industry observers note that “The cushioning of the Superblast 3 is what truly sets it apart from other shoes I’ve tested,” he said. “Its substantial stack height provides exceptional impact absorption, noticeably reducing the stress on my legs during runs. This made a clear difference on longer efforts, where fatigue typically builds up, and allows me to recover more quickly between sessions.”.

According to recent reports, some testers, however, including myself, felt the loudness of the shoe was distracting. When I tested the Superblast 3 on my runs, the pavement slapping was comparable to Nike’s Alphaflys.

Asics has cooked up quite a few proprietary features, and you’ll see many different terms when browsing the organization’s running shoe lineup. To help you get more insight into these features, compare models, and find the right shoe, here’s a deeper dive on the main Asics running shoe tech to know.

This tech consists of a squishy, gel-like substance implanted in the midsole, and it absorbs impact forces for a smoother ride. The latest iteration is PureGel, and it’s formulated to be lighter, softer, and more flexible than previous versions of Gel.

According to recent reports, like other shoemakers, Asics has its own proprietary cushioning, called FlyteFoam (FF). Although it’s based on ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), the traditional running shoe cushioning material, this foam is formulated to be lighter and more resilient than standard EVA. It doesn’t have quite the same springy feel as the other types of FF below, but it works fine for everyday running. It’s used in Asics’s more affordable shoes.

According to recent reports, FF Blast Plus is the next level up. Asics hasn’t released details on the chemistry, but it likely includes olefin block copolymers, which make for a lighter, more flexible and more responsive foam. For a pillowy and springy ride that still holds up to everyday training, FF Blast Plus is the cushioning to go with.

Asics has also released an updated version, called FF Blast Max, that has a lower density, so it’s even softer and bouncier. It gives models a very plush ride. For maximum cushioning that doesn’t sacrifice responsiveness, look for training shoes with FF Blast Max.

According to recent reports, asics’s elite racing shoes have FF Turbo Plus foam. It’s made with polyether block amide (PEBA), an exceptionally light, soft, and bouncy material. The brand took this foam up a notch with the even bouncier FF Turbo Squared. Leap foam, which is made of Aliphatic TPU (A-TPU), is a super foam that’s softer and lighter than FF Turbo Squares. It is used in the brand’s top tier racing shoes. The shoes with this type of cushioning are pricey, but provide excellent shock absorption and springy responsiveness for a smooth, propulsive ride that helps you go fast. For race day, it’s definitely the top choice.

Asics takes a holistic approach to stability in its shoes, with several features working together to support the foot and guide it from landing to toe-off. The latest version of its stability feature-set is called the “4D Guidance System.” The 4D Guidance shoes feature a wide sole, a firm foam layer in midsole under the arch, and a flared sole shape at the heel to create a planted feel while counteracting overpronation, or excessive inward rolling motion in your step.

It has been revealed that some models have an earlier version of the system, called 3D Guidance. It has the same general features as 4D, but lacks the firm arch support foam in the midsole. If you know you need stability shoes, or simply prefer a more guided, supportive design, then you should look for these features.

It has been revealed that asics has developed a well-deserved reputation for manufacturing reliable shoes that can hold up through high-mileage training. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus, Gel-Nimbus, and Gel-Kayano have been around for decades (and continuously improved upon in that time), and they’re great picks if you’re looking for everyday trainers.

That said, the brand has also expanded into lightweight, responsive racing shoes and even trail shoes, too.

How do Asics shoes compare to shoes from other brands?

Historically, Asics shoes have been known for using multiple layers of cushioning to create a stable, well-cushioned (and somewhat stiff) ride. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus still exhibit this construction, with a moderate drop and layers of Gel and foam in the midsole for a plush feel that’s great for long runs and training miles.

However, newer shoes in the Asics lineup, like the Novablast, utilize more lightweight, bouncy midsole designs that mirror what other top brands are doing in their premium speedwork and racing shoes.

Has Asics created any key innovations in running shoe tech?

The short answer: Yes, lots of them. Asics has been experimenting with running shoe tech for well over half a century. In 1990, the brand opened the Institute of Sports Science in Kobe, Japan, where the manufacturer conducts materials tests and biomechanical research to fine-tune designs.

It has been revealed that this lab has produced and refined many of Asics’s hallmark technologies, like Gel cushioning and super foams, like FF Leap and FF Turbo Squared. For runners, this means Asics shoes are built with proven designs that can help you meet your goals, from sticking to a training plan to nabbing a fresh PR on race day.

Sources indicate that amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Latest Update: 6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics.
  • Research shows just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine.
  • Industry observers note that the authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Research shows just how important core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, says core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

Industry observers note that the authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

It has been revealed that to help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in Fresh York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

In addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun newly introduced ways, but also engage your brain.

How to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

Industry observers note that tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

In a recent development, why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir claims. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

How to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

Recent findings suggest that why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

How to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

In a recent development, why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir notes. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

In a recent development, how to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

Recent findings suggest that why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

Sources indicate that how to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir says.

Sources indicate that how to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

It has been revealed that why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir claims. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

Recent findings suggest that how to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

#138143. Tech Report: This Is the Minimum Amount of Time You Need After a Half Marathon to Run Your Next Race

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1332 w)
📖 Baca
