Tech Report: This Is the Minimum Amount of Time You Need After a Half Marathon to Run Your Next Race

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race.
  • But jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results.
  • Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race. You might only get a few chances per year to run a marathon, but you can stack up multiple half marathons, 5Ks, and 10Ks per season, as long as you balance those harder efforts with sufficient recovery time.

But jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results. Even if you feel ready to race again soon after a half marathon, specifically, you might need more time than you think. So what’s the ideal reset time after 13.1 and when should you be able to line up again?

Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.

In general, it’s a good idea to take two to four weeks off from high-intensity work after a half marathon before racing again, notes Laura Norris, a Seattle-based certified personal trainer and run coach with a master’s in applied exercise science.

You should first take three to five days postrace off completely to clear up any muscle damage and let your body fully recover, then stick exclusively to easy running for the rest of that two- to four-week period.

It has been revealed that “There’s new research that shows the half marathon stresses the heart pretty decently for two weeks postrace,” Norris states. While it’s not the same level of stress as a full marathon, it’s still vital to take sufficient time to recover before tackling another high-intensity effort.

With that in mind, you can make adjustments to your timeline:.

The harder you push, the longer it takes to recover, so Norris suggests waiting those three to four weeks before racing again if you just ran your fastest half marathon, even if you feel good.

However, you can consider your upcoming race distance and goal: If you’re jumping into a Turkey Trot 5K for fun, for example, you can probably get away with just two weeks of recovery, but wait at least the entire four weeks before gearing up for a full marathon, Norris suggests.

Sources indicate that after a race where you feel really beat up, you’re extra sore, mentally drained, or fatigued, it’s a good idea to take those first three to five days off followed by two to four weeks of really easy running, Norris states. But that doesn’t mean you jump right into another race.

According to recent reports, in this case, “it might be worth spacing your races at least six to eight weeks apart, maybe even a full training season apart,” she says. Otherwise, you could enter into a vicious cycle of overtraining, not recovering fully, and entering another race underprepared and beating yourself up again, Norris explains.

It can feel really disappointing to train hard for months for your race and not have results to reflect that work, but it’s notable to honor your recovery and health more than performance.

According to recent reports, the amount of time you give yourself to recover from a bad race depends on the reason the race went poorly, Norris claims. If you just had a bad day, dealt with a difficult course, or struggled with fueling, you might stick to three to four weeks before another race.

But if you were dealing with an illness after your event or you undertrained leading into it, then in addition to taking days completely off and a few weeks of easy running, you probably want another few weeks of adding in speed before jumping into another race, Norris suggests. This would give you an opportunity to prepare more for your next race, while allowing your body to heal.

Wait a minimum of six weeks before racing again. “That’s at least two weeks to recover, four weeks to navigate training again, and also a few weeks to make sure that you aren’t impulsively making a decision based on high postrace emotions,” Norris indicates.

In a recent development, norris notes that you have to evaluate how poorly you feel and listen to your gut, too. It’s always a good idea to get pain or potential injury addressed by a physical therapist and navigate your timeline from there.

In a lot of cases, you can use post-half marathon fitness to your advantage to tackle another race and see how much better you can do. “If you want to race in a couple weeks once your legs feel better and you’re not sore, it might not be a bad time to do a 5K,” indicates Christine Rockey, an exercise physiologist, RRCA-certified run coach, and principal lecturer at Coastal Carolina University.

But there’s a difference between setting your sights on another PR and jumping into a fun family 5K. Here’s how you should prepare in training for your next race, depending on your goal.

Sources indicate that norris suggests slowly ramping back up with about a week of 30-minute easy runs after the three to five days of rest. “They won’t feel great at first, but we just want to get the legs moving now that most of the muscle damage has started to repair,” she states.

According to recent reports, then, continue with easy running during the following week, but try to aim for about 75 percent of your peak volume during half marathon training. For example, if your peak long run was 14 miles, you might aim to cover 10.

If you have two more weeks, you can add in some race pace work to sharpen your speed during the first of those two weeks, then give yourself a week to taper. It’s always easier to maintain fitness than it is to build, and you want to avoid being overtrained before your next race, Norris says.

In a recent development, as you lace up for your next race, keep a realistic goal in mind. It’s always good to be an ambitious runner and gain more race experience, but remember to keep your expectations in check, Rockey claims. “I think if you go in thinking the next five races you do are all going to be PRs, I think you’re going to end up disappointed and you might even get so frustrated that you stop running,” she says.

According to recent reports, you have a bit more leeway to do lower volume and run a few short easy runs every other day, for example. Norris indicates you can coast on 50 percent of your peak half marathon volume and know that you’ll still be fit enough to jump into a last-minute 5K.

It’s important not to go back to a completely sedentary state if you proposal on racing again. “If you were to sit on the sofa [instead of easy running] and do absolutely nothing for three weeks, you would begin to detrain,” Norris adds. “It might not be that serious, but it would probably make the race not feel as good.”.

Plus, going from the couch to another half marathon can lead to aches and pains, Norris adds. “If you go from doing nothing for three weeks to doing 13 miles, that’s a huge jump in single-session load,” she notes, pointing to a study published in 2025 that demonstrates jumping up your single-run volume by more than 10 percent in a 30-day span can increase injury risk.

Keeping up with a couple easy runs in between efforts will help you race your best—even when your best means having the most fun.

New Balance SC Elite V5 + FuelCell Rebel V5 Running Shoes.

According to recent reports, black Friday sales are notorious for flooding inboxes with endless discounts on triathlon gear you might not actually need. Triathlete’s editors are no exception: for the past two months, they have received a deluge of notifications teasing Black Friday deals from just about every triathlon brand.

In a recent development, but our staff, who test and review gear year-round, know not every sale is worth shopping. After all, what good is a big Black Friday discount on cheap triathlon gear if it requires replacement in a few months?

To separate the signal from the noise, we asked our very own Triathlete editors to share the items sitting in their online shopping carts this holiday season. From reliable daily trainers and high-end smartwatches to cold-weather layers and budget-friendly pool essentials, here are the Black Friday deals our team is actually buying with their own money.

In a recent development, have you ever found that pair of shoes where it was immediate love at first stride? You just knew you’d found yourself in a newly introduced, long-term relationship, and for the next several weeks, you were in the honeymoon phase – enjoying running more and convincing yourself that running in carbon shoes was fine because this was the only shoe you wanted to run in. Forever.

Recent findings suggest that that was me with the New Balance SC Elite V4. That might surprise a few people, as it’s not the fastest or flashiest of shoes – and very few pros wore it. Yet it just ticked all the boxes: a wide toe box, stable, grippy, and breathable. They’re the not-intimidating super shoe I recommend to everyone looking to try super shoes. And to top it off, they lasted two seasons and far more miles than you’re ever supposed to put on them.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why the SC Elite V5 is on my shopping list. It’s not only well past time to replace my current pair, but the new version promises to be lighter and faster, with a couple of small issues, like the short tongue, addressed. Alex Yee and Laura Philipp both wore this shoe to great effect, and now I think it’s my turn.

Sources indicate that but I can’t just run in these for every session. Sigh. I must also shop for a daily trainer that matches the love I have for the Elites, and that’s why I’m shopping for the FuelCell Rebel V5. After temporarily trading my trusty Adidas EVO SLs for a friend’s upcoming Rebels for a couple of laps around the track, I was immediately hooked. Again, even though they might not be as popular as the SLs, it’s all about your relationship with the shoe – and I knew I’d just found my next pair of daily trainers.

With both on sale at Running Warehouse for way less than they deserve, it’s time to stop talking about relationships with shoes and just get them. Otherwise, my wife will say I should just go on dates with them instead.

-Travis Mundell, social media manager.

According to recent reports, I’ve entered the payoff phase of parenting where my oldest son is becoming a fun companion for activities. We’re running our first 5K together in December. While our outerwear will be holiday sweaters, he needs some base layers to stay warm from the December chill.

Backcountry has decent prices on Smartwool’s kids’ base layers, ideal for little ones who will likely outgrow the apparel after just one season (though my 3-year-old has proudly proclaimed she will be running cross “crunchy,” so the base layers will get good use).

According to recent reports, while I’m shopping, I’m also going to replace some of my threadbare running socks, which I’ve been avoiding. Smartwool is one of my favorite durable sock brands and they are 25% off.

– Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

As someone who tests a lot of endurance-focused smartwatches (pretty much all of them that have been made in the last decade), I know a good watch — and a good deal on a watch — when I see one.

When the Suunto Race 1 came out in 2023, I reviewed it for Triathlete. At the time, I gave it 4.5 out of 5 stars, only dinging it for a slow raise-to-wake/processor that was slightly behind the competition. Pros included a giant, bright AMOLED touchscreen, excellent offline mapping and a useful rotating digital dial, and shockingly solid battery life for a major-screened AMOLED smartwatch. The other major pro was what I considered an incredibly thrifty price — $500 at the time for the titanium model with more storage than the even cheaper (and heavier) steel $400 version.

Three years later, I still consider the original Suunto Race a menace to the rest of Suunto’s line: The Race 2 somehow had less battery life than the original, but cost way more; and I don’t even consider the Race 3S a worthy challenger to either of the previous models in function or price.

So now that this fully triathlete-approved smartwatch with a gigantic screen and handy rotating dial (best for navigation) is available at $320 in the Titanium version and a category-shattering $280 for the steel version, you can’t even compare it to those other ill-fated Race models nor other smartwatches like the capable-but-not-nearly-enough-storage-for-offline-mapping (and small-screened) Coros Pace 4 ($250).

Industry observers note that and equivalent Garmin models like the Forerunner 570 (on sale for $450 down from $550) can’t even remotely compete on price or battery life. Don’t be turned off by the age of this watch; pick it up now, be satisfied for years, and take the money you save and put it toward some holiday gift-giving.

– Chris Foster, editor-in-chief.

It’s the end of the season, which means two things:.

Industry observers note that naturally, Black Friday serves as the perfect time to bag a few latest suits and swim necessities. To me, the fresh gear equals a fresh mindset as I enter a swim-focused block of winter training. These Three Offseason Strength Exercises Can Help You Break Through Your Climbing Plateau

  • For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside.
  • The workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time. If you’re thinking about winterizing your bike for the season, then it’s the perfect time to start looking at your strength training proposal for the offseason.

For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside. For others it takes form as time on fat bikes, skis, or even a pair of running shoes. Regardless of how your winter activities take shape, be sure to add some strength training to make sure you can hit your 2027 goals.

The workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training. Each exercise targets a different part of the body to dial in the strength you need when you are trying to power up climbs next year. The workout can be done as a stand-alone set of exercises or it can be added on to your current strength training blueprint.

So many cyclists want to just spend time in the saddle for training—that’s great up to a point. Eventually we all need to get off the bike and spend some time strength training to help break through those frustrating plateaus. These three overlooked exercises can help you elevate your climbs for 2027.

Recent findings suggest that today I had my first hill-focused ride after a few weeks focusing on running and trainer rides. The first steep pitch rapidly reminded me how much I use my upper body while getting up a hill on the bike. As I climbed, I felt myself pulling on the handlebar with each pedal stroke while gravity was trying to pull me back. Developing the pull muscles is something that will benefit the whole kinetic chain while climbing. Bent-over rows in particular are a great upper-body exercise for this because they engage multiple muscle groups for one movement pattern. Rows can be done with so many different types of equipment: dumbbells, kettlebells, TRX Suspension Systems, elastic bands, and more. Here’s how I recommend doing them with dumbbells.

One of the reasons I love deadlifts for cyclists is because they are exercises that works almost all the muscles through the kinetic chain in one simple move. As we climb, we are pulling energy through our upper body, driving through the hips, and pushing the power through our legs into the pedals. This exercise trains the muscles through your arms, back, and core, while simultaneously working the muscles throughout your legs. Another reason deadlifts are one of my go-to exercises is that they can be done with several different types of equipment. My favorite equipment for this exercise is a barbell, but deadlifts can be done with dumbbells and kettlebells too.

It has been revealed that recovery Tip: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is very real, and depending on the person, your muscle burn can last for a few days after your training session. Plan accordingly for your rides following a heavy weight day. Listen to your body and add a recovery ride or off-bike activity if that's what you need.

Sources indicate that your core is what ties everything in your body together, so it is integral to grow your stability and power here. While riding today, I was trying to really be in tune with how I was using my core when climbing. When I was in the saddle I felt like the focus from my core was on stability, allowing for a sound upper body while pushing power through my legs and out of the pedals. My simple go-to core exercise to improve climbing is a plank with cross-body knee taps. This works stability through your core while working the internal obliques through the cross-body motion of the knee tuck. This exercise will really show its gains when you get out of the saddle as the climb pitches up.

In a recent development, A quick note on consistency: strength training will give you the best results when you incorporate it in your blueprint week after week. It will offer significantly diminished results if you are sprinkling it in sporadically. If you are able to, try to commit to adding strength training consistently for a four- to six-week block and see how that impacts your rides.

Sources indicate that our strength training program can help get you started with a more in-depth workout blueprint. It’s important to remember it does not matter where you are in your cycling journey, there are gains to be found from adding some level of strength training to your calendar.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Latest Update: 3 Subtle Breathing Exercises You Can Do at the Dinner Table

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are certain occasions that call for covert calm.
  • Practicing breathwork, even the quiet kind, can affect your physiological, mental, and emotional state, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and easing your entire being out of panic mode.
  • Industry observers note that if you’re already dealing with low-level overwhelm, drawing attention to yourself and your nerves is likely the last thing you want to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are certain occasions that call for covert calm. You know what I mean. Those times when you’re incredibly stressed, uncomfortable, or anxious but can’t really extricate yourself from the situation. Take, for example, the occasion dinner. If the thought of a large gathering and non-stop (as well as unfiltered) conversation fills you with even a slight sense of unease, subtle breathing exercises might just be your new favorite mindfulness practice.

Your breath is a powerful tool. Practicing breathwork, even the quiet kind, can affect your physiological, mental, and emotional state, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and easing your entire being out of panic mode. Known as pranayama in yoga, breathwork is a broad category, allowing you to find the breathing that resonates with you and return to it whenever signs of stress arise.

Industry observers note that if you’re already dealing with low-level overwhelm, drawing attention to yourself and your nerves is likely the last thing you want to do. So, rather than jumping up from the table for a quick yoga pose or engaging in a liberating round of lion’s breath, subtle breathing exercises invite you to remain in your chair, appearing engaged as you regulate your nervous system.

Sources indicate that start with a count of 3 or 5 rounds of each of these breaths and see how you feel. If the tension is still palpable, take as many as you need to self-soothe. And if you forget any of the below in your situation, simply lengthen your exhalations.

Sources indicate that also known as diaphragmatic breathing, belly breathing invites you to take your deepest breath possible. At it’s core, this breathing exercise is about (surprise!) inhaling into your belly. This is, of course, anatomically incorrect. But think of the larger goal here, which is to direct your inhalations toward your belly without exaggerating the movement in your ribs. The results is the diaphragm lowers and creates space to breathe into your actual lungs.

In a recent development, belly breathing also gets your breath out of your upper chest, which is the sort of shallow, stunted breathing that often accompanies anxiety. Slowing and deepening your breath signals safety, reminding your animal self that this is not a moment for fight, flight, or freeze—even if it feels like one.

Sometimes evening things out is the answer. Box breathing involves a simple pattern of inhaling for a count of four, holding for a count of four, exhaling for a count of four, and holding for a count of four, thus (figuratively) creating a sort of square shape with your breath. If four is too short of a count for your natural breathing, you can change your number to five, six, or beyond, so long as each part of the breath (inhalation, exhalation, and holds) remains even.

Turning even part of your attention away from the group and toward your own breath gives you a break from the noise while demonstrating the power of your own body and mind. Box breathing is often used for focus, so don’t be surprised if you return to the conversation with more interest and alertness.

The simplest option on this list, equal breathing is all about matching your inhalations to your exhalations. This is a practice of balance, so track the count of a deep inhalation, and if it feels okay in your body, apply it to your exhalation. It’s also the most adaptable, so feel free to vary the count slightly. You don’t want to stress yourself out, after all.

In addition to providing the aforementioned benefits of breathwork, redirecting your focus places your entire being in neutral, enabling you to consider your current circumstance with more clarity and calm.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the best folding treadmills give you a real running experience without permanently eating up your floor space.
  • If you're like me and you want to be able to run a treadmill at home, but you can’t give away valuable space to a huge piece of fitness equipment?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that the best folding treadmills give you a real running experience without permanently eating up your floor space. I adore having a folding treadmill at home, because, living in a smaller space, I can easily stash it away or bring it out for a go. And this time of year, when there's sleet and snow? I don't want to miss out on a workout.

If you're like me and you want to be able to run a treadmill at home, but you can’t give away valuable space to a huge piece of fitness equipment? We get it. There’s a solution, though: A folding treadmill gives you the ability to pack up and store your ’mill between runs. Their compact size and light weight comes at a cost: They often don’t have as many convenient features we expect from a top-of-the-line model, nor do they offer huge inclines and top speeds. That stated, most can do the basics effectively when you need them to, then fit in your closet when you’re done. The best folding treadmills, as we see them, offer a range of sizes and prices for casual runners and athletes in training.

The dream of shoving your treadmill under your bed between runs is alive in the Echelon Stride-6. This high-performance mill features a full-size, 20.5- by 60-inch running deck that can hit a max speed of 12.5 mph, but still manages to fold up tight. Personally, I store mine upright against a wall, sometimes hidden behind a curtain. It takes up about as much space as a few snowboards or a couple of winter coats. No, I'm not kidding, it's just that compact.

Industry observers note that the Stride-6’s belt features low-response cushioning that creates a ride that feels closer to outdoor road running than treadmill running, which I love when I’m training for road races. Also, as an autistic sensory seeker, sometimes I really enjoy beating the hell out of the deck after a bad day. Are you also a sensory seeker, or have one in your life? If so, this is a solid choice. At full speed, with a 12 percent incline, this machine gives as good as it gets, too.

This treadmill does not have a touchscreen, though. Instead, it syncs directly to a running watch or tablet, for which it has an extra-large holder. The pre-loaded running programs are fine and dandy, but nothing to write home about. Echelon produces a paid workout video library like NordicTrack’s iFit, which you can access via an app, but it’s no different than any other virtual workout platforms without native support on the treadmill.

Let’s talk a little more about the folding mechanism, though, because that’s the reason to buy this treadmill. It is one of only a handful of options that doesn’t require any assembly. Unbox this beauty, unfold it, plug it in, and you’re good. It has an “autofold” feature that makes collapsing the treadmill feel seamless. All that you do is press the foot pedal, and the crossbar and board fold onto the surface of the treadmill. You can then store it flat on the ground or upright, which is a win for anyone who doesn’t have the permanent floor space available.

According to recent reports, also, after testing treadmill after treadmill in my house, I can confidently say my cats prefer the Stride-6, and I have no idea why. They're obsessed and I can't figure it out. It is also the easiest to store, fun to run on, and it's by far the easiest to move around.

It has been revealed that when this treadmill is folded, it practically disappears. Fully folded, it drops to under 11 inches tall, which is easily flat enough to slide under a bed or stand upright in a closet corner. For anyone training for a marathon in an apartment, a spare bedroom, or a shared space, you know the value there. The SwiftFold mechanism handles it in one motion, and there’s no assembly required.

According to recent reports, what I appreciate is that folding this flat usually means compromising on the machine underneath. This one doesn’t. You still get a dual brushless 4.0 HP motor, a 0–12 percent auto-incline, a 12.5 mph top speed, and a 300-lb weight capacity that matches most treadmills in its class. The 51.18 x 18.9-inch deck is a touch narrow for tall runners, and that is, admittedly an concern.But, when you add the real marathon course maps and an AI coach, along with that magical fold? At around $900 to $1,000 it’s a ‘mill that’s hard to say no to.

Urevo CyberMega Treadmill Review.

Industry observers note that I will be the first to admit I was incredibly skeptical about this machine. I mean, it folds up to be smaller than your average card table. I have luggage that’s bigger than the G5i. But, I hear the cawing coming because I need to eat crow. It’s surprisingly stable and fun to run on. It’s really pretty smooth. It is more road-like than cushioned, so if you’re expecting pillowy surfaces, you’ll be disappointed. But if you’re worried you’re going to feel the fold seam, or feel super penned in, you won’t.

Recent findings suggest that no, this is not a treadmill for tall runners. I’m 6-feet tall, and I’m at the tippy top end of the range of someone who should throw miles on this. But, that being remarked, if you’re shorter than I am, starved for space, and you want a folding treadmill with serious speed and incline, this is a fantastic option. One thing I will note, though: that first fold when you’re folding it isn’t as soft as you’d expect, and it’s kinda loud. But considering the fact that you could store it just about anywhere, and that it takes less than five minutes to set up and assemble? It’s freaking impressive as all get out. Like, truly wild territory, here.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for a serious running machine that also happens to fold, then you can’t do better than the NordicTrack Commercial 1750. Both Dengate and I really appreciated the feel of running on this machine, which has he called “Goldilocks” cushioning. The deck is firm enough that you don’t feel like you’re running on rubber but soft enough that it wasn’t as hard on our joints as a road run would be. We were also sold on the quick controls for both speed and incline changes, which are both easy to identify and toggle. I found that it stops a bit more abruptly than other NordicTracks: It’s not “knock you off your feet” fast, but there’s a little learning curve.

Sources indicate that the Commercial 1750 has a large running surface, which I appreciate as someone who tends to wander on the ’mill a bit. All NordicTracks come with a trial subscription to iFit, the brand’s virtual workout library, which gives you dozens of programs, like marathon training companions, guided runs, and more. It costs extra after the first 30 days, but I think it’s a distinctive and worthwhile option if you like a guided workout. Of course, you can run on this treadmill without iFit, too.

In a recent development, on to the folding: The frame is huge–it weighs over 300 pounds–so it needs the hydraulic lift help that gets it to fold. The process could be a hair easier, but the balanced weight makes it fairly simple. Moving the 1750, on the other hand, is tricky. Sure, it technically has wheels so that you can roll it around, but that requires tipping the machine and balancing it while you do. Once you place it, you can fold it, but you’re better off leaving it where it is.

The Horizon 7.0AT was the easiest treadmill to get started and learn how to use, but its simplicity holds it back from being the outright best. It’s an old-school treadmill with no touchscreen display or video components, and that limits options for programming. That being stated, it’s a very affordable option that gets the job done so long as you don’t need a guided workout or on-board entertainment.

The Horizon 7.0 does exactly what you expect and does a great job of it. It has a 20- by 60-inch running deck that’s plenty large enough for the majority of runners. I wish that it felt a little firmer underfoot, but other members of our team did not have the same complaint. The pre-loaded programs are easy to find if you know your way around a treadmill. (Most of the runners I spoke with are “set and forget” or running with program apps—which you can link through your watch or tablet—so it’s not a worry.) The toggles for speed and incline are intuitive and easy to use.

In a recent development, folding this one is nice and easy, thanks to a hydraulic assist mechanism. Moving it around is pretty easy, too: The wheels line up in a better place than the 1750. It shrinks by nearly 40 percent when folded, which is genuinely impressive when you consider its massive build and huge incline range. One thing to keep in mind, though: That steep incline lifts you fairly high, so I do not recommend it for basement gyms unless you blueprint on running flat, or you live in a fancy place with 9-foot basement ceilings.

Read Full Horizon 7.0AT Treadmill Review.

It has been revealed that I’ve never met a treadmill that folds up smaller than the WalkingPad R2. In keeping with the brand, it’s made for walking, with a top speed of 3.7 mph and speed walking at 7.5 mph. And honestly? It’s so compact that you could reasonably put one of these in your home as a more portable complement to a standard, non-folding treadmill without feeling cramped. Use it as an under-desk treadmill or move it around to wherever you can find some free space.

It’s a fantastic treadmill for anyone who wants to get moving when they’d otherwise be sitting around. It features a smaller deck, super-responsive cushioning, and whisper-quiet motor. You could walk on it during a Zoom call with your microphone unmuted, and people would be hard-pressed to hear it. The cushioning means that you’re not going to wear yourself out while you work, and keeps you from bouncing around so badly that you can’t type.

According to recent reports, one little thing I like about this folding treadmill is its smart “automatic mode,” which automatically detects your speed changes depending on where your feet are hitting the deck and adjusts as you go. That alone is worth the cost of the machine.

Sources indicate that folding this treadmill is a cinch, and so is storage, thanks to its low weight and small footprint. Even if you store it in a different room from where you use it, it’s only 55 pounds, so you can just haul it from space to space without any issue.

Sources indicate that the team at Runner’s World has been testing all things running for decades. We work year-round on everything from shoes to treadmills. Personally, I have been running for over 20 years, running multiple marathons and ultras, and treadmill training is a huge part of my regimen. And I’ve been professionally reviewing products for nearly a decade.

According to recent reports, runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate designed a rigorous testing protocol to measure a number of critical features in each and every treadmill that we test, and I wrote a specific rubric to test folding treadmills based on that protocol. This year alone, I have run on over 40 models, racking up almost 200 miles in the past several months. Dengate, who is “never not running,” has also put in miles on many of these models. With folding treadmills, there are several specific qualities we examine to separate the best from the just ok:.

Having the ability to fold should not make a treadmill any less useful. While it’s impossible for them to maintain all of the features of certain non-folding treadmills, many or most of them are every bit as good. Some are so gozZod that they even appear on many of our guides.

Sources indicate that even with a compact folding model, it’s key to plan ahead and measure out the spaces where you plan to use and/or store your treadmill. Keep in mind that you need at least 2 feet of clearance surrounding your treadmill in every direction while you’re running. As someone who has put a Cat-shaped hole in the wall of her basement because I lost my footing, I cannot recommend this enough.

There’s a Right Way to Fold and a Wrong Way to Fold.

This sounds like a no-brainer, but a folding treadmill should become more compact and easy to store when folded. There are a ton that technically have a folding mechanism but are not all that much smaller in their folded form. If the folded treadmill is too tall for a room, or if it doesn’t clear very much floor space, it doesn’t make sense.

A small running platform can prevent you from feeling comfortable at your full running stride, so we generally think that longer is better. (There are exceptions, of course: A walking pad doesn’t need a long belt.) Width is crucial for people with a wider stride or who tend to wander a bit, or those of us who run a bit duck-footed. A narrow belt can feel constricting when you’re running.

Don’t Worry Too Much About Max Speed and Incline.

It has been revealed that with folding treadmills especially, you only want as much power as you actually need. A faster max speed requires a bigger motor, which makes for a bigger, heavier treadmill. Most people will be just fine with 10 mph for running, and 3 or 4 mph for walking, so a huge motor isn’t necessary.

Inclines are controlled by a separate motor, so the same rule applies. Most of us don’t want to pretend we’re climbing Everest at the gym, so a 15 percent incline is overkill. It’s nice to have occasionally, but not a dealbreaker to go without.

What are some ways to stay safe on the treadmill while training?

Recent findings suggest that with the treadmill setting the pace for you, it is important to select a pace that you feel capable of walking or running at, and use the safety equipment provided. Be sure you know where the automatic stop switch is and where the speed adjustment buttons are before starting to run/walk.

Should I adjust my mileage while using a treadmill?

It has been revealed that because treadmill running can be easier than road running, you may need to increase your mileage (or adjust speed and incline) when training on the treadmill to get the same level of workout you get from running outdoors. However, many people find treadmill running far less mentally stimulating, making it difficult to do longer distances indoors.

Is a treadmill a good way for newbie runners or walkers to start?

In a recent development, there are benefits of starting your training on a treadmill. The external pacing of the treadmill allows you to set a desired pace, then not have to think about maintaining it once it’s set. Treadmills are also indoors, which means inclement weather can’t stop you from running. They also can have screens attached, allowing you watch reveals or follow a video workout instead of just listening to music. However, walking outdoors has been shown to be beneficial for mental health with the changes in scenery as you walk, increased vitamin D production from being in the sun, and decreased sensory stimulation with the absence of screens.

Over a five-night stay, you're looking at a cash outlay of $2,500 to $7,500. That's a trip many families save years for. With World of Hyatt points, that same night costs **25,000 points**. At a cash rate of $1,000 per night (a very achievable number at peak Ziva properties), you're extracting **4 cents per point** in value — and at $1,500 per night, you're pushing **6 cents per point**. The industry benchmark for a "good" hotel redemption is 1-2 cents per point. You're doubling or tripling that benchmark on a family vacation. The pricing inefficiency here is structural and beautiful: Hyatt's award chart is **fixed**, meaning they set a category for each property based on its tier, not its cash price. All-inclusive resorts are priced in the award chart like any other Hyatt — but the cash rate includes *every meal, every drink, every activity*. The loyalty program hasn't fully "priced in" the all-inclusive premium. That gap is your opportunity. For families pursuing FI, this redemption is especially powerful because the value scales with family size. Four people eating and drinking all day at a resort adds up fast in cash — but costs exactly the same 25,000 points whether it's two people or a family of six. The bigger your family, the more you win.

The core insight here is understanding what the 25,000 points actually buys — and why Hyatt's award chart creates an accidental arbitrage for all-inclusive resorts.

The key word is fixed: your points cost doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash prices do. Breaking: Think Your Saddle Is Too High? The Signs Every Cyclist Should Know Before Their Next Ride

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours.
  • Sources indicate that and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix.
  • To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A too-high saddle can feel fast for 10 minutes and terrible for the next two hours. It can show up as pain behind the knee, pressure in the saddle, numbness, or that familiar feeling that you’re reaching for the pedal instead of driving through it.

Sources indicate that and because saddle height is the foundation of bike fit, getting it wrong can send you chasing the wrong fix. Riders often blame the saddle itself, their bib shorts, or even their flexibility when the glitch is simply that the seat is a little too high.

To get the most out of your ride, consider a full bike fit—not just a saddle height change. Check out Bicycling’s Guide to the Perfect Bike Fit.

That said, saddle height is also where fit advice gets messy. There isn’t one perfect number that works for everyone, and the usual rules of thumb are only starting points. Your ideal height depends on your body, your mobility, your injury history, your cleat setup, and more.

Quick Signs Your Saddle May Be Too High• Pain behind the knee • Saddle sores or numbness • Discomfort where your hamstrings meet your glutes • Rocking hips while pedaling • Reaching for the pedal at the bottom of the stroke Quick Fix• Lower the saddle a few millimeters, do a real ride, and reassess.

Here’s how to tell whether your saddle may be too high and a simple at-home check you can do before your next ride.

In a recent development, saddle height is one of the first things riders adjust, and for good reason. When it’s close, you feel smoother and more comfortable. When it’s off, the problems can spread everywhere.

Sources indicate that but this is where people get tripped up: saddle height is important, but it is only one element in an interconnected system. If your cleats are in the wrong place, your saddle is too far forward or back, or your crankarms don’t suit you, changing saddle height alone may not solve much. It’s the beginning of fit, not the whole thing.

Industry observers note that A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel. Two riders with the same height and inseam may still end up at different saddle heights because bodies aren’t identical and neither are pedaling styles.

In a recent development, pain is the clearest warning that something in your position needs attention. Riding is hard. Suffering through an interval is one thing. Pain caused by pressure, strain, or repeated irritation from a bad setup is another.

A saddle that’s too high often highlights up in a few predictable ways:.

In a recent development, this is the classic one. If you feel pain at the back of the knee, especially after longer rides or harder efforts, a too-high saddle is one possible cause.

But not the only one. Fit problems tend to overlap. So treat this as a clue, not a verdict.

If the back of your pedal stroke feels strained, tight, or tuggy, especially when you’re trying to make power, your saddle may be a little high.+.

Industry observers note that A high saddle can make you unstable on the bike. Instead of sitting planted, you start shifting and searching. That extra motion can increase friction and pressure, which can mean hot spots, sores, and numbness.

If your hips are dropping side to side at the bottom of the pedal stroke, there’s a decent chance you’re compensating for too much saddle height.

In a recent development, some riders point their toes naturally. But if you’re really reaching at the bottom of the stroke and compensating by going toes-down, that can be another sign the saddle is too high.

Rocking hips can also happen with a saddle that’s too low. So can a toes-down pedaling style. Tight hamstrings, limited mobility, weak core stability, and other fit issues can all muddy the picture. Back-of-knee pain can come from saddle height, but it can also come from saddle fore-aft, cleat setup, or a combination of things.

That doesn’t make the signs worthless. It just means you should think in patterns, not absolutes.

If you have knee pain plus hip rocking plus pressure and instability in the saddle, now the case gets stronger.

Todd Carver, Specialized’s human performance manager, shared a simple check that can help flag a saddle that may be too high.

If the distance from heel to pedal is more than about one centimeter, your saddle could be too high.

The result is a prompt to look closer, not a green light to make significant changes without further investigation.

According to recent reports, don’t make a giant change. That’s how you turn one problem into several problems.

Industry observers note that start small. Lower the saddle a few millimeters at a time, then ride it long enough to notice whether the change actually helps. One short spin around the block is not enough. You want enough ride time to see whether the pain eases, whether your pedaling feels smoother, and whether you stop shifting around on the saddle.

If you’re dealing with persistent pain, don’t keep self-diagnosing forever.

A good fit pro can sort out whether saddle height is the actual problem or just the most obvious symptom.

Riders fixate on saddle height because it feels fundamental. And it is. But it’s also just one part of a system.

A high saddle can absolutely cause trouble. So can cleat position. So can saddle setback. So can crank length. So can your mobility. The goal is not to chase some magic formula you found online. It’s to get to a position that lets you pedal smoothly, make power comfortably, and finish rides feeling worked, not damaged.

That’s why the best takeaway is a modest one: use the common signs, do a quick check, make small changes, and listen to what your body tells you.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

The first snowfall can be magical, but overcast skies and visible breath during a run can dampen the enthusiasm of any runner impatient for spring. To survive the everlasting cold, the trick is to layer properly so you don’t feel miserable during winter training. Stocking up on a winter running jacket, leggings, and pants is a no-brainer, but don’t forget to accessorize. I’m talking gloves here.

As a constantly cold person who has three sweatshirts piled onto the back of her office desk chair, I’ll never forget that one Santa 5-Miler when I left my gloves in my car. As I squeezed my hands into fists trying to retain warmth as I raced, I swore to never again run a winter race without full coverage over my five digits.

This winter has tested my cold-weather tolerance, dipping below zero degrees Fahrenheit more than once. But it’s a perfect breeding ground for glove—and mitten—testing. Here are my top picks.

According to recent reports, I’ve worked at RW for eight years and started running XC in high school. I learned to embrace the cold this year, testing most of the gloves included on this list. I judged them by insulation, dexterity, and fit. I also had a little help from male staffers, who tested the men’s version of gloves—and became aghast learning that the women’s wasn’t similar.

Contributor Nick Hilden also provides tips on what to look for when shopping for gloves and answers your frequently asked questions on when to wear them, and on sizing and fit.

Recent findings suggest that the Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove is included in our Best Winter Gear for Runners guide because it checks off all the boxes: double-knit insulation, reflective lining, windproof panels, and touchscreen-compatible fingertips. The stitching on the long cuffs ensures a secure, tailored fit around the wrists.

Sources indicate that the Active Fleece kept my fingers warm for an hour during 32-degree and slightly below freezing runs. When the temperature dropped to 20, my fingers started to ache after a half hour in the cold.

Sources indicate that my main critique is that they’re unisex sizing only. Even the smallest size, extra small, left some room above my fingertips, which made it difficult to grasp items I pocketed and zippers. The patch on the palm didn’t reach past my thumb and forefinger, which would have provided a soft area for nose wiping.

Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated Glove Review.

It has been revealed that these gloves by the Swoosh are great for easing into cold weather. The sizing is sex-specific and true-to-size. They’re favorable for their sleek construction, making dexterity possible when you need to refuel midrun—or just grab your apartment key—and don’t want to remove your gloves.

It has been revealed that because of their thinness, your fingertips may start to ache once the thermometer hits below freezing. Still, they’re a great pair when you’re transitioning into colder weather or have a higher threshold to the cold.

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com.

When you’re pitting gloves against mittens, it’s dexterity versus warmth. Gloves allow you to use your fingers, but mittens keep them together, thereby minimizing heat loss.

Even though I felt like I was running with oven mitts on my hands (the sizing is small/medium, medium/large), the Convertible Zip Mittens were great for braving workouts that dipped into the teens—and tens. The extra room also allows for doubling up if you really want to head out when it’s minus 1 degree Fahrenheit or less.

The Velcro tabs allow you to tighten the fit around the wrists, and the interior lining feels as plush as the felt on my very authentic Robin Hood hat from Nottingham.

According to recent reports, if you’re prone to losing a mate when things come in pairs, TrailHeads sees you: a buckle guarantees your left and right mitt won’t be separated. Afraid of losing both mitts? Attach them to a carabiner on your duffel using the loops on the cuffs. The reflective zipper is a nice touch if you need to use your fingers midrun.

My one issue with the mittens: the material on the thumbs leaves snot trails.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

My coworkers thought I was heading out on the slopes or wearing garden gloves, but the Ibex Kilometer isn’t just for skiers (or gardeners). After a stretch of testing during a brief stay in Newly introduced York City, the Kilometer gets my runner seal of approval. I tested them while logging runs in Central Park and the Hudson River Greenway, hitting gusts of wind on rolling hills and by the water. Temperatures varied from 20 to 40 degrees Fahrenheit; the Kilometer made my workouts more bearable.

It has been revealed that the leather palms had excellent grip when I ran holding my phone, trying to find the best route back to my hotel. My fingers were shielded from the river’s wind chill and the ribbed cuffs kept my wrists toasty. But the biggest win for me was the soft, absorbent patch of fabric on each thumb. They were perfect for swiping my very runny nose when the wind speed was 15 mph.

Industry observers note that if you run with your phone and whip it out a bunch of times midrun, these are your gloves; almost the entire palm is patterned with silicone grips. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible and sizing is sex-specific, which translates to no bunched fingers or agitation trying to scroll.

These gloves aren’t for extreme weather, but they’re great when things start to get nippy or when you’re heading out for a short winter run. However, there’s one thing TrailHeads must rectify: It’s a travesty that only the men’s version has a nose wipe patch. Why did they skimp on this feature with the women’s edition?

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

These aren’t the cotton gloves you wore in grade school. The Smartwool Liner offers so much more in terms of warmth and quality; it all starts with the woven material.

The fabric is merino wool, which regulates warmth, controls odors, and dries fast. The fingertips are touchscreen-compatible, and you’re not limited to a small patch on the thumb when you need to wipe your nose (the glove itself is real estate). The ribbed cuffs fit snug, even on small wrists. They’re great to wear when the temperature is mid-30s; maybe even lower if you don’t have near-Raynaud’s hands like mine.

Sources indicate that despite coming in unisex with no extra-small option, I was surprised how well the small Vortex Gloves fit my hands and how easy it was to use my phone and text. The fleece layer feels soft on my skin and I’ll honestly never understand why a glove/mitt hybrid is so underrated. The mitten hood serves as wind protection; it’s great on gusty runs or when the temperature slowly rises. You can tuck in the entire hood above the wrist, with the hi-vis tape still partially showing.

Industry observers note that the gloves aren’t for extreme cold, however. I ran in the Vortex Windblock when the temperature dipped in the teens and not even the mitt hood could stop my fingers from aching. That’s not the worst knock, since we’ve had abnormal weather below 10 degrees and most gloves on this list either didn’t make the cut or only lasted for half an hour before I had to ball my hands in the palms.

The Vortex Windblock also has snaps on the cuffs so you can store them attached.

Sources indicate that prone to losing your gloves? The snap on the lululemon Fast and Free prevents accidental separation and it’s just one standout reason you should buy this pair.

These sleek gloves have silicone grippers to keep you from dropping your phone midrun midtext, as well as “screen-conductive” finger pads that allow you to use your touchscreen.

Striking reflectivity details the back of the Fast and Free. That fabric is also soft enough to swipe your nose without causing the skin on your nostrils to peel.

Shop Men’s at shop.lululemon.com | Shop Women’s at lululemon.com.

What to Consider by Nick Hilden.

It has been revealed that winter runners should look for a pair of lightweight gloves that are warm enough to keep your hands cozy, but breathable enough to let air circulate. Look for technical fabrics—polyester and other synthetic materials are often your best bet for finding that balance.

In a recent development, some blends are better than others though. In case of bad weather, it also makes sense to keep an eye out for a weather-resistant material that can protect against rain and snow, as well as cold, cutting winds. Moisture-wicking materials, such as merino wool, can also help deal with sweat and mitigate the impact of cold rain.

I also like when a glove fabric contains a small amount of a stretchy material, such as spandex or elastane, to ensure the gloves fit comfortably and snug. That said, skip the stretch if you like a glove that feels roomy inside.

On the other hand, I recommend avoiding heavy gloves made from nylon or polyurethane. These materials are often thicker, warmer and weatherproof, so they’re more likely to make you overheat. (Depending on the design, they may also make it hard to use your phone or check your smartwatch.).

Recent findings suggest that everyone has their own Goldilocks spot for how much warmth they need from their gloves. The crucial thing to keep in mind is that your body feels warmer while you’re running–speaking broadly, we recommend dressing for a run as if it's 10- to 20 degrees warmer than the temperature outside (including the wind chill.) That’s a good rubric for determining both when to start wearing gloves in the winter, and the level of protection you want against the cold.

According to recent reports, thinking about gloves specifically, your running gloves probably shouldn’t be as warm as your everyday winter gloves. A warmer glove will keep you going in colder temperatures but will cause you to sweat more, so it may not feel comfortable for long.

According to recent reports, winter nights come early, so visibility is an essential concern for all cold-weather running gear. If you frequently run near a road, or in areas with little street lighting, every item of clothing you wear, head to toe, should feature a reflective or high-visibility element.

Sources indicate that in fact, gloves are among the most important pieces of reflective running gear you can wear. They catch drivers’ eyes especially well because your hands move as you run, creating a more noticeable effect.

When should I start wearing running gloves in the winter?

It has been revealed that every person feels differently about gloves, but as I noted earlier in the piece, experts recommend dressing for a run as if it’s 10 degrees warmer than the effective temperature with the wind chill. If you normally wear gloves on a 50-degree day, start putting on gloves when it’s 40 degrees.

A good running glove should fit snug around your hand. If there’s room for your hand to move inside the glove, your skin may rub against the fabric and start to chafe. At the same time, it’s important to make sure they aren’t too tight, which might reduce circulation.

Industry observers note that one way to check if you have the right fit is by doing a pinch test. Put on one glove, then pinch the fabric at the tip of a finger with your other hand. Ideally, you should have about a quarter inch of extra room.

Recent findings suggest that most glove brands use one of two measurements to determine sizing: The circumference of your fingers at the knuckles (without the thumb), and full hand length from the base of the hand to the tip of the middle finger. Check the product listing on the glove to see how the brand measures.

Sources indicate that to measure the knuckle circumference, hold your fingers together, then wrap a measuring tape around your knuckles. Don’t squeeze your fingers too tight, though.

When measuring your full hand, make sure your middle finger is fully extended to ensure a proper measurement.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Recent findings suggest that nick Hilden is a writer, globetrotter, and jack-of-many-talents who has written gear reviews for the likes of  Runner’s World, Popular Science, Men’s Health, Thrillist, the Daily Beast, the Los Angeles Times, Greatist, and the Manual, and his lifestyle, culture, and tech writing has also appeared in Scientific American, Afar, Salon, Vice, Healthline, and many others. Before entering journalism some 15 years ago, he worked as a bartender, brewery manager, sound engineer, recording and touring musician, cook, teacher, and in a variety of other trades. These days, he lives all over the world, performs music sporadically, and spends a lot of time thinking how to best improve his Honda Element conversion.

Industry News: Best Cheap Exercise Bikes That Feel Surprisingly Expensive

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, there are plenty of reasons to start riding inside.
  • Sources indicate that recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, there are plenty of reasons to start riding inside. Questionable weather, overly packed schedules, and less daylight can cause outdoor riders to head inside for some indoor saddle time. It’s also possible you’re someone who doesn’t ride outside and you just want a good low-impact workout in the comfort of your own home—without breaking the bank.

Sources indicate that recently we did extensive testing in the office on different exercise bikes. I found that some people who don’t ride bikes outside may actually prefer some of the less expensive exercise bike options. Some of the higher-end exercise bikes we tested feel like a real bike outside—and pair with specific apps like Zwift for when you want to get some group rides or racing in. If you aren’t used to a bike outside, then getting comfortable in that position can be a hard transition. More narrow saddles, a more aggressive position, and controls that simulate the shifters on a bike may not be what you want. Largely, these more inexpensive exercise bikes have more upright positions, wider and more padded saddles, and controls that would resemble the exercise bike you might see on the floor of a fitness center.

Keep in mind that inexpensive is relative—the bikes we have on this list range from about $200 up to $700. If you’re looking to boost your mood, stay consistent, or supplement your training with an affordable indoor cycling bike, these cheap exercise bikes deliver the best mix of value, performance, and reliability.

If you're further along in your indoor training journey and none of the bikes on this list feel like the right fit, take a look at our reviews of the Peloton, Zwift Ride V2, and other premium models.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike operates a 35-pound flywheel that provides a smooth and quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable via a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately, if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches, and allows riders to adjust the handlebar height as well as the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Using the single-button monitor, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned as you exercise. Just below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame is designed to provide stability and durability, but it's easy to move if you tip it up onto the small wheels on the front edge.

It has been revealed that besides being designed to look like an entry-level Peloton, the Yesoul S3’s biggest selling point is its Bluetooth connectivity, which pairs with the Yesoul Sports App (on both iOS and Android) and works with Zwift and other interactive training apps. All your workout data, including distance, time, calories burned, speed, heart rate, odometer, and cadence, is tracked and easy to access.

The bike has a quiet belt drive and magnetic resistance, with 100 levels that are easy to adjust with a knob. With a height- and distance-adjustable seat and handlebar, the S3 is built to fit riders from 4-feet-9-inches to 6-feet-2-inches—though riders at the higher end of that range and those with disproportionately longer legs might find the riding position to feel a bit “off.” The bike is easy to move on two small transport wheels, and it comes in both white and black models for a sleek, Peloton-like aesthetic.

This is a fantastic price for a budget bike that delivers a Peloton-like experience. It has the same sleek silhouette, with a saddle that adjusts both up/down and fore/aft, plus an adjustable handlebar height—just like the real thing. The belt-drive system is another big plus, keeping noise to a minimum so the only sounds you hear are your own effort (and hopefully some music to cover it up).

Industry observers note that to keep costs down, this bike skips the large built-in display, instead offering a tablet holder and Bluetooth connectivity. That means you can ride with any third-party app you prefer—including Peloton classes—using your own device. At this price, it’s a fair trade-off. But if you want a built-in screen, Merach offers a similar model with that feature for about $450 more.

According to recent reports, merach’s newest bike, the A26 Aura, is one of the best Peloton competitors I’ve seen. It follows the familiar design cues of premium exercise bikes — a sturdy frame, heavy flywheel, and whisper-quiet belt-drive system. The seat adjusts up and down as well as fore and aft, and the handlebar also moves vertically for a comfortable fit.

At its current sale price, the Merach A26 Aura makes a compelling case as one of the best values on this list.

Recent findings suggest that the Echelon Connect Sport 2 delivers a Peloton-like experience at a more affordable price. It connects via Bluetooth to the Echelon Fit app, allowing you to track speed, distance, and calories. If you’re taking a live class, you can also view your ranking on the leaderboard. The app offers over 40 live classes daily and a library of more than 15,000 on-demand sessions. While the bike doesn’t have a built-in screen, its device holder accommodates tablets up to 8 inches wide.

That remarked, you don’t need the connected features to get a great workout. At its core, this is a solid, well-built exercise bike with a heavy flywheel and 32 resistance levels, manually adjusted with a knob behind the handlebar. The bike features a “one size fits most” design, with adjustable saddle and handlebar positions to suit most adults. However, some shorter riders have reported difficulty positioning the saddle close enough to the handlebars for a comfortable fit.

In a recent development, with Bluetooth and USB connectivity to the Schwinn ConnectTM, Zwift, and MyFitnessPal apps, this stationary bike is a great option for interactive workouts—particularly if you want to work through pre-programmed sessions and track your progress over time. The bike has the standard DualTrack console shared by similar-level Schwinn and Nautilus products, which has two sharp, backlit LCD screens loaded with 29 workouts.

Unlike many of the bikes we've selected that adjust gradually in difficulty at the turn of a knob, this model has 25 preset levels of magnetic resistance, which provides a nice range in difficulty. The seat and handlebar adjust by height and angle to fit users from 4-feet-6-inches to 6-feet-6-inches; however, as always, those at the far ends of the range might have more difficulty getting a comfortable fit. Ultimately, the bike is a solid package for the price—especially if you can catch one on sale for around $400.

According to recent reports, looking for a cheap home exercise bike that will neither take over your space nor break the bank? When not in use, this compact device folds down to half its size and can be easily rolled into a closet or tucked under a bed.

Recent findings suggest that while it may have a minimalist design, it still has the basic functionality needed for a workout. It touts 12 levels of magnetic resistance, adjusted via a knob below the handlebar, that allows you to adjust the intensity as needed. The built-in LCD screen, although very basic, keeps track of key workout stats, including distance, time, speed, calories burned, and heart rate.

Sources indicate that consumers love how quiet this bike is, making it perfect for multitasking or watching TV while riding. Though it may not provide the high resistance some hardcore riders seek, many praise it as a “sturdy, well-built machine” with a “comfortable seat and great height adjustability.”.

Recent findings suggest that just like with a regular bicycle, if you want the best experience on your indoor bike, it’s important to get the proper fit. Josh Taylor, a global brand ambassador for the online fitness site Spinning, recommends finding an indoor cycling bike that puts you in the same position as the bike you’re accustomed to riding outside.

For example, if your daily rider is a road bike, look for an indoor cycling bike with a handlebar option that incorporates a traditional bullhorn bar and mimics the hand-position options of drops and brake hoods. However, if you’re already used to taking studio classes, an indoor cycling bike with just the traditional bullhorn-style bar will work great, claims Ben Sharp, three-time Order of Ikkos medal recipient and founder of Sharp Coaching.

Sources indicate that if you don’t ride at all outside or in a spin class yet, then it will take a bit more playing around with the exercise bike to figure out sizing and position. Start with getting saddle height set up correctly, then if you can adjust reach to the handlebars that’s step two. For the reach shoot to have a slight bend in the elbows and remember to keep your shoulders relaxed and away from your ears. Matt Phillips, Senior Test Editor at Bicycling, recently published a story on dialing in saddle height. What applies to saddle height on an outdoor bike largely applies to exercise bikes as well. “A common starting point is a height that provides around 30 degrees of knee bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock position). But that is a starting point only, not gospel,” claims Phillips.

Join Bicycling All Access for more in-depth gear reviews.

When you’re riding an outdoor bike, you’re mostly working against inertia as you pedal. In order to recreate that sensation and effort on a stationary bike, manufacturers have to simulate that resistance in some way. Most choose to use a fan or a flywheel (a weighted disc that spins as you pedal).

Flywheels work by storing inertia as they spin, and smoothing out the pedal stroke to eliminate that choppy up and down motion you’d otherwise experience. For most budget spin bikes, a heavier flywheel means a smoother ride, though some bikes opt for a light (8-pound) flywheel that maintains its inertia by spinning four times as fast instead.

Since the pedals on spin bikes are fixed to the flywheel (no coasting), the smooth-moving mechanism helps keep your pedaling consistent. These bikes will usually have a knob or lever that allows you to adjust the resistance, making it harder or easier to pedal, independent of your cadence (how fast you’re spinning the pedals). If you’re used to riding a bike outside, then think about it like riding a fixed-gear bike or fixie.

Fan-operated resistance bikes are a bit simpler: As you pedal, the fan blades push against the air around the machine. Your cadence is directly related to the amount of effort required to push the pedals, meaning these bikes don’t allow you to spin at a fast cadence with low resistance, which can be nice for warming up or cooling down.

#138131. After a Decade of Refusing to Use a Treadmill, I Finally Gave In. Here’s How It’s Making Me a Better Runner.
