  • Lie on your back with your arms and legs straight, as if you were in Savasana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve been feeling ultra stiff lately, a five-minute yoga-inspired stretching routine break to release physical tension can feel like a full-body reset, helping you feel better in your body—and even more productive—so you can do all of your favorite activities.

Industry observers note that this short practice is ideal when you need a short break during the workday, but it can also serve as a grounding moment before you sit at your desk or when you’re winding down in the evening. You only need a yoga mat and a sturdy surface to practice on. Come exactly as you are.

Lie on your back with your arms and legs straight, as if you were in Savasana. Take some small movements, maybe wiggling your fingers and toes or moving your head side to side. Then let yourself relax for a moment. Inhale as you reach your hands overhead and your feet away from you, stretching your entire body from head to toe. Exhale and release.

Bend your knees, plant your feet on the mat about hip-distance apart, and rest your arms at your sides. Inhale, press your hands and feet into the mat, and lift your hips in Bridge Pose. Exhale and lower your hips to the mat.

Separate your feet slightly wider than your hips. Bend your elbows and draw your arms into a cactus shape. Exhale and allow your knees to lower toward the left. Inhale and return your knees to center. Exhale and lower your knees toward the right. Repeat Windshield Wipers two more times on each side.

Hug both knees toward your chest, grasping your shins or the backs of your thighs with your hands.

Industry observers note that come to a comfortable sitting position. Lift your shoulders toward your ears, then roll them back, down, and forward. Continue drawing circles with your shoulders in one direction for a few rounds, then switch directions.

Interlace your fingers behind your head with your elbows out to the sides. Exhale as you draw your navel toward your spine, round your back, and lower your chin toward your chest in a Cat Pose variation. Inhale as you lift upright and arch your back, drawing your elbows back slightly in a Cow Pose variation. Repeat a few times.

Inhale and reach your arms overhead. Exhale and twist your chest toward the left. Place your right hand on your left knee and your left fingertips on the mat behind you. Take a few breaths here.

Sources indicate that still sitting, come back to center and bring your arms into a cactus shape. Open your hands as wide as you can, spreading your fingers apart. Then shut your hands into tight fists. Repeat opening and closing your hands as many times as feels good.

It has been revealed that sit on the mat with your knees bent, your feet flat on the mat, and your hands on the mat behind your hips, fingertips pointing toward you or toward the back of the mat. Press into your hands and feet as you lift your hips off the mat. Draw your chin toward your chest and gaze forward. Take a few breaths here, then lower your hips to the mat.

Recent findings suggest that draw the soles of your feet together. Inhale and lift your chest. Your feet can come closer to you or stay farther away. Exhale and fold forward, grasping your ankles or feet in Bound Angle Pose. You can stack your fists on top of each other and rest your forehead on them. Breathe here.

Lie on your back with your arms resting at your sides and your palms pressing into the mat. Bend your knees toward your chest and straighten your legs so your feet are reaching toward the ceiling. Keep your legs slightly bent if it’s more comfortable. Take a few breaths here, then shake out your arms and legs and lower your feet to the mat.

In a recent development, lie on your back, resting your arms, legs, hands, and feet against the mat in Savasana. Or find a comfortable seated position. Take a few deep breaths before returning to the day.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines at the moment offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity.
  • According to recent reports, here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike.
  • Recent findings suggest that at Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines at the moment offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity. Popular in the CrossFit community, this fan bike consists of a belt-driven system and a heavy-duty steel frame, making it a great tool to build both endurance and strength.

According to recent reports, here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike. We put it through hours of strenuous cardio workouts to see if it could take on the challenge. In this Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X review, we’ll highlight our results, how well the bike ranked in testing, and how it compares to other fan bikes.

Recent findings suggest that at Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment. We have a product testing team that has put hundreds of machines through the wringer, using them for everything from gentle warm-ups to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workouts. Many of our staff members are home gym owners themselves and use these products nearly every day.

With the knowledge we’ve gained over the years, we created a proprietary scoring system that we used to rank the AssaultBike ProX in various categories. Not only did we evaluate how the bike performed on its own, but we also compared it with nearly 30 other exercise bikes to see how it stacked up against the competition.

From the founders of the AssaultRunner (one of the best treadmills to train with), the Assault Bike ProX is made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat that helps keep it corrosion-resistant and capable of standing the test of time. It is a top-tier fan bike that can provide a brutal workout for any athlete.

In a recent development, in addition to its tough and durable frame, it incorporates a belt-driven system for a quiet, smooth training experience. It also requires less upkeep than chain-driven systems, which should come as a relief to busy individuals who can’t be bothered with complicated maintenance protocols.

It has been revealed that at the time of writing, the Assault Bike ProX costs $899. Fortunately, there is also an option to finance it at around $82 a month through Affirm. For comparison, the Assault Bike ProX is more expensive than the AssaultBike Classic at $699 but cheaper than the Concept2 BikeErg, which costs around $1,100.

According to recent reports, the Assault Bike ProX also provides free shipping, which is a significant deal for equipment this size. Buying an air bike from another brand could set you back another $100 in shipping costs.

All of the above considered, we’ve rated this bike 4 out of 5 stars for its shipping rate, finance options, and value.

The Assault Bike ProX weighs 125 pounds, has a max user weight of 330 pounds, and boasts a heavy-duty steel frame with a corrosion-resistant black powder coating finish. We love this type of frame and finish because it means less maintenance over time.

It’s also similar to what you would see with the Rogue Echo Bike, which has a black powder coating and almost looks like it was built from scraps of a heavy-duty squat rack! But the Assault Bike ProX isn’t as bulky as the Rogue Echo Bike, making it more compatible with small spaces, which our product testers enjoyed. For comparison, the ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high, while the Echo Bike is 55 inches long, 29.5 inches wide, and 52.25 inches high.

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX provides a wide padded seat that can adjust to 11 different heights and six different directions either forward or backward. These adjustments were the same on the Assault Bike Pro, which the ProX replaces. The rubber handles on the ProX help you maintain your grip and keep your hands comfortable throughout the workout as well.

Recent findings suggest that this fan bike also comes with footpegs at the base of the handlebars for you to place your feet. This gives you the option to do an upper body-only workout, which is great for injury recovery or arm day.

Based on the quality and construction of the Assault Bike ProX, we rated it 5 out of 5 stars.

According to recent reports, we gave the AssaultBike Pro X 5 out of 5 stars for delivery and assembly because of how straightforward it was to build. The bikes arrived at our testing facility 75 percent built, so all we had to do was attach the LCD console, pedals, handlebars, seat post, and saddle. Assault Fitness provides all the tools needed to build your air bike, and it should take roughly 35 to 45 minutes.

When testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a smoother and quieter ride than what we’ve experienced with other air bikes, like the Titan Fan Bike or the AssaultBike Classic. This is predominantly thanks to the belt-driven system. A belt-driven system requires less maintenance than a chain-driven system, but it is also harder to use. When you pedal, the steel fan wheel generates resistance based on your effort. The harder you pedal, the more resistance is applied.

Sources indicate that however, once you stop pedaling, the fan wheel will stop moving, requiring more effort to get it started again. This might be tough if you’re not prepared for a high-intensity workout. Due to this, we gave the Assault Bike ProX a 4 out of 5-star rating for performance.

The Assault Bike ProX’s LCD monitor provides seven built-in training programs and a competition mode for those ready to take on the challenge. Through the Assault Fitness App, which we’ll review below, there is also an option to follow instructor-led programs or create customized workouts.

All in all, we give it a 3 out of 5 star rating in this category. The included workouts aren’t as robust as what you’d see in a more interactive bike like the Peloton. However, we do appreciate having them and think they can be valuable for people who may not know where to start.

It has been revealed that while the AssaultBike Classic was only compatible with the Polar T34 heart rate chest strap, the Assault Bike ProX is compatible with other brands, like Garmin. You can link a heart rate monitor through the bike’s Bluetooth features. However, you need to purchase a compatible one separately, which is why we only rated it 4 out of 5 stars here (though to be fair, this is common for most exercise bikes).

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX comes with a five-inch by eight-inch monitor, which is a common size amongst other fan bikes. This high-quality LCD monitor is powered by four AA batteries, which Assault includes with your purchase. The console is great for tracking stats such as calories, distance, heart rate, speed, watts, and RPM. It also connects to the Assault Fitness App.

Our product testers loved that it could track power output in addition to distance and speed, which is a great measure of energy expenditure to quantify workout intensity. The Rogue Echo Bike monitor doesn’t provide feedback such as watts and RPM on its monitor, which gives the Assault Bike ProX the edge.

All things considered, we’ve given this bike 5 out of 5 stars for its display and tracking capabilities.

Sources indicate that when testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a ton of conveniences. First, the air bike requires no electric outlet, and we loved being able to use it anywhere. This feature is also a welcome benefit for commercial CrossFit gym owners, as you don’t have to worry about your members tripping over power cords.

In a recent development, other conveniences include a device holder and a water bottle holder. Some fan bikes like the Titan Fan Bike also include these conveniences. Others, like the Rogue Echo Bike, don’t (though they are available to purchase separately). We always appreciate it when a brand throws in little extras like this. They allow you to have all your workout essentials within reach. Plus, you don’t have to worry about potentially placing multiple orders or paying extra shipping fees to get them.

Industry observers note that overall, our product testers rated the conveniences 4 out of 5 stars. The only reason we docked a point is that we wish the bike came with a wind guard to prevent cold air from blowing in our faces when training in a cold garage. There is one available on the Assault Fitness website, but you have to buy it separately for an additional $39.

The Assault Bike ProX is a part of the Assault Fitness line of exercise machines that operate using the Assault Fitness app. The app was one of our product testers’ favorite features.

Free to download from the App Store and Google Play, the Assault Fitness App provides you with a multitude of instructor-driven workouts. You can do these workouts on your own or compete against other athletes virtually. Many of the workouts also integrate other types of equipment, such as dumbbells and kettlebells, to help you get more well-rounded programming.

Sources indicate that while we enjoyed the app, we only gave it 4 out of 5 stars. As of this writing, it’s not available on the most recent version of Android. Athletes with newer Android phones may not be able to use it.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is Bluetooth-enabled. We don’t necessarily consider Bluetooth connectivity a standout feature, as dozens of cardio machines we’ve tested now come with it. But we’ve also tried inexpensive cardio equipment that doesn’t have this feature, and even Assault Fitness’s classic AssaultBike lacks Bluetooth capabilities. As such, we rated the ProX 5 out of 5 stars here.

Sources indicate that when comparing other fan bikes we tested, the Assault Bike ProX generated less noise due to its belt-driven system. The belt-driven system operates more smoothly than chain-drive systems such as those on the Schwinn Airdyne. A noisier system can make it tough to perform workouts at home, especially if you train early in the morning or late at night when others are sleeping.

That remarked, no fan bike will be completely silent, so you should still expect some noise as air travels through the flywheel. Due to this, we give the noise level of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX offers some portability, thanks to two small transport wheels at the front. To move it, all you need to do is tilt it onto its wheels to help glide it across the floor. However, although it might be easy for some athletes to move this fan bike, others might struggle to relocate it because it weighs 125 pounds. Based on these findings, we give the portability of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

According to recent reports, the Assault Bike ProX has a three-year non-wear parts warranty and a seven-year frame warranty. The three-year non-wear parts warranty doesn’t cover normal wear and tear on parts like the seat, pedals, and handle grips. This may seem like a drawback, but in our experience, this is common in warranties on other brands’ fan bikes. But the length of Assault’s warranty is longer compared to Rogue, who only offers a two-year warranty on their Echo Bike, and Titan, who only offers a one-year warranty on their fan bike. We gave the warranty of the Assault Bike ProX 5 out of 5 stars for this reason.

The Assault Bike ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high. Compared to the classic AssaultBike, these dimensions are one to two inches bigger in each category. If you’re between the two, we definitely recommend measuring carefully to ensure you choose the one that will best fit your space.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is a fan bike, meaning it builds resistance based on how much air you recruit in the fan wheel as you work. The harder you pedal, the more air resistance is applied, making your workout more challenging.

In addition to air resistance, the ProX uses a belt-driven system, meaning it only operates when you begin to pedal. If you stop pedaling, the machine stops moving. This makes it harder to operate compared to a chair-driven system, like what you’d see with the AssaultBike Classic.

The weight capacity of the Assault Bike ProX is 330 pounds. This is more than the Classic bike, which holds 300 pounds, but less than the Elite, which holds up to 350 pounds.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike ProX can accommodate most body sizes with 11 different height settings and six front-to-back settings. These adjustment levels are relatively standard based on what we’ve seen on other fan bikes. However, some competitors like the Rogue Echo Bike only have five front-to-back seat settings.

In a recent development, because the Assault Bike ProX does not require an electrical outlet, you can transport it wherever you want to go —outdoors or indoors. The monitor, however, does require AA batteries to operate.

At first glance, it seems the Assault Bike ProX and Rogue Echo Bike have many similarities. When you analyze them more closely, you’ll find that there are several key differences between the two.

Below are the dimensions of both fan bikes:.

Industry observers note that even though the Rogue Echo Bike is bulkier in material and dimensions, it has the same 330-pound weight capacity as the AssaultBike ProX. Both of these fan bikes are also powered by movement, so no electrical outlet is needed. Further, weighing in at 123 and 125 pounds, respectively, the Rogue Echo Bike and the Assault Bike ProX are equally portable, especially given they both have wheels.

Finally, both products use belt-driven mechanics, providing a smooth and quiet riding experience. But the Assault Bike ProX gives more metrics on the monitor, such as watts and RPM. This feature alone could make or break your decision, depending on how important tracking is to your training.

In a recent development, the Assault Bike ProX comes in with a strong 4.6 out of 5-star rating on the Assault Fitness website. Many users claim that it is super easy to set up, requires low maintenance, and is a favorite piece of equipment in their home gyms. Customers also praise its sturdiness and its ability to handle a tough workout.

One user mentioned that the left peg became loose during their workout. Another buyer mentioned that the Assault Bike ProX was very noisy and didn’t think it was as stable as other reviews might suggest — note, however, that complaints like this are in the minority.

According to recent reports, after extensive research and testing of the Assault Bike ProX, we can say that this air bike is worth it. Made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat, it can take on the toughest workouts. It’s ideal for anyone looking for a full-body, high-intensity interval training machine for improving both endurance and strength.

Industry observers note that the smoother and quieter experience you get with the Assault Bike ProX is thanks to the belt-driven system integrated into the design. Although this system might require more effort to operate, this bike can still be a great purchase for everyone from CrossFitters to health and fitness enthusiasts.

The Assault Bike provides a great workout, combining air resistance and a belt-driven system for a tough cardio and muscular endurance workout. You can use both the foot pedals and the arm handles to get a full-body workout. Or you can just use the arm handles to work out your upper body exclusively.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike Pro X is a belt-driven system. The fan bike only works when you operate the pedals and/or handlebars. The belt-driven system also offers a smoother and quieter workout.

Sources indicate that the AssaultBike alone may not aid fat loss if you’re eating too many calories. However,  it can provide a strong enough stimulus for an intense enough workout to help you burn more calories and hit multiple health and fitness goals.

It has been revealed that because the AssaultBike Pro X requires a full-body effort and utilizes a belt-driven system, you could potentially build a small amount of muscle by using it consistently. However, resistance training with implements like dumbbells or barbells (and following a diet that supports muscle growth) will be your best bet if you want to pack on as much muscle as possible.

#138118. Best GPS Bike Computers of 2026: 10 Editor-Tested Picks for Navigation, Training Data, and Battery Life

📅 25 Jun 2024 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2920 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

Best GPS Bike Computers of 2026: 10 Editor-Tested Picks for Navigation, Training Data, and Battery Life

📅 25 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.
  • I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides. Head units display common metrics like speed, distance, and power, and track and record your data, so you can download it and crunch the info after your rides. They’re also great for ride navigation and following pre-planned routes. Today’s leading head units put features from turn-by-turn GPS navigation to real-time performance analytics at your fingertips.

I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride. I do this to test more devices and log the many miles I pedal on different bikes and equipment. An upside of always riding with a GPS-equipped computer is mid-ride exploration and changing rides on the fly. Now, if I’m curious about a road or potential shortcut, I can check whether it goes where I think. And rerouting features on many computers let me cut rides short and head home if weather changes.

Sources indicate that many new bike computers integrate with popular platforms such as Strava, Trailforks, and Garmin Connect. Our favorite models offer real-time hill profiles on climbs and feature data-rich maps for precise navigation, even when descending switchback roads at speed. Some models even feature solar charging and real-time weather alerts. But beyond the fancy features, every bike computer does the same basic job—record your ride and display the data you need.

Sources indicate that since our editors and test team use cycling computers on nearly every ride, we’re constantly riding the newest models. Brands offer dozens of cycling-specific computers, and many have similar shapes, screens, and button layouts. However, as our testing has proven, the differences are in the details. And picking the right cycling computer for your needs makes rides much more enjoyable.

Buying Advice: Modern cycling computers operate a lot like cell phones (the Hammerhead is actually an Android-based platform). So, think of their operating systems like using a mobile device. What works for someone else might not be right for you, but that doesn’t make it a bad computer. Try computers before buying (if possible), because you cannot change the interface without getting a fresh device.

The Wahoo Elemnt Bolt V3 combines excellent features at a great price, making it a strong option for a wide range of cyclists. In his review of the Bolt V3, Test Editor Dan Chabanov dug into the revamped computer’s details. Its features include a 2.3-inch high-resolution display with 16 million colors for increased clarity and improved battery life (up to 20 hours). The Bolt’s interface still prioritizes information in an easy-to-read format and uses buttons rather than a touch screen.

According to recent reports, the Bolt displays grade and climb profiles that show difficulty by assigning different background colors depending on the hill’s gradient (red being the steepest). This makes it easy to see at a glance what the climb ahead of you will be like.

Wahoo computers feature an easy setup process and an intuitive companion app that connects to third-party tools. The Bolt V3 has 32 GB of onboard storage, which is enough to store maps for the United States and thousands of routes. The Elemnt Bolt V3 gives you everything you need (and nothing you don’t).

Garmin introduced the all-latest Edge 850 late last year. It features a slightly larger and brighter screen, an integrated bell, voice prompts, and more. However, it also adds $150 to the price. For this reason, we’re still substantial fans of Garmin’s Edge 840.

Sources indicate that while the Edge 840 features less functionality than the newer Edge 850, it costs significantly less and has a longer battery life. The 840 provides riders with all the data they need to manage a training program and track progress. These include VO2 max output (when paired with a heart monitor), recovery time, training load, and heat and altitude acclimation. It also offers cycling dynamics like position, right/left balance (when paired with a power meter), and bike setup. The Edge 840 provides plenty of detailed info if you like charts and analyzing data.

Overall, the 840 is an excellent option for riders who love training and digging into data. It offers a reasonable balance of price and features in the generally pricey Garmin bike computer lineup. If you need more battery life, choose the 840 Solar, which extends usage up to an impressive 32 hours.

It has been revealed that if you want the maximum possible battery life for a cycling computer, Coros’ recently debuted Dura 2 is your standout choice. Although the new Dura costs double the original, the Dura 2 features a sleeker design, improved maps and navigation, and clean pairing with devices such as power meters, heart rate monitors, and electronic drivetrains.

Like the original Dura, the second-gen model gets exceptional battery life, and that’s without considering its solar charging capabilities. Coros claims the Dura 2 achieves up to 120 hours of use on a single charge. In Dan Chabanov’s testing, he still had 77 percent battery remaining after 30 hours of ride time—that’s frankly exceptional for a cycling computer.

Industry observers note that however, with its great battery life and solar charging come a couple of downsides. Notably, the price: the Dura 2 costs $499 compared to the original model’s $250 price tag. The other notable miss is the Dura 2’s rerouting. It requires a connection to Coros’ smartphone app, and we found it hit-or-miss in our testing.

If you don’t have the budget for a Wahoo, Garmin, or Hammerhead computer, you still have a few solid options. For only $100, Magene offers a full-color touchscreen, turn-by-turn navigation, and even has a hill gradient feature and Strava segment integration (with a firmware update). That puts the mighty little C506 in the league of its big-name competitors at a fraction of the price.

Sources indicate that the low price, however, means the C506 isn’t quite as polished as the pricey head units. For example, you must pair your smartphone to upload routes. Some users also report touchscreen lag and software bugs. However, to its credit, Magene’s firmware upgrades have added a lot of functionality and improved shortcomings. If you have a limited budget and don’t mind a few usage quirks, the C506’s price and low weight make it hard to pass up.

Since launching two and a half years ago, Hammerhead’s Karoo computer has consistently remained my go-to head unit for road and gravel rides. Why? Because it’s the right size, has excellent navigation, pairs well with SRAM components, and features my favorite user interface.

According to recent reports, the Karoo’s navigation and touchscreen are best-in-class. On-the-fly route planning is easy—I love its ability to navigate to any Google Maps destination (shared via the Hammerhead app) and use the feature often. The Karoo’s UI is very intuitive, and it’s easy to find functions or customize the screens (compared to the bloated interfaces on some competitors’ cycling computers).

While the Karoo doesn’t look much different from its predecessor, the Karoo 2 (yes, it’s called the Karoo even though it’s the third-gen), it offers many solid updates: A dedicated power button, improved battery life (up to 35 hours), an ambient light sensor, and automatic backlight control.

It has been revealed that hammerhead’s smartphone app offers automatic ride uploads and live tracking—you can send a link to family or friends to track your ride progress. Another Hammerhead strong suit is its bi-weekly software updates that remedy bugs and add useful features. Combined with the ability to sideload third-party apps, the Karoo’s function constantly improves.

For AXS-equipped bike owners, the Karoo integrates tightly with SRAM’s electronic components. For example, you can program AXS shift buttons (including the bonus buttons on Force and Red hoods) directly from the computer. Read more about this integration in Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips’ story “SRAM Launches its Fresh Red AXS Road Group.”.

If you only need a cycling computer for the basics (speed, distance, heart rate, power, etc.) and don’t want a cellphone-sized device hanging off your bar, the Cycplus M2 is a great option. This tiny computer covers all the bases at a fraction of the cost of substantial-name competitors. It also has great styling that won’t look out of place on lightweight bikes, and it's small enough to use on the trail.

It has been revealed that while the M2 lacks amenities such as a touchscreen display or mapping, it features a 70-hour battery life, GPS tracking, and ANT+ and Bluetooth connectivity to your power meter and HRM. Cycplus’s app will also sync your rides to Strava to track your progress.

Recent findings suggest that overhauled in 2025, Wahoo’s Elemnt Roam is consistently one of our favorite cycling computers. Updates to the Roam V3 over the V2 include a larger touchscreen display, dual-band GPS for enhanced connection in mountains and dense woods, 64GB internal storage, and improved battery life.

In a recent development, in addition to the V3’s larger size and weight, Wahoo added a speaker for voice navigation and an integrated bell (activated with a quick two-finger tap on the screen). However, Wahoo removed the V2’s fan-favorite LED status lights. Additionally, we found the screen brightness a bit dim in our testing compared to Garmin and Hammerhead displays.

Recent findings suggest that as Chabanov noted in his detailed review of the Roam, beyond its overall solid reliability, the Roam is a standard mid-tier bike computer. It features a slew of handy navigation features, including turn-by-turn directions, navigate to start, back on track, mountain bike trail integration, saved locations, retrace route, and take me to.

After using the Edge 1050 for almost six months, the best word to describe Garmin’s range-topping computer is “major”. This computer is big in size, features, and price. But all of this bigness provides an experience unlike anything found on other cycling computers—and if not for the 1050’s price, it would be vying for the Best Overall Computer title.

In a recent development, there is no getting around the Edge 1050’s size, and at 2.4” x 4.7” x 0.6”, it takes up a lot of real estate on your bar. In fact, the 105 is so long that it’s incompatible with many standard mounts. However, the enormous size makes it easy to read data, follow routes, and scroll screens.

Navigation features include turn-by-turn directions, maps showing the popular routes locals use, and recalculation when you stray from your course. And while they might not like the 1050’s dimensions, mountain bikers will love its integration with the Trailforks app. However, this is merely scratching the surface of the Edge 1050’s superpowers; if you want to see the data, the 1050 is probably logging it, and Garmin most likely has a screen for it buried in the long list of data fields.

The Edge 1050 also offers some thoughtful safety features, including the ability to automatically send an emergency message to your specified contacts when it detects a crash, group messaging, and a ‘follow my ride’ feature that shares your real-time position with friends and family.

If you like these features but want a smaller package (and slightly lower price), check out the Garmin Edge 850. You can dig into the details on the 850 in Dan Chabanov’s full-length review.

Like Garmin’s Edge 1050, Wahoo goes similarly huge with its Elemnt Ace. The screen’s 3.8-inch size is impressive, as is its battery life (up to 30 hours). Plus, the Ace features Wahoo’s signature user-friendliness. Matt Phillips summed up his full review of the Elemnt Ace, saying, “If you crave significant and bold, this is your cycling computer.”.

The Ace’s super-sized screen offers room for large and easy-to-read data fields. The touchscreen function is also excellent, even while wearing gloves. Wahoo’s signature page zoom function—use the up and down buttons to zoom in on fewer fields or out on more fields—swiftly makes prioritized fields even larger. This helps if you want to concentrate on one metric or have vision challenges. It also provides a very massive map (or a large map plus additional data fields) and spoken turn-by-turn directions.

Compared to most cycling computers, the Ace is overkill in almost every way. However, if you want one computer with a big screen and impressive battery life, then the Ace is your ticket.

It has been revealed that do you wax nostalgic for the days of simple cycling computers—but still want to upload your rides and training data to Strava? Then the Omata is the computer for you. Years ago, our computers only displayed the basic riding metrics like speed, ride time, distance, and elevation. Your rides weren’t interrupted by constant pinging from notifications, messages, navigation, and target training zones.

Silca’s Omata computer is to your rides like a vinyl turntable is to listening to music. Sure, you can stream your favorite band on Spotify, see the songs’ lyrics in real time, and skip tracks you don’t like, but digital audio lacks the tactile experience of a record player. That’s what riding with the Omata is like; it features dials to display your current speed, distance traveled, elevation gain, and riding time—nothing more, nothing less.

It has been revealed that yet, behind the scenes, the Omata also captures critical riding data, like power, heart rate, and GPS route. This means you can still track your rides and get Strava kudos from your friends. However, the Omata comes at a steep price—$800—but it‘s an experience you will not find in any other device.

One of the biggest differences between GPS cycling computers is the technology ecosystem you’re buying into—much like choosing a smartphone. While you can pair most sensors, regardless of brand, with most computers via Bluetooth or ANT+, these devices work best when used with their corresponding companion apps. Although some budget-friendly computer options require an app to unlock full functionality, premium models from brands like Hammerhead, Wahoo, and Garmin let you perform most tasks without an app.

Recent findings suggest that while bigger isn’t always better, a large, easy-to-read display—like the one on the Wahoo Elemnt Ace—makes navigation and data viewing significantly more convenient. When testing the gargantuan Elemnt Ace, Matt Phillips initially found the screen’s sheer size off-putting, but he eventually grew to appreciate it.

According to recent reports, navigation capabilities vary widely. Even budget models, such as the $120 iGPSport BCS300T, support turn-by-turn directions with downloadable routes. High-end models such as the Hammerhead Karoo and Garmin Edge models take it further, allowing on-the-fly route changes—such as finding a coffee shop—without adjusting settings in the companion app.

Battery life used to be a major concern, but modern bike computers are built to last. Most can handle a full week of riding without recharging. Some, like the Coros Dura and Garmin Edge 840 Solar, even feature solar charging. In fact, the Coros Dura’s battery is so robust that some customers report they haven’t been able to completely drain it after months of use, making its claimed 120-hour battery life seem entirely plausible.

The computers in this story are optimized for cycling and intended for on-bike use. If you participate in events like triathlons or duathlons—or also need a device for running or hiking activities—consider a smartwatch with cycling functionality. Our guide to Garmin watches can help you select the right one for your rides and runs.

With expert instruction from pro rider Chaz Turmon, this program features motivating follow-along video sessions and flexible workouts you can do almost anywhere to help you ride faster, train smarter, and watch your numbers climb.

This holistic program covers all the tips and tricks needed to improve your riding technique, master cadence, stack speed and endurance workouts, build strength off the bike, and fine‑tune gear in order to achieve the speed gains you dream about.

Watch as host Alison Tetrick takes you through everything you need to know to ride your first (or fastest) century. Along with other cycling experts, she explains how to find the best gear, build endurance, fuel your body during the ride, and much more.

Cycling is the best way to stay fit as you age. With the help of host Peter Abraham and other experts, you’ll learn everything you need to get started and stay riding into your golden years, including choosing a bike, finding a initiative, and optimizing recovery.

Whether you’re constantly feeling aches or you want to maximize your performance gains, you need the right bike fit. With this guide, host Jenna Foley and certified bike fitter Jonathan Blyer walk you through the process and offer up DIY tips.

Recent findings suggest that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Latest Update: The World’s Hardest Beer Run? This Brutal Race Sends Runners Up a Mountain—With a Keg of Beer on Their Back

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Running up a rocky and technical trail more than a mile above sea level is tricky enough.
  • Male entrants in the race shoulder a traditional wooden carrying frame, which resembles a sled but is loaded high with a 30-liter (about 8 gallons) keg of beer, plus other supplies (including large bottles of water) that add up to more than 130 pounds (60 kg).
  • Industry observers note that since 1985, this unique annual race has been taking place on the unforgiving flanks of the High Tatras mountains in Slovakia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Running up a rocky and technical trail more than a mile above sea level is tricky enough. Imagine doing it with a keg of beer strapped to your back—because this is exactly what competitors in the Sherpa Rallye, held on October 24, had to contend with.

Male entrants in the race shoulder a traditional wooden carrying frame, which resembles a sled but is loaded high with a 30-liter (about 8 gallons) keg of beer, plus other supplies (including large bottles of water) that add up to more than 130 pounds (60 kg). Women commonly carry cases of beer and materials that make their load weigh about 44 pounds (20 kg).

Industry observers note that since 1985, this unique annual race has been taking place on the unforgiving flanks of the High Tatras mountains in Slovakia. It starts just above the town of Starý Smokovec and finishes at Zbojnícka chata, a mountain refuge perched like an alpine eyrie 3.5 miles up the steep and rough track.

The High Tatras are home to Europe’s last remaining group of old-school mountain porters, many of whom take part in the race, which was started by a porter named Viktor Beránek to help bring workers together. They are locally and colloquially known as horský šerpa (mountain sherpas)—although they have no connection to the Sherpas of the Tibetan Himalaya, a distinct ethnic group, and are more correctly called horský nosi (mountain carriers).

Sources indicate that however you refer to them, each season they manually transport heavy supplies to the mountain huts, refuges, and chalets that hikers use for shelter while trekking the local trails. And herein lies the rub, because once the Sherpa Rallye runners reach Zbojnícka chata, they don’t even get to celebrate by supping the goods they have just transported up to the hut—it goes in the stores for use over winter.

Your gym bag is probably packed with some of the best supplements for building muscle, including protein powder, creatine, and pre-workout. Crucial for boosting energy and strength during a gym session and reducing muscle soreness afterward, you wouldn’t dare train without them. But imagine a single supplement that combines the benefits of all three.

Sources indicate that enter XWERKS Motion — an innovative supplement formulated to enhance endurance during intense exercise and support a quick post-workout recovery. Sounds too good to be true? We’ll find out in this XWERKS Motion review.

In a recent development, our team of personal trainers, CrossFit coaches, nutrition experts, and competitive weightlifters shared their feedback on the formulation, price, taste, and solubility of this one-of-a-kind product. As a registered dietitian nutritionist, I’ll do a deep dive into the ingredients and potential health benefits of XWERKS Motion, so you know if it’s worth adding to your supplement stack.

In a recent development, medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

Our Breaking Muscle product testing team has tried nearly 20 of the best BCAA supplements, gaining a thorough understanding of what meets customer standards and what falls short. Here’s how our expert testers rated the following categories after trying XWERKS Motion themselves.

In this XWERKS Motion review, we’ll explore the product’s cost, formula, flavors, taste, and more. We’ll include honest, reliable feedback straight from our Breaking Muscle expert testers, so you’ll know exactly what to expect from this supplement. With transparency in mind, we include the good and not-so-good aspects of XWERKS Motion to give you the full picture.

In comparison, Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine costs $1.33 per serving, while Jacked Factory BCAA Powder is available at $0.67 per serving at the time of this writing. XWERKS Motion is on the pricier side, earning this category a 3.5 out of 5, but also contains ingredients not found in most other BCAA supplements.

XWERKS Motion is thoughtfully and originally formulated, earning it a 4 out of 5. It is unlike other BCAA supplements in that it contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbohydrates, also known as highly branched cyclic dextrin (HBCD). Cluster dextrin passes through the stomach into the intestines rapidly, where it can be absorbed into the bloodstream and taken up into muscle cells to replenish glycogen content and provide a quick energy source. (1).

Industry observers note that human studies suggest that when used before or during a workout, cluster dextrin carbs may decrease perceived exertion and enhance endurance when compared to maltodextrin and glucose, especially when prior carb intake is low. (1) However, those who eat plenty of carbs may not experience any added benefits when supplementing cluster dextrin.

According to recent reports, in addition to carbs, each serving offers three grams of branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). The product contains the BCAA ratio 2:1:1 of leucine, isoleucine, and valine. BCAAs are essential amino acids (EAAs), meaning you must consume them because the body doesn’t synthesize them on its own. Leucine is often thought of as the king of BCAAs because it activates muscle protein synthesis, which is necessary for muscle growth and recovery. (2).

In a recent development, other active ingredients include calcium, magnesium, and sodium. During exercise, you lose electrolytes through sweat that need to be replenished. The electrolytes in XWERKS Motion help prevent dehydration and maintain proper muscle function during a workout.

Enhanced with natural flavors, sucralose, and citric acid, this product contains ingredients that add sour and sweet notes.

Sucralose is an artificial sweetener considered safe when consumed in moderation. Unlike table sugar, most research shows sucralose has little to no effects on blood sugar levels or insulin. (3) However, some animal studies suggest it could disrupt healthy gut bacteria and increase inflammation when consumed long-term, but more human studies are needed. (4).

You won’t have any difficulty picking a flavor if you choose to try XWERKS Motion, considering there is only one option available — Raspberry Lemonade. Obviously, if you prefer to stick with one flavor on repeat this won’t be a problem. For those who like to switch things up, the lack of variety may leave you feeling bored, hence the middle-of-the-road rating on flavor.

Luckily, the Raspberry Lemonade flavor delivers. Our expert tester was more than pleased with the taste of the raspberry lemonade supplement, rating it an impressive 5 out of 5. She noticed hints of the tart lemonade with a more robust berry flavor overall. The supplement wasn’t too sweet and had a very refreshing taste to it. Our tester even went as far as to say that she could happily sip on this drink all day.

Industry observers note that another winning category of XWERKS Motion is solubility, which our tester rated a perfect 5 out of 5. She didn’t experience any clumping, grittiness, floaties, or difficulty mixing — a feature you’ll want when drinking it at the gym or on the go. Because the cluster dextrin in this product is highly soluble in water, it dissolves easily and forms a smooth, uniform mixture. Several customer reviews on the XWERKS website rave about the product’s superior solubility, mentioning it “blends so smooth” and is “easy to mix.”.

Cluster dextrin is believed to be safe for consumption, with no apparent safety concerns. (5) Our product tester didn’t experience any adverse side effects during her use of this product. As for beneficial effects, she didn’t notice any superhuman strength or noticeable bursts of energy, but she did feel good during longer lifting sessions.

Switching gears, BCAAs are considered safe when consumed in appropriate dosages. It’s best to adhere to the suggested dosage instructions on the product label for optimal safety and effectiveness.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, always consult with your healthcare provider before adding a upcoming dietary supplement to your routine, particularly if you have pre-existing medical conditions or are presently taking prescribed medications. This precaution ensures that the supplement aligns with your individual health needs and won’t pose any risks or interactions.

All of the above considered, XWERKS Motion gets a 4 out of 5 rating for the lack of side effects from its formulation.

Unfortunately, there’s no mention of third-party testing on the XWERKS Motion product page, which is why we gave it a 1 out of 5.

We always encourage consumers to consider supplements that are third-party tested, because it serves as a quality control measure, ensuring that products are safe, effective, and meet certain regulatory requirements. Third-party testing enhances transparency and builds consumer trust by verifying that high-quality products contain what’s on the label and don’t include harmful levels of heavy metals or contaminants.

According to recent reports, XWERKS Motion and XTEND Original BCAA powder have both commonalities and differences. To start, both products contain BCAAs and electrolytes to enhance muscle recovery, reduce muscle soreness, and maintain hydration.

Recent findings suggest that however, that’s where their similarities end. While XTEND Original BCAA powder doesn’t contain any carbohydrates, XWERKS Motion contains 25 grams of cluster dextrin carbs for extra energy and prolonged endurance.

Recent findings suggest that XTEND Original BCAA powder also has a much higher BCAA content of seven grams, compared to the three grams in XWERKS Motion. The Original BCAA powder even contains a whopping three and a half grams of leucine, exceeding the recommended two to three grams per day to maximize muscle-gaining capabilities. (2) The same can’t be said for the leucine content of XWERKS Motion.

It has been revealed that customers on the XWERKS website give Motion a 4.4 out of 5-star rating. There are only 35 reviews on the product page. Motion is not available on Amazon at the time of writing.

Industry observers note that one happy customer says, “Great taste! No issues with digestion, gives you the fuel needed during most intense workouts.” Another customer says, “It mixes well, I like the flavor, and have no digestive or other issues. Performance-wise I feel great. I feel more energetic during my workouts and that I’m getting more out of them.”.

Reviews from customers who were less pleased with the product were written over a year ago, and the formulation and flavors may have changed. One customer states, “I’m not sold on this product. I don’t really notice any difference on the days I take this. Also, it takes a blender to get this stuff mixed! That’s a deal breaker for me.” Other customers complain of the grape flavor, which is no longer available.

It has been revealed that XWERKS Motion provides a synergistic blend of cluster dextrin carbs, BCAAs, and electrolytes to support endurance and recovery during and after a workout. Those who enjoy leisurely activity and consume enough carbs to sustain their energy levels may not benefit from this product.

In a recent development, however, it might be worth it for endurance athletes and bodybuilders with high training loads. Taking XWERKS before, during, or after intense physical activity may reduce perceived effort, extend the time to exhaustion, and decrease muscle soreness.

Recent findings suggest that you can consume BCAAs pre, post, or intra-workout depending on your fitness goals. Some prefer to take BCAAs before or during a workout to provide their muscles with amino acids to help prevent muscle protein breakdown. Others like to take BCAAs post-workout to support muscle repair and recovery.

In a recent development, if you eat a whole-food diet high in protein, then you likely consume enough amino acids and may not experience further benefits by supplementing them. If you struggle to eat enough protein, BCAAs may support endurance, helping you train at a higher intensity for longer. Additionally, BCAAs may reduce muscle damage and DOMS post-workout.

In a recent development, BCAAs are a group of three EEAs—leucine, isoleucine, and valine— that must be consumed through the diet. They get their name from their unique molecular structure. While all EAAs are vital, BCAAs are thought to play an important role in protein synthesis, muscle recovery, and preventing loss of lean mass.

It has been revealed that BCAAs may provide an extended feeling of energy and delay the onset of muscle fatigue, enabling you to work out longer. Moreover, BCAAs might diminish muscle damage, inflammation, and DOMS post-workout. Lastly, BCAAs may aid in preserving lean muscle mass during periods of fat loss, contributing to weight loss efforts.

Sources indicate that there are no official recommended daily requirements for BCAAs. The suggested sweet spot for leucine intake is often cited as two to three grams per day to optimize muscle building. (2) Avoid exceeding the recommended serving size on the product label. If you take protein powder or eat a high-protein diet, BCAA supplements likely won’t provide added benefits.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Industry observers note that after months of long runs and tough workouts, you’ve finally crossed the finish line of your goal race. Now, it’s time to recover—and figure out what’s next.

While you can scale back your running in the offseason, it’s worth making room for strength training. Even a short time in the weight room can help you build a stronger foundation for your next training block.

The good news? You don’t need to spend all your newfound free time in the gym to make progress. By hitting the following minimum amount of strength work each week, you set yourself up to handle more mileage and run more efficiently when it’s time to chase a fresh goal.

In the first two weeks after your race, you should focus mainly on rest and getting back into easy jogging. After that, aim to add at least two strength sessions per week to your routine, exercise physiologist Heather Milton, C.S.C.S., previously told Runner’s World. Milton states these offseason strength sessions should focus on heavier weights (just make sure you work up in weight!) and a low-to-moderate number of reps.

During these heavy lifting workouts, athletes should aim to complete four to six sets of one to five reps of each exercise, pausing for two to four minutes in between each set, strength coach and physical therapist Lisbeth Hoyt, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., previously told Runner’s World.

While running is your main focus during marathon training (or any race distance, for that matter), strength sessions often help you maintain the strength you already have, Milton explains. But between training blocks, you can put more emphasis on building strength.

“Plus, when you start training for your next marathon, you’ll be in a stronger position to increase your running volume again because you’ve strengthened all of the areas of your body that were impacted by your previous race, which can help prevent injuries,” Milton adds.

You might associate heavy lifting with short sprinters or football players—athletes who focus on quick, explosive movement, rather than steady endurance. But building stronger muscles through heavy lifting supports long-distance running, too.

In a recent development, for starters, lifting heavier weights helps you build muscular strength, which translates to improved running economy, New York City-based strength and run coach Yusuf Jeffers previously told Runner’s World. Meaning, heavy lifting can help you use less energy to run at a given pace.

It has been revealed that research backs this up. A review published in Sports Medicine in 2023 examined several types of strength training in middle- and long-distance runners, including lifting heavy, submaximal lifting, isometric exercises, and plyometrics. The researchers found that lifting high loads—at least 80 percent of a person’s one-rep max—had the greatest effect on improving running economy at faster speeds. (Plyometrics worked particularly well for improving economy at slower speeds.).

According to recent reports, the benefits extend beyond your muscles, too. Hoyt explains that strength training can support connective tissues and bone health.

Industry observers note that it’s vital to remember lifting “heavy” looks different for everyone. If you’re upcoming to strength training or you’re unfamiliar with a particular movement, start by learning proper form and gradually work up in weight, Hoyt notes.

Hoyt suggests focusing on movements such as squats, deadlifts, lunges, and rows, encouraging athletes to move slowly and with control.

Industry observers note that matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

Industry News: Our Favorite Men’s and Women’s Mountain Bike Shorts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • In a recent development, A good pair of mountain bike shorts should stay out of your way through long climbs, rough descents, and everything in between.
  • The Pearl Izumi Summit Shorts scored well across the board, with a comfortable fit, effective water repellency, and well-placed pockets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

In a recent development, A good pair of mountain bike shorts should stay out of your way through long climbs, rough descents, and everything in between. The right fit leaves room to pedal and wear knee pads without bunching or snagging, while a secure waistband and well-placed pockets keep the shorts comfortable on the trail. We’ve tested options for different budgets and riding styles, from lightweight shells to shorts with a padded liner. These are the pairs we’d choose for our next ride.

The Pearl Izumi Summit Shorts scored well across the board, with a comfortable fit, effective water repellency, and well-placed pockets. At 191 grams, they’re relatively light and breathe well (though the Velocio Ultralight MTB Shorts below are yet lighter and more breathable). The Summits still move enough air for all-day trail rides without noticeable moisture buildup.

Industry observers note that their four-way-stretch ripstop nylon has held up through multiple seasons of testing and riding, resisting tears without feeling rough or abrasive. For nylon, it’s surprisingly soft.

Sources indicate that A lined mountain bike short at this price is rare. The Ally has a forgiving fit and plenty of waist adjustment (Velcro sizing tabs and belt loops), which makes it easier to wear than many shorts. On the bike they feel relaxed and comfortable (but not floppy), and move with you well. The included liner means you don’t need to buy a chamois separately. Plenty of pockets let you stash a phone and ride essentials, though all those zippers can feel like a lot—and like potential failure points over time. The unisex sizing means there’s no separate women’s version.

With a 13-inch inseam in the men’s version, the Landfarer covers the tops of most knee pads without feeling heavy. The stretch fabric is lightweight, and the broad range of men’s and women’s sizes makes it easier to find a good fit. Patagonia also uses recycled nylon in the fabric and makes the shorts in a Fair Trade Certified™ factory, so the vibes are good. The range of waist sizes can help you find a tailored fit, but the elastic waistband has no adjusters. The low-friction fabric and forgiving waist can let the shorts slip more easily, so make sure you get the right size.

The Ultralight lives up to its name. It’s extremely light and quick-drying, with a cut and fit dialed for long days with lots of pedaling. Despite the light material, these have proven surprisingly durable, shrugging off slides and brushes with rocks and trailside vegetation. I tested the latest version, which features a fresh elastic waist that greatly improved the fit and made it more forgiving of weight fluctuations. One caveat: that waistband change appears to be rolling through production, so not all pairs and colors have the new waist yet. These are also expensive.

The Flexair keeps things low-key and streamlined. Its low-profile cut and ratchet closure make for a clean look and a secure fit on the bike. The leg opening sits close to the thigh, so these work best with very low-profile knee pads; bulkier pads may feel crowded. Stretch fabric and laser-cut perforations help keep the shorts light and ventilated, but there’s no liner. The waists run small, so try them on if you can and be prepared to size up.

Industry observers note that there are plenty of great bike shorts out there—but most of them play it safe with earth tones and muted colors. Wild Rye bucks that trend. This women-led brand out of Sun Valley, ID makes technical “apparel that inspires more women to get outside”—and look good doing it. The standout designs and bold colors are just as impressive as the performance of the gear itself. If you want high-quality apparel with flair and personality, this is your brand.

The Riley 10” Bike Short checks all the right boxes. A high-rise waist prevents sagging in the back while riding, and a stretch panel across the rear waistband adds comfort and flexibility. Along with a side zip pocket that fits a phone, the shorts also have two front pockets for smaller essentials. The 10-inch inseam will suit most riders, though it may not pair perfectly with all knee pads.

Pro tip: Check the sale page for deals on last year’s designs.

Recent findings suggest that A company that builds only women’s athletic apparel typically nails it in every category, and these super-comfortable, breezy shell shorts from Shredly are no exception. With a versatile 11” inseam and a wide, high, soft waistband, these pair really well with a slightly longer chamois liner or waist shorts, and sit high on the waist to reduce gapping during rides.

The shorts material has 9 percent spandex for structure and four-way stretch that lends maximum range of motion. These are built for a woman’s hips and waist, and have an articulated taper that doesn’t impede pedaling.

It has been revealed that A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.
